lenses.body: Most AI answers one question and stops. An agent is more like a helper you give a whole chore to: it figures out the steps itself and keeps going until the chore is done, checking in only when it needs to.

An agent is an identity that acts, so treat it as an access-control problem first: its own credentials, scoped permissions, an allowlist of tools, and full logging of every action it takes, exactly as you would a new employee with unknown judgment.

The defining engineering shift is initiative between instructions: your system now decides its own next step, which means error handling, loop limits and permission boundaries matter more than prompt quality once you move from single-call to agentic design.

Software that pursues a goal across multiple steps rather than answering one question, which changes what needs governing: not just what it says, but what it does, what it can touch, and who is accountable when it acts wrongly.

terms.origin: Emerged from decades of AI research; the current usage solidified with the 2023-2024 wave of LLM-based agents.
terms.example: A research agent that searches, reads, and compiles a briefing from one request.
terms.definition: An AI system that takes a goal, breaks it into steps, and carries those steps out using tools, rather than answering a single question and stopping. The defining trait is initiative between instructions: the agent decides what to do next.

lenses.body: When one AI helper passes a job to a second helper partway through, like tagging in a relay race. If the second one does not get the full story, it might ask you to repeat everything.

Each handoff is a point where permissions and context cross a boundary, and should be logged and scoped the same way a privilege escalation would be, since a poorly bounded handoff can let a low-privilege agent inherit access it should not have.

Design the handoff payload explicitly rather than relying on the receiving agent to infer context; a lost-context handoff is one of the most common causes of a multi-agent system that feels broken to the end user even when each agent works correctly alone.

A poorly designed handoff between AI systems creates the same bad experience as being transferred between departments who did not talk to each other. Ask how state and context are preserved across any multi-agent workflow you deploy.

terms.example: A support triage agent passing a billing dispute, with full conversation history, to a specialist billing agent.
terms.definition: Transferring control, context, and accumulated state from one agent to another mid-task. Done well, the receiving agent continues without re-asking; done badly, context is lost at the seam and the user repeats themselves.

lenses.body: A notebook the AI keeps so it remembers things about you and past conversations, instead of forgetting everything the moment you close the chat. Some notes are short-term, some are kept for a long time.

Split retention policy deliberately: short-term working memory can be ephemeral and cleared aggressively, but anything promoted to long-term storage needs its own access control, deletion path and audit trail, since it is now a standing data store, not a chat transcript.

Persistent memory is what makes an assistant feel personalized, and it is also a new category of stored personal or business data that needs a retention policy, access controls and a way to honor a deletion request.

A company's claimed "memory" moat is only as durable as its data governance around it; ask how memory is scoped per user or per tenant, since a memory leak across accounts is both a security incident and a trust-destroying story.

terms.example: An assistant that remembers your reporting format from last quarter without being retold.
terms.definition: A persistent store that lets an agent recall facts, preferences, and prior work across sessions instead of starting cold each time. Typically split into a short-term working scratchpad and a long-term store, each with different retention and privacy implications.

lenses.body: The part that tells all the different AI helpers and tools what order to work in, and what to do if one of them fails or is slow, so the whole job actually gets finished.

This is where most production complexity lives, not in any single model call: retry logic, timeout handling, and deciding which component owns a given failure mode are the actual engineering work of shipping an agentic system.
The management layer that turns individual AI capabilities into a working system end to end. A vendor who has a good model but no orchestration story is selling you a part, not a product.

Orchestration, not the underlying model, is often where defensibility actually sits, since base models are increasingly commoditized while reliable coordination across tools and failure modes is hard-won engineering.

terms.example: A planner agent assigning research, drafting, and review to three worker agents and assembling the result.
terms.definition: Coordinating multiple agents, tools, and steps toward one goal, including sequencing, retries, and deciding which component handles what. It is the management layer that turns individual capabilities into a working system.

lenses.body: When a company calls something an "AI agent" but it is really just a fixed set of steps that cannot change or adapt, the way a real agent would if something unexpected happened.

The practical test: give it a scenario outside its expected script and see whether it adapts or breaks. A true agent replans; a washed one fails or produces nonsense because there was never any decision-making underneath the label.

Before buying an "agentic" product, ask what happens when the situation deviates from the happy path. If the answer is that it breaks or requires a human to intervene immediately, you are likely buying a scripted workflow with agent branding.
A useful diligence question for any "AI agent" pitch: demo a scenario the founders did not prepare for. The gap between a real agent and a rebranded workflow shows up immediately under improvisation.

terms.origin: Analyst coinage, popularized by Gartner in 2025 vendor-claim critiques.
terms.example: A vendor rebranding a five-step form automation as "agentic AI" in a sales deck.
terms.definition: Marketing a simple scripted workflow as an autonomous agent to ride the trend. The tell is that the "agent" cannot deviate from its script when conditions change.

lenses.body: Most AI answers a question and stops. An agent is given a goal instead, and takes steps by itself to reach it, like being told to tidy your room rather than being told exactly where to put each toy.

An authenticated identity that acts, which makes it an access-control problem before it is an AI problem. Give it its own machine identity rather than a human's credentials, scope permissions to the task, allowlist tools, log every action for reconstruction, and assume any content it reads may attempt to redirect it.

A model in a loop with tools, memory and a stopping condition. The hard parts are not the model calls: they are error recovery when a step fails, preventing loops, bounding cost and steps, and deciding what the agent is permitted to do without asking. Design the permission boundary before the prompt.

Software that pursues an objective across several steps rather than answering one question. That changes the risk profile: an agent takes actions with consequences, so the governing questions become what it may touch, what it may spend, what is logged, and who is accountable when it acts wrongly.

terms.origin: Industry usage from roughly 2024 onward, as tool-using LLM systems reached production.
terms.example: A procurement workflow where the AI requests quotes, compares them, and drafts the purchase order.
terms.definition: AI capable of planning and acting autonomously toward a goal, using tools and adjusting course based on results. The term marks the shift from AI that answers to AI that does, which is also the shift that creates most new governance exposure.

lenses.body: A set of AI steps done in a fixed order every time, like a recipe, as opposed to an agent that can decide to change the order if something unexpected happens.

Prefer a fixed workflow over an agent whenever the task path is genuinely known in advance; the added unpredictability of agentic decision-making is only worth it when the task actually requires adapting to conditions you cannot fully anticipate.

If your process is the same steps every time, a fixed AI workflow is usually the safer and cheaper choice over a more flexible "agent," since it is more predictable and easier to check that it is working correctly.

The key distinction from an agent is that the path is designed in advance by a person rather than chosen at run time by the system, which makes workflows more predictable and easier to audit, at the cost of flexibility when conditions change.

terms.example: Invoice intake, extraction, validation, and posting running as one automated sequence.
terms.definition: A coordinated, repeatable process in which AI performs defined steps, usually with fixed order and human checkpoints. Distinct from an agent in that the path is designed in advance rather than chosen at run time.

lenses.body: How much an AI helper is allowed to do on its own before it has to ask you first, from "just suggest something" all the way up to "just go ahead and do it."

Autonomy level should map directly to a documented risk tier per action type, and any change to that level, especially raising it, should go through the same change-control process as a permissions escalation for a human user.

Set this per task, not per system: a coding agent might warrant approve-to-execute for a deploy but suggest-only for a database schema change, and hardcoding one autonomy level for an entire agent ignores that different actions carry very different risk.

One of the core governance decisions for any AI deployment: deciding, deliberately and in writing, which actions require human confirmation and which do not, rather than letting the default settings make that call.

terms.example: An agent allowed to draft emails freely but required to get approval before sending.
terms.definition: How far an agent may act before a human must confirm, ranging from suggest-only through approve-to-execute to fully autonomous. Setting this level deliberately, per task, is one of the core agent governance decisions.

lenses.body: An AI that can use a website the way you do: clicking buttons, filling in forms, and reading what is on the page, instead of just answering questions in a chat box.

A browser agent inherits whatever session and credentials it is given, and can be redirected by content on a page it visits; scope its permissions narrowly, log every action, and never give it a logged-in session with standing access it does not need for the task.

Treat every page it visits as untrusted input, since hidden text or instructions embedded in a page can attempt to redirect the agent's behavior; sandbox the session and constrain what actions it can complete without confirmation.

Genuinely useful for research and procurement tasks, and also a new category of system access, one that operates like a person with a browser, that most security reviews built for APIs and applications have no slot for yet.

terms.example: An agent comparing supplier pricing across a dozen vendor portals.
terms.definition: An agent that operates a web browser the way a person does: navigating pages, filling forms, clicking, and extracting data. Powerful for research and procurement tasks, and a new category of access that security reviews often have no slot for.

lenses.body: An AI that can read a whole codebase, make changes to fix problems, run tests to check its work, and then suggest the change for a person to approve, similar to a junior programmer.

The review burden shifts rather than disappears: someone still has to read and understand machine-generated diffs before merging, and a coding agent that "passes its own tests" is not the same guarantee as a human reviewer catching a subtle logic error.

Compresses development time meaningfully, and raises a real question your engineering leadership needs an explicit answer to: who reviews machine-written code changes, and with what rigor, before they ship.

A coding-agent product's real differentiator is usually not raw model capability but the surrounding scaffold: test integration, review workflow, and how it handles a task it cannot complete, since those determine whether it is trusted in production.

terms.example: Claude Code fixing a failing test suite and submitting the patch for human review.
terms.definition: An agent that reads a repository, edits files, runs tests, and opens pull requests with limited supervision. It compresses development time and simultaneously raises the question of who reviews machine-written changes.

lenses.body: An AI that can control a computer screen directly, clicking and typing the way you do, even in old programs that were never built to talk to AI at all.

Treat a computer-use session with the same rigor as handing a contractor a logged-in laptop: scope what it can access, monitor the session, and assume anything on screen, including content the agent did not expect, could influence its next action.

Software with no API is exactly the software with the fewest guardrails, so a computer-use agent operating a legacy application often has more effective access and less oversight than the same task done through a proper API integration would.

Extends automation to systems that were never designed for it, which is powerful and also means your existing security review process, built around APIs and known integrations, likely has no framework yet for what this agent can actually touch.

terms.origin: Introduced as a named capability by Anthropic in October 2024.
terms.example: An agent processing claims inside a legacy desktop application.
terms.definition: An agent capability to operate a graphical interface directly, reading the screen and issuing clicks and keystrokes. It extends automation to software that has no API, which is exactly the software with the fewest guardrails.

lenses.body: How an AI actually does things in the real world instead of just talking about them, by sending a structured request to a specific tool, like calling a weather app instead of guessing the weather.

Every function the model can call is an attack surface; apply least privilege the same way you would to any service account, and assume prompt injection can attempt to trigger an unintended tool call through content the model processes.

This is the boundary where a text-generation system becomes a system with side effects; validate and constrain every tool call server-side rather than trusting the model's output, since a model can be manipulated into calling a tool with unintended arguments.

The mechanism that turns "the AI can answer questions" into "the AI can take actions with real consequences," which is exactly the point where your governance and review process needs to tighten, not loosen.

terms.origin: Introduced commercially in OpenAI's June 2023 API release; now standard across providers.
terms.example: A model calling a weather API, then a calendar API, to reschedule a site visit.
terms.definition: The mechanism by which a model invokes external tools, APIs, or code through structured requests instead of plain text. It is what connects a language model to real systems, and therefore where read-only assistance becomes action with consequences.

lenses.body: A rule that says the AI has to stop and ask a person "is this okay?" before doing certain important things, rather than just going ahead on its own.

Audit approval logs periodically for evidence of rubber-stamping, such as approval times too short to reflect actual review; a HITL control that exists on paper but has degraded into automatic approval provides no real risk mitigation.

Placement matters more than presence: a checkpoint on every trivial action trains approval fatigue, so people start rubber-stamping requests, which quietly defeats the control on the rare high-stakes action that actually needed scrutiny.

This control is only as strong as where the checkpoints sit. If your team approves so many low-stakes prompts that they stop reading them carefully, the checkpoint on a genuinely risky action gets the same rubber stamp.

terms.origin: Borrowed from control-systems and human-factors engineering, decades before LLMs.
terms.example: A manager approving each AI-drafted payment before release.
terms.definition: A design that requires human approval at defined checkpoints before an AI action takes effect. The control is only as good as the checkpoint placement: approval fatigue on low-stakes items trains people to rubber-stamp the high-stakes ones.

lenses.body: A safety limit that stops an AI helper from trying the same failed thing over and over forever, wasting time and money chasing something that is never going to work.

Set hard ceilings on iterations, wall-clock time and spend for every agent loop, not just a soft retry count; an agent chasing an impossible goal will happily consume unbounded resources unless something external forces a stop.
A basic but essential cost control: without one, a single misconfigured agent task can run indefinitely and generate a large, unexpected bill before anyone notices something is wrong.

Ask any AI-agent vendor how they bound run-away cost and time; the absence of a hard loop guard is an operational risk that eventually surfaces as a support incident or a customer's unexpectedly large bill.

terms.example: A cap of 25 steps and $5 of inference per task, after which the agent stops and reports.
terms.definition: A hard limit on iterations, time, or spend that stops a runaway agent loop. Agents that retry failed steps can burn unbounded cost pursuing an impossible goal unless something external ends the attempt.

lenses.body: Several AI helpers working together on one big job, each doing a different part, like a team where one person researches, one writes, and one checks the work.

Each agent in the system needs its own scoped identity and permissions rather than a shared credential, since a compromised or misbehaving single agent should not be able to act with the combined privileges of the whole system.

Coordination failure is the new failure mode this architecture introduces: agents can disagree, duplicate work, or wait on each other indefinitely, so design explicit handoff protocols and timeouts rather than assuming the pieces will cooperate smoothly.

Can meaningfully improve output quality on complex tasks by specializing roles, but it also adds a layer of coordination complexity and cost that a single well-scoped agent does not have; use it where the task genuinely needs it.

terms.origin: A named research field since the 1990s; revived in LLM form from 2023.
terms.example: A researcher agent, a critic agent, and a writer agent producing a due-diligence memo.
terms.definition: Several specialized agents collaborating, delegating, or debating to solve a task no single agent handles well. The architecture improves quality and adds coordination failure modes that single-agent systems do not have.

lenses.body: One AI acts like a manager, breaking a big job into smaller pieces and handing them to other AI helpers, then putting all their work back together into one final answer.

This is the pattern behind most production "deep research" systems, and the reason a single user request can quietly fan out into dozens of model calls; monitor and cap that fan-out explicitly, since cost scales with delegation depth.

Explains why a seemingly simple AI request can carry a surprisingly high cost: one user query can trigger many worker-agent calls behind the scenes, which matters for both budgeting and latency expectations.

Cost and latency scale with delegation depth in this pattern, so a vendor's unit economics on an "orchestrated" product depend heavily on how tightly they bound worker fan-out; ask about that control before crediting a margin claim.

terms.example: A lead agent splitting a market analysis into five parallel research threads.
terms.definition: A lead agent decomposes a task and delegates subtasks to subordinate agents, then assembles their outputs. The pattern behind most production "deep research" systems, and the reason one user request can fan out into dozens of model calls.

lenses.body: The part of an AI agent that figures out the list of steps to take before actually doing any of them, like planning a route before starting to drive.

Plan quality is the ceiling on agent quality: a flawless step-executor working from a bad plan still fails, so debugging a failing agent should start by inspecting the plan it produced, not the execution of individual steps.

When an agent fails at a complex task, the root cause is often a bad plan rather than a bad execution of a good plan; ask your team to distinguish the two before concluding the model itself is at fault.

terms.example: A task graph turning "prepare the board pack" into gather, draft, chart, and review steps.
terms.definition: The component that decomposes a goal into an ordered set of steps before execution begins. Plan quality bounds agent quality: a flawless executor of a bad plan still fails.

lenses.body: Connecting several AI steps in a row, where each one's answer becomes the next one's question, like a relay where each runner hands off to the next.

Still the right tool when the task path is genuinely known in advance; reach for full agentic architecture only once you need the system to decide its own next step, since a fixed chain is simpler to debug and more predictable to run.

A good, simpler starting point than a full "AI agent" if your task follows the same steps every time: break it into a chain of prompts rather than paying for the complexity of a system that can improvise.

The direct predecessor of full agentic systems: it introduces the idea of multi-step AI processing, but the sequence and path are fixed in advance by the designer rather than chosen dynamically by the system, which is the boundary that separates it from a true agent.

terms.example: Extract key figures, then summarize them, then format the summary as an email, as three chained calls.
terms.definition: Connecting prompts in sequence so each step's output feeds the next step's input. The predecessor of full agents, still the right tool when the path is known in advance.

lenses.body: The scribbled notes an AI writes to itself while it is figuring something out, before giving you its final answer. Reading those notes is often the best way to see how it got there.

Often the fastest debugging tool available for an agent that produced a wrong or strange result: inspecting the scratchpad reveals the reasoning path that led to the output, which the final answer alone does not show.

Scratchpad contents are a window into intermediate reasoning, but they are not a guaranteed faithful account of the actual computation producing the answer, which is an active and unresolved question in interpretability research.

terms.example: A coding agent's plan file listing which modules it intends to touch and why.
terms.definition: A working area where a model writes intermediate reasoning, notes, or plans that inform its final answer but are not the answer. Inspecting it is often the fastest way to see why an agent did what it did.

lenses.body: A smaller AI helper spun up just to do one specific piece of a bigger job, then it reports back and disappears, like a temp worker hired for one task.

Scope each subagent's permissions independently rather than inheriting the parent agent's full access; a subagent handling one narrow subtask should not be able to act outside that scope even if it is manipulated.

Design subagents with the minimum context and permissions their slice of work requires, not the full context of the parent task; that isolation is the point, and it limits blast radius if a single subagent misbehaves or is compromised.

terms.example: A subagent given read access to one folder to summarize its contents, and nothing else.
terms.definition: A scoped agent spawned to handle one subtask and report back, then terminate. Isolation is the point: the subagent gets only the context and permissions its slice of work requires.

lenses.body: The official list of tools an AI helper is allowed to use, with rules about what each tool can do, so the AI cannot suddenly use something it was never given permission to touch.

Treat the tool registry the same way you treat an access-control list: review it on a schedule, remove unused entries, and require a change-control process before adding a new tool, especially one with write access or financial consequences.

This is the practical control surface for agent blast radius: an agent literally cannot misuse a tool that is not in its registry, so keep the registry minimal and task-specific rather than granting broad access "in case it is needed."

The documented tool registry for an agentic system is a natural artifact for demonstrating bounded authority: it shows precisely what the system was permitted to do, which supports an accountability claim after an incident far better than a general description of intended behavior.

terms.example: A registry granting the finance agent report-generation tools but not payment execution.
terms.definition: The catalog of tools, with their schemas and permissions, that an agent is allowed to call. It is the practical control surface for agent blast radius: an agent cannot misuse a tool it was never granted.

lenses.body: Trying really hard to break your own AI system on purpose, the way a locksmith tries to pick their own locks before selling them, so you find the weaknesses before someone with bad intentions does.

Goes beyond functional QA specifically: the tester behaves like an adversary, probing injection paths and boundary conditions, not confirming the happy path works. Budget for this as a distinct activity from feature testing, since the two have genuinely different goals and skill sets.

A distinct activity from normal quality testing, worth its own line item and its own team or vendor; confirming a feature works is not the same exercise as trying to break it, and skipping the second leaves real gaps undiscovered until an actual attacker finds them.

Increasingly expected as part of a documented pre-deployment risk assessment for higher-risk AI systems; the absence of any adversarial testing evidence is itself a meaningful gap in a conformity or risk assessment record.

terms.example: Running injection, boundary, and output tests against a customer-facing chatbot before launch.
terms.definition: Deliberately attacking your own AI system to find what breaks before someone else does. It goes beyond functional QA: the tester behaves like an adversary, probing injection paths, boundary conditions, and output handling rather than confirming the happy path works.

lenses.body: A clear, written-down list of exactly what an AI agent is and is not allowed to read, change, or trigger, so everyone, including the people checking its work later, knows precisely where its limits are.

Writing boundaries down is the control: an undocumented boundary cannot be audited, and in a boundary matrix the empty cells are findings, not omissions. Treat any agent without an explicit, current boundary document as unreviewed, regardless of how well it seems to be behaving in practice.

Ask for the written boundary document, not just an assurance that an agent "is scoped appropriately," for any deployed agent that matters; an unwritten boundary is not a real control, whatever the intention behind it.

A documented agent boundary is a natural evidentiary artifact for demonstrating bounded authority in an incident review or conformity assessment, since it shows precisely what the system was permitted to do at deployment time.

terms.example: A grid showing each agent's permitted data sources, write targets, and downstream actions, with every blank cell explained.
terms.definition: The documented limit on what an agent may read, write, and trigger. Writing boundaries down is the control: an undocumented boundary cannot be audited, and in a boundary matrix the empty cells are findings, not omissions.

lenses.body: A written document that explains exactly what an AI system is for, what safety controls it has, and how it is being watched over time, using a standard format so anyone reviewing it knows where to find the important information.

Extends the long-standing system security plan discipline to AI, giving assessors one consolidated place to see what the system does and how it is protected; maintain this as a living document, updated as the system and its controls change, not a one-time artifact.

A standard, expected documentation artifact for any AI system of real consequence; its absence for a system your organization operates is a genuine governance gap worth closing before an auditor or regulator asks for it and it does not exist.

A structured, standardized documentation format specifically designed to make AI systems assessable using the same established discipline applied to conventional system security plans, which supports consistent review across different organizations and systems.

terms.origin: NIST SP 800-18 Revision 2, which extended system security planning to AI systems.
terms.example: An SSP-style document covering a deployed RAG system's data sources, access controls, and monitoring.
terms.definition: Documentation of an AI system's purpose, controls, and monitoring, in the format NIST SP 800-18r2 defines. It extends the long-standing system security plan discipline to AI, giving assessors one place to see what the system does and how it is protected.

lenses.body: A standard scoring system that rates how serious a specific AI security weakness is, so a team can decide which problems to fix first instead of guessing or fixing things in a random order.

Scores are what turn a pile of findings into a sequenced remediation roadmap; adopt a consistent scoring methodology like this one rather than triaging AI vulnerabilities by gut feeling, since a defensible, documented prioritization is what stands up under later scrutiny after an incident.

A concrete way to ask your security team a specific, answerable question: what are our highest-scored open AI vulnerabilities, and what is the remediation timeline for each, rather than a vague assurance that "we are working on AI security."

A structured scoring methodology specific to AI vulnerabilities, analogous to the well-established CVSS for conventional software, that supports more consistent and comparable severity assessment across different organizations' AI risk documentation.

terms.origin: OWASP AI Vulnerability Scoring System project.
terms.example: Ranking a prompt-injection exposure against a model-exfiltration risk to decide which gets fixed first.
terms.definition: An OWASP scoring method for rating the severity of AI-specific vulnerabilities, the AI analog of CVSS for conventional software flaws. Scores are what turn a pile of findings into a sequenced remediation roadmap.

terms.term: Annex I / Annex III (EU AI Act)

lenses.body: Two different ways an AI system can get classified as "high-risk" under Europe's big AI law: one way is if the AI is part of a product that was already regulated before, and the other is if the AI does specific listed jobs, like helping decide who gets hired or who gets a loan.

The classification pathway determines which specific technical and documentation controls, risk management, logging, human oversight, apply to a given system, which means security control implementation planning should follow, not precede, this legal classification determination.

Determine early, with legal counsel, which annex any EU-facing AI system falls under, since this single classification decision cascades into your entire compliance timeline and obligation set; do not assume high-risk status or lack thereof without this specific determination.

Which annex applies decides the obligation set and the compliance deadline; determining the correct classification pathway early is foundational to building an accurate compliance timeline, since Annex I and Annex III systems can face different assessment routes and deadlines under the current amended schedule.

terms.origin: EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; deadlines amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus.
terms.example: An AI hiring screener landing in Annex III and inheriting the full high-risk obligation stack.
terms.definition: The two routes into high-risk classification under the EU AI Act: Annex I covers AI embedded in already-regulated products, Annex III lists stand-alone high-risk use cases such as hiring and credit. Which annex applies decides the obligation set and the compliance deadline.

lenses.body: Every single point where someone trying to break in could possibly reach or influence a system. AI adds a bunch of brand new points that did not exist before, like the box where you type questions to it, and the documents it reads to look things up.

AI expands it in kind, not just degree: inference endpoints, prompt channels, retrieval sources, and tool calls are all new entry points the pre-AI threat model never listed. Rebuild your threat model explicitly for these new categories rather than assuming your existing web application security review already covers them.

Deploying an AI feature genuinely expands your organization's attack surface in ways that traditional software security review was not designed to catch; confirm your security team has specifically updated their threat model to account for these new AI-specific entry points.

A meaningfully expanded attack surface is a relevant factor in risk assessment for any AI system, since traditional security assessment methodology built around conventional software attack vectors does not automatically transfer to cover prompt-based and retrieval-based entry points unique to AI systems.

terms.origin: Long-standing security-engineering concept, predating AI.
terms.example: An inventory that adds the chatbot's prompt box and its retrieval store to the classic network and application entries.
terms.definition: Every point where an attacker can attempt to reach or influence a system. AI expands it in kind, not just degree: inference endpoints, prompt channels, retrieval sources, and tool calls are all new entry points the pre-AI threat model never listed.

lenses.body: A protected, tamper-proof record showing exactly who did what and when, and with what authority, so if something goes wrong later, there is a real record to investigate instead of just people's memories and guesses.

Agent actions belong in it exactly as human actions do; an agent that acts outside the logged record is an agent that cannot be investigated. Ensure every agent action is logged with the same rigor as a human user action, since an unlogged agent action is functionally unauditable when something goes wrong.

Confirm agent actions are captured in the same audit trail as human employee actions, not in a separate, less rigorous log or not logged at all; an agent acting outside a proper audit record leaves you unable to investigate or explain what happened if a problem arises.

A tamper-resistant, comprehensive audit trail covering both human and AI-agent actions is a foundational evidentiary requirement for demonstrating accountability after an incident; its completeness and integrity should be a specific point of examination in any compliance review.

terms.example: A log entry showing which agent approved a refund, under which delegation, at what time.
terms.definition: A tamper-resistant record of who did what, when, and under what authority. Agent actions belong in it exactly as human actions do; an agent that acts outside the logged record is an agent that cannot be investigated.

lenses.body: How much damage could actually happen if a specific AI system or account got hacked or went wrong, before anything stops it. An account that can only look at information causes less damage than one that can actually change things.

Read access leaks data; write access changes systems, which is why write permissions are what make a blast radius large. Minimize write permissions specifically and aggressively for any agent or identity, since read-only compromise is contained and recoverable in a way write-access compromise often is not.

Ask specifically what an agent or system could do at maximum if fully compromised, not just what it is intended to do; the gap between intended behavior and maximum possible damage under compromise is the real risk exposure your organization is carrying.

A documented blast-radius assessment, specifically distinguishing read from write access and their respective consequences, is a meaningful component of a risk assessment for any consequential AI system, since it directly informs the appropriate level of required oversight and control.

terms.origin: Borrowed from site-reliability engineering; applied to AI agents from roughly 2024.
terms.example: Measuring what a hijacked procurement agent could actually order, cancel, or pay before a control intervenes.
terms.definition: How much damage a compromised identity or agent can cause before anything stops it. Read access leaks data; write access changes systems, which is why write permissions are what make a blast radius large.

lenses.body: A label a manufacturer puts on a product to say it meets Europe's legal requirements and can be sold there. It is a statement that the right paperwork process was followed, not a promise that the product is actually secure against attacks.

A regulatory market-access marker, not a security control; a CE-marked AI product still requires your own independent security assessment before deployment, since the marking speaks to regulatory process completion rather than to demonstrated resistance to attack.

A necessary but not sufficient signal when evaluating a vendor's AI product for the EU market; it confirms a compliance process was completed, not that the underlying system is actually secure, which requires its own separate verification.

A statement of product compliance, not a security assurance: a CE mark says the conformity process ran, not that the system resists attack. Do not conflate CE marking with a security guarantee when assessing a vendor's claims; ask separately about actual security testing and results.

terms.origin: EU product-conformity regime, extended to AI by the EU AI Act.
terms.example: An AI-enabled medical device carrying a CE mark while still needing its own security assessment.
terms.definition: A manufacturer's declaration that a product meets EU requirements and may be sold in the single market. It is a statement of product compliance, not a security assurance: a CE mark says the conformity process ran, not that the system resists attack.

lenses.body: A temporary backup safety measure used when the real, preferred safety measure cannot be put in place right away. It reduces risk in the meantime, but it comes with an implied promise that the real fix is still coming, not a permanent substitute.

Every compensating control carries an implicit promise to install the real one; track compensating controls explicitly with a target date for replacement, since without active tracking they have a strong tendency to quietly become permanent, undocumented risk acceptance instead of temporary bridges.

If your team reports a compensating control in place for a known gap, ask specifically for the target date when the actual preferred control will be implemented; a compensating control with no planned end date is effectively an unacknowledged permanent risk acceptance.

A documented, time-bound compensating control with a clear remediation plan is a legitimate and often necessary interim risk management approach; an undocumented or open-ended one is a meaningfully weaker position in any compliance review.

terms.origin: Standard audit and compliance vocabulary, notably from PCI DSS.
terms.example: A WAF rule blocking a known exploit pattern while the underlying patch waits for a maintenance window.
terms.definition: A substitute control applied when the preferred control cannot be deployed in time. It buys risk reduction now at the cost of tracking debt: every compensating control carries an implicit promise to install the real one.

lenses.body: The official process of proving a product actually meets legal safety and quality rules before it can be sold. Depending on how risky the product is considered, this proof either comes from the company itself or from an independent outside checker.

Understand which specific technical controls and documentation your system needs to have in place before assessment begins, since starting the conformity assessment process without the underlying technical control implementation already complete typically results in a failed or substantially delayed assessment.

Budget for meaningfully longer timelines if your system requires third-party conformity assessment rather than self-assessment; notified-body capacity constraints mean this route can take considerably longer than internal teams typically plan for.

Depending on classification it is self-assessed or third-party assessed, and the difference determines cost, timeline, and who signs; confirm early which assessment route applies to a given system, since third-party assessment involves substantially longer lead times and dependency on notified-body capacity.

terms.origin: EU product-safety law; central to the EU AI Act's high-risk regime.
terms.example: A high-risk AI system routed through a notified body instead of a self-declaration.
terms.definition: The formal process of demonstrating a product meets regulatory requirements before it goes to market. Depending on classification it is self-assessed or third-party assessed, and the difference determines cost, timeline, and who signs.

lenses.body: Making sure one person's private questions, information, and results never accidentally get mixed up with or shown to a different person using the same AI system, so nobody sees information that belongs to someone else.

Failures here are leaks with no attacker involved: the system volunteers one tenant's data to another through shared context or cache. Test multi-tenant isolation explicitly and adversarially, since this failure mode requires no attacker skill at all, only a design flaw in shared infrastructure.

A specific, serious risk category for any multi-tenant AI product, worth a direct question to your vendor or internal team: has cross-tenant context isolation been explicitly tested, not just assumed to work because it was designed to?

A cross-tenant data leak caused by context isolation failure is a serious privacy incident regardless of whether any malicious actor was involved, since the system itself caused the exposure; this failure mode should be a specific focus of privacy impact assessment for multi-tenant AI systems.

terms.example: A multi-tenant assistant that never lets tenant A's retrieved documents surface in tenant B's answers.
terms.definition: Keeping one user's prompts, retrieved data, and cached results out of another user's session. Failures here are leaks with no attacker involved: the system volunteers one tenant's data to another through shared context or cache.

terms.term: COSAiS (Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems)

lenses.body: A project that takes the government's big list of standard security controls and figures out exactly how each one applies specifically to AI systems, giving teams a detailed, practical guide instead of having to figure it out themselves from scratch.

The implementation detail beneath the Cyber AI Profile: where the profile says what outcomes matter, the overlays say which controls produce them. Use this mapping directly when implementing SP 800-53-based controls for an AI system, rather than independently reinventing an AI-specific interpretation of each control.

A structured mapping of an established, widely recognized control catalog onto AI-specific implementation guidance supports more consistent security control implementation and assessment across organizations, reducing ambiguity in how conventional security frameworks apply to AI systems.

terms.origin: NIST Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems project.
terms.example: Selecting the overlay controls for a generative AI deployment instead of hand-picking from 800-53.
terms.definition: A NIST project mapping the SP 800-53 control catalog onto AI systems. It is the implementation detail beneath the Cyber AI Profile: where the profile says what outcomes matter, the overlays say which controls produce them.

lenses.body: A government guide that applies the standard cybersecurity rulebook specifically to AI, covering three angles: keeping AI systems themselves secure, using AI to help defend against attacks, and stopping attacks that use AI as the weapon.

It bridges CSF 2.0 and the AI RMF so security teams do not need two disconnected frameworks; use this profile as your primary reference when integrating AI-specific security considerations into an existing NIST Cybersecurity Framework-based security program, rather than maintaining entirely separate AI and general security frameworks.

A useful reference framework if your security team is building or maturing an AI security program on top of an existing NIST CSF-based general security program, since it is specifically designed to integrate rather than replace that existing foundation.

A structured bridge between two previously separate NIST frameworks, the Cybersecurity Framework and the AI Risk Management Framework, that supports more coherent and less duplicative security and AI governance program design across regulated organizations.

terms.origin: NIST IR 8596.
terms.example: Mapping an existing CSF 2.0 program onto AI systems using the profile's Secure, Defend, and Thwart lenses.
terms.definition: A NIST profile applying the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 to AI, organized around securing AI systems, defending with AI, and thwarting AI-enabled attacks. It bridges CSF 2.0 and the AI RMF so security teams do not need two disconnected frameworks.

lenses.body: A European law requiring products with any digital or software components to be built and maintained securely their whole life, from how they are developed through how security problems get fixed and updates get delivered.

Lifecycle security obligations, secure development, vulnerability handling, update delivery, under this regulation should be built into your standard product security practices from the start, since retrofitting them after a product is already in the field is considerably more costly and disruptive.

A regulation with real overlap and interaction with the EU AI Act specifically for products with digital elements; coordinate compliance planning across the two regimes rather than treating them as entirely independent obligations, since meeting one can partially satisfy the other.

Its Article 12(1) deems CRA compliance to satisfy part of AI Act Article 15, tying the two regimes together; understand this cross-reference explicitly when building a compliance program, since demonstrating CRA compliance can directly support part of your AI Act security obligation rather than requiring entirely separate evidence.

terms.origin: EU Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847.
terms.example: A software vendor's CRA conformity work counting toward its AI Act cybersecurity obligations.
terms.definition: An EU regulation setting lifecycle cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, from secure development through vulnerability handling and updates. Its Article 12(1) deems CRA compliance to satisfy part of AI Act Article 15, tying the two regimes together.

lenses.body: Security tools that watch for sensitive company information trying to leave the building, usually by checking emails, uploads, and computers. Most of these tools were never built to watch what people type into an AI chat box, which has become a major, often unwatched way information actually leaks out now.

Classic DLP is rarely tuned to watch a prompt box, which is now one of the busiest exfiltration channels in the building; explicitly extend DLP coverage to AI prompt and file-upload channels, since this is a real and currently underprotected gap in most existing DLP deployments.

Ask specifically whether your organization's existing data-loss-prevention tools cover what employees type into AI chat tools, since most legacy DLP deployments were built before this channel existed and were never extended to monitor it, leaving a real and current gap.

A meaningful and currently common gap in data protection controls, since legacy DLP infrastructure predating widespread AI tool adoption frequently does not cover this new exfiltration channel, worth specific attention in any data protection or security assessment involving AI tool usage.

terms.origin: Established security control category; AI-channel coverage is the current gap.
terms.example: Extending DLP policies to inspect what employees paste into public AI tools.
terms.definition: Controls that detect and block sensitive data leaving the organization. Classic DLP watches email, uploads, and endpoints; it is rarely tuned to watch a prompt box, which is now one of the busiest exfiltration channels in the building.

lenses.body: A verified, trustworthy record showing exactly where a piece of data actually came from and what it is legally allowed to be used for. Rules about consent, licensing, and where data is allowed to be stored all travel along with the data into whatever AI model uses it.

Maintain provenance documentation as a first-class security and compliance artifact alongside your data inventory, since consent, licensing, and residency obligations travel with the data into every downstream system that touches it, including trained models.

Ask specifically about data provenance, not just data availability, before approving any custom model training initiative; data being technically accessible does not mean its use for AI training was legally authorized, and this gap is a real and growing source of litigation.

Provenance is what makes a training set defensible rather than merely available; require documented provenance as a standard part of any AI training data review, since data availability alone says nothing about whether its use for training is actually legally permitted.

terms.example: Tracing a fine-tuning dataset back to its licensed sources before a customer audit asks.
terms.definition: A verified record of where data came from and what it may be used for. Consent, licensing, and residency obligations travel with the data into every model that touches it, so provenance is what makes a training set defensible rather than merely available.

lenses.body: A real, dated document owned by someone specific that proves exactly what a company knew and when they knew it. Being confident about something is not the same as being able to actually prove it later with a real paper trail.

Build documentation practices around producing genuinely defensible evidence, dated, owned, specific, for every significant security and governance decision, rather than relying on institutional memory or informal assurance that would not hold up under later scrutiny.

Assurance is an opinion; evidence is a document, and a regulator or plaintiff accepts only the second. Push your team past verbal assurances toward dated, owned, documented artifacts for any claim that might later need defending, since confidence without documentation carries no evidentiary weight.

The standard a regulator or court will actually apply when assessing whether an organization exercised appropriate diligence; verbal or undocumented claims of awareness or action carry essentially no evidentiary weight compared to dated, owned artifacts.

terms.example: A signed risk assessment with a date and an owner, produced in response to a regulator's request.
terms.definition: A dated, owned artifact that answers what the organization knew and when it knew it. Assurance is an opinion; evidence is a document, and a regulator or plaintiff accepts only the second.

lenses.body: A 2026 package of changes to Europe's big AI law that pushed back some deadlines and changed how compliance checking works, but did not actually remove any of the underlying requirements, just gave companies more time to meet them.

Recalibrate your compliance program timeline to the specific new dates this package established, noting that different obligation categories, like Annex III high-risk duties versus transparency requirements, moved on different schedules and need to be tracked separately.

Do not mistake this deadline extension for reduced compliance scope; the underlying obligations remain, and this is genuinely additional planning time to meet them properly, not a signal to deprioritize the work.

Its practical effect is calendar relief, not obligation relief: Annex III high-risk duties moved to December 2027 while transparency dates held. Communicate this distinction clearly to stakeholders, since the deadline extension does not reduce the underlying compliance burden, only the timeline for meeting it.

terms.origin: EU Digital Omnibus package, 2026.
terms.example: Replanning an AI Act compliance roadmap around the deferred Annex III date instead of the original 2026 deadline.
terms.definition: The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment. Its practical effect is calendar relief, not obligation relief: Annex III high-risk duties moved to December 2027 while transparency dates held.

lenses.body: A required, documented study of privacy risks that must be done before certain kinds of high-risk data processing begins. Many AI projects trigger this requirement because they process people's personal information in genuinely new ways and at a much bigger scale than before.

Build a trigger-check process into your AI deployment pipeline specifically asking whether a given project processes personal data in a way that requires this assessment, since many AI use cases trigger the requirement in ways that are not immediately obvious without deliberate review.

Confirm this assessment has actually been completed, not just assumed to be unnecessary, before launching any AI feature that processes personal data at meaningful scale; many organizations discover the requirement applied to them only after a regulator asks for the document.

The DPIA is often the first document a supervisory authority requests; ensure this assessment is genuinely completed and current for any AI deployment involving personal data processing at scale, since its absence or staleness is typically the first and most visible compliance gap an authority identifies.

terms.origin: GDPR Article 35.
terms.example: Completing a DPIA before deploying an AI system that screens customer communications.
terms.definition: A documented assessment of privacy risk required before certain high-risk processing. Many AI deployments trigger the duty because they process personal data in new ways at scale, and the DPIA is often the first document a supervisory authority requests.

lenses.body: A specific European technical standard that, once officially recognized, lets a company assume it has met a legal requirement just by following that standard, which shifts the burden onto anyone who disagrees to prove otherwise.

Build technical control implementation directly against the specific requirements of any applicable harmonised standard, since demonstrated adherence provides a legal presumption of conformity that a custom, non-standard approach, however technically sound, does not automatically receive.

Ask your compliance team specifically which harmonised standards apply to your AI systems and whether you are actually following them; this is the practical, lower-cost compliance route wherever an applicable standard exists, and missing it means taking a harder, more burdensome compliance path unnecessarily.

Following the standard becomes the practical route to compliance because it shifts the burden of proof onto anyone claiming otherwise; identify and follow applicable harmonised standards specifically where available, since they represent the lowest-friction compliance pathway currently recognized.

terms.origin: EU standardisation system under Regulation (EU) 1025/2012.
terms.example: Building an AI quality-management system against the harmonised standard instead of arguing conformity from first principles.
terms.definition: A European standard that, once cited in the Official Journal, gives a presumption of conformity with the regulation it supports. Following the standard becomes the practical route to compliance because it shifts the burden of proof onto anyone claiming otherwise.

lenses.body: A written, practiced plan for what to do when a security problem happens: how to notice it, stop it from getting worse, and recover afterward. Actually practicing the plan ahead of time matters enormously, because the real first incident is the worst possible moment to be figuring it out for the first time.

The rehearsal is the substance: an untested plan is treated as no plan, because the first live incident is the worst possible rehearsal. Schedule and conduct actual tabletop exercises against realistic AI-specific incident scenarios, not just general security incidents, since AI incidents have genuinely different characteristics worth practicing for specifically.

Ask when your incident response plan for AI-specific incidents was last actually rehearsed, not just documented; an untested plan provides false confidence and often fails in ways that only surface during a real, high-stress incident, which is the worst time to discover them.

A documented but untested incident response plan is meaningfully weaker evidence of genuine organizational readiness than one with a demonstrated rehearsal history; this distinction should be a specific point of inquiry in assessing an organization's actual incident preparedness.

terms.origin: Codified in NIST SP 800-61.
terms.example: A tabletop exercise walking the team through a prompt-injection incident before one happens.
terms.definition: The documented and rehearsed process for detecting, containing, and recovering from a security event. The rehearsal is the substance: an untested plan is treated as no plan, because the first live incident is the worst possible rehearsal.

lenses.body: A digital login or credential that belongs to a piece of software rather than to a human person, things like service accounts, API keys, and certificates. There are now more of these than actual human employee accounts in most companies, and every new AI agent adds even more of them.

They now outnumber human identities in most environments, and each new agent adds several more; extend your identity governance and access review processes explicitly to cover machine identities with the same rigor as human accounts, since most existing review processes were designed around and still focus primarily on human users.

Ask whether your organization's identity and access management program actually covers machine identities as rigorously as human employee accounts; given that machine identities now typically outnumber human ones, a gap here represents a large and growing portion of your actual attack surface.

The often-overlooked but numerically dominant category of organizational identities in an AI-adopting environment; access governance frameworks and their assessment should explicitly account for machine identity coverage, not assume traditional human-identity-focused review processes are sufficient.

terms.example: An inventory pass that finds five machine credentials for every employee login.
terms.definition: Any credential belonging to software rather than a person: service accounts, API keys, certificates, tokens. They now outnumber human identities in most environments, and each new agent adds several more.

lenses.body: A legal judgment about whether something that happened is important enough that it has to be officially reported to investors or regulators. For public companies in the US, deciding a cyber incident counts as "material" starts a strict four-business-day countdown to disclose it.

A materiality determination on a cyber incident starts the SEC's four-business-day disclosure clock, which makes the determination itself a governed process; have a clear, pre-established, documented process for making this determination quickly, since the disclosure clock starts running the moment materiality is determined, and delay in making that determination is itself a governance risk.

A public company's process for determining materiality on AI-related incidents is worth understanding specifically, since a slow, poorly governed determination process creates real disclosure timing risk that can itself become a securities law issue independent of the underlying incident.

A well-documented, consistently applied materiality determination process is a meaningful indicator of organizational governance maturity around incident disclosure; an ad hoc or undocumented process for such a consequential and time-sensitive determination is a real governance gap.

terms.origin: SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules, 2023.
terms.example: A materiality assessment convened within hours of discovering a breach involving an AI system.
terms.definition: Whether an event is significant enough to require disclosure to investors or regulators. For US public companies a materiality determination on a cyber incident starts the SEC's four-business-day disclosure clock, which makes the determination itself a governed process.

lenses.body: A public library that catalogs real, documented attacks people have used against AI systems, similar to a well-known crime database that helps security experts recognize patterns instead of having to guess what attacks might look like from scratch.

It turns AI threat modeling from speculation into pattern-matching against documented attacks; use this as a direct reference when threat modeling any AI system, since it provides documented, real-world attack patterns rather than requiring your team to speculatively imagine what an AI-specific attack might look like.

A useful, credible reference your security team should be actively using; if your organization's AI threat modeling process does not reference this or an equivalent documented knowledge base, it is likely relying on speculation rather than known, real-world attack patterns.

A well-established, community-maintained knowledge base of documented AI-specific adversary tactics that provides a credible, external reference point for assessing whether an organization's threat modeling for its AI systems is grounded in known attack patterns rather than purely speculative.

terms.origin: MITRE ATLAS, launched 2021.
terms.example: Mapping a deployed model's exposures against ATLAS techniques during a threat-modeling session.
terms.definition: A public knowledge base of observed adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, the ATT&CK equivalent for AI. It turns AI threat modeling from speculation into pattern-matching against documented attacks.

lenses.body: The actual trained pieces that make up an AI model, its learned settings and any extra fine-tuning it received. This counts as a real, valuable business asset with its own backup and recovery needs, since losing it can mean losing a capability that no ordinary code backup can bring back.

Losing it can mean losing a capability no backup of the surrounding code can restore; ensure model artifacts have their own dedicated backup and recovery procedure, distinct from standard code and infrastructure backups, since standard software recovery processes typically do not account for these large, specialized files.

Confirm your organization treats trained model weights as a distinct, valuable business asset with its own backup and disaster recovery plan; treating it as just another file in a general backup process risks losing a capability that took significant time and money to originally produce.

A company's trained model weights represent real, embedded capital investment; ask specifically about backup, recovery, and access control practices for these artifacts, since their loss or theft represents a genuine and sometimes underappreciated business continuity and IP risk.

terms.example: Including model weights and adapters in the disaster-recovery inventory with defined restore objectives.
terms.definition: The weights, adapters, and tuning data that constitute a trained model. It is a production asset with recovery requirements: losing it can mean losing a capability no backup of the surrounding code can restore.

lenses.body: Stealing a copy of an AI model's knowledge or behavior by asking it a huge number of carefully designed questions over time and piecing together the answers, rather than stealing the actual files directly. Each individual question looks completely normal; the theft only becomes visible when you look at the whole pattern together.

Each request looks legitimate on its own; the theft only appears in the aggregate pattern, which is why per-request controls miss it. Implement query-pattern and volume-based monitoring specifically for this attack type, since request-level access controls alone are structurally unable to detect an attack that only becomes visible in aggregate.

A genuine and hard-to-detect risk for any proprietary model exposed through an API, since standard access controls checking individual requests will not catch it; ask your team whether monitoring specifically looks for the aggregate query patterns characteristic of this attack.

A documented and technically demonstrated attack category worth including explicitly in risk assessments for any organization exposing a proprietary or sensitive model through an accessible API, since standard access control auditing does not naturally surface this pattern.

terms.example: Rate and pattern monitoring that flags a customer account systematically mapping a model's decision boundary.
terms.definition: Extracting a model's behavior or training data through repeated queries. Each request looks legitimate on its own; the theft only appears in the aggregate pattern, which is why per-request controls miss it.

lenses.body: Rules from bank regulators about carefully checking and overseeing any AI or computer models used in important decisions, including having someone independent double-check the model, watching it over time, and clearly writing down its known limitations.

Independent validation and ongoing monitoring requirements under this discipline apply specifically and explicitly to AI and machine learning models now, not just traditional statistical models; ensure your model governance program has been extended to cover AI systems with the same rigor previously applied only to conventional models.

If your organization is a regulated financial institution using AI in consequential decisions, confirm your model risk management program has been updated to reflect the current framework that replaced the older SR 11-7 guidance in April 2026.

SR 26-2 and OCC 2026-13 replaced the long-standing SR 11-7 in April 2026, extending the discipline explicitly to AI and machine learning models; ensure your model risk management program has been updated to the current framework, since the earlier SR 11-7 has been formally superseded and citing it now reflects an outdated compliance posture.

terms.origin: Federal Reserve SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13, April 2026, superseding SR 11-7.
terms.example: A bank's validation team independently testing an AI credit model before it touches a lending decision.
terms.definition: Supervisory expectations for validating and governing models used in regulated decisions: independent validation, ongoing monitoring, and documented limitations. SR 26-2 and OCC 2026-13 replaced the long-standing SR 11-7 in April 2026, extending the discipline explicitly to AI and machine learning models.

lenses.body: Everything an AI model actually depends on that your own organization did not build itself: the original base model, the data used to fine-tune it, the training process, and the outside services hosting it. Each of these inherited pieces brings its own risks that never got specifically evaluated when the model was originally chosen.

Each inherited component carries inherited risk that procurement never priced; map your model supply chain explicitly, base weights, tuning data, training pipeline, hosting service, the same way you would map a conventional software supply chain, since each link carries its own distinct risk that a simple vendor contract review does not surface.

Ask specifically what your model supply chain actually looks like, not just who your primary AI vendor is; a vendor's own model may itself depend on base weights, data, or infrastructure from other parties whose risk was never separately evaluated in your procurement process.

Model supply chain dependency and diversification is a real risk factor worth understanding for any AI company; heavy, unexamined reliance on a single upstream base model or data source represents concentration risk comparable to conventional supply chain concentration risk.

terms.example: A register listing the base model, dataset sources, and pipeline dependencies behind each deployed AI system.
terms.definition: Everything a model depends on that the organization did not build: base weights, tuning datasets, training pipelines, and the services that host them. Each inherited component carries inherited risk that procurement never priced.

lenses.body: The official government document that defines "zero trust" security: check every single request no matter where it comes from, always assume a break-in has already happened somewhere, and only give the minimum access actually needed. It was written before AI agents existed, so applying it to AI means stretching its ideas to cover a kind of actor it never anticipated.

It was written before agent traffic existed, so applying it to AI means extending its identity and policy model to non-human actors it never anticipated; explicitly extend your zero trust architecture's identity and policy model to treat AI agents as first-class subjects, since the original framework's examples and assumptions were built around human and traditional service traffic.

Confirm your organization's zero trust security architecture has actually been extended to treat AI agents as first-class identities requiring verification, rather than assuming the existing framework automatically covers this newer category of actor it was not originally designed for.

A foundational, well-established security architecture reference that requires deliberate extension and interpretation to properly cover AI agent traffic, since its original scope predates the emergence of autonomous AI agents as a distinct category of network actor.

terms.origin: NIST SP 800-207, published 2020.
terms.example: Using 800-207 tenets to design per-request authorization for agent tool calls.
terms.definition: The NIST publication defining zero trust architecture and its tenets: verify every request, assume breach, grant least privilege. It was written before agent traffic existed, so applying it to AI means extending its identity and policy model to non-human actors it never anticipated.

lenses.body: Any account or identity that can log in and take action without an actual person present, including service accounts, cloud workload identities, and now AI agents too. This is the group of accounts most security reviews accidentally miss, because those reviews were built with only human employees in mind.

It is the population most access reviews miss, because review processes were designed around employees; explicitly extend periodic access review processes to include non-human identities with the same rigor, cadence, and ownership accountability as human employee access reviews, since this population is both large and frequently overlooked.

Ask specifically whether your organization's access review process includes non-human identities, service accounts, agent credentials, workload identities, or only human employees; given how numerous these have become, a gap here represents a substantial and growing unreviewed risk surface.

A category of identity increasingly numerous and consequential in AI-adopting organizations that traditional identity and access governance frameworks, built around human employee lifecycle, do not naturally cover; access governance assessment should explicitly probe for this coverage gap.

terms.example: An access-review cycle that includes agent credentials with the same rigor as user accounts.
terms.definition: Any identity that can authenticate and act without a person present: service accounts, workload identities, and now AI agents. It is the population most access reviews miss, because review processes were designed around employees.

lenses.body: An officially approved outside organization allowed to formally check whether certain products meet European legal requirements. Right now there are not very many of these approved checkers for AI systems specifically, which means the actual checking process can become a real bottleneck.

Begin technical documentation and control implementation early enough to accommodate potential queuing delays for notified-body assessment; the current capacity constraint in this market means assessment timeline, not just your own preparation timeline, needs to be factored into project planning.

Engage with a notified body well ahead of any compliance deadline requiring third-party assessment, given documented capacity constraints in this market; waiting until close to a deadline risks being unable to secure assessment in time regardless of your own internal readiness.

Notified-body capacity is the current constraint: obligations can arrive faster than assessors can be accredited; factor current notified-body capacity constraints explicitly into compliance timeline planning and communication, since the regulatory deadline and the practical availability of assessment capacity to meet it are currently not well matched.

terms.origin: EU conformity-assessment regime; designated per regulation including the AI Act.
terms.example: Booking a notified-body assessment slot months ahead of a high-risk system's market date.
terms.definition: An accredited organization designated to carry out third-party conformity assessment under EU product law. For the AI Act's high-risk systems, notified-body capacity is the current constraint: obligations can arrive faster than assessors can be accredited.

lenses.body: Checking an AI's generated answer one more time right before it actually gets sent out, and blocking or hiding anything that should not be shown. It is the very last safety check, catching problems that slipped through everything else, whatever caused them.

It catches what retrieval pulled in, what the prompt coaxed out, and what upstream controls missed; treat this as a genuine defense-in-depth layer, not a replacement for upstream controls like input validation and access control, since it is specifically valuable as the last line catching what everything earlier in the pipeline missed.

A meaningful, worthwhile safety layer, but ask whether it is your organization's only control or one layer among several; relying on output filtering alone, with no upstream controls, leaves you dependent on catching every problem at the very last possible moment, which is a fragile single point of failure.

A valuable and expected control for high-risk AI systems, though its presence alone should not be treated as sufficient risk mitigation without corroborating evidence of upstream controls, since an output filter catching problems at the last stage indicates gaps existed earlier in the pipeline that ideally would also be addressed.

terms.example: A filter redacting account numbers from a support bot's answers regardless of how they entered the context.
terms.definition: Inspecting generated responses before release and blocking or redacting what should not go out. It is the last line: it catches what retrieval pulled in, what the prompt coaxed out, and what upstream controls missed.

lenses.body: A widely trusted, agreed-upon list of the biggest security risks specifically for AI applications, ranked by how serious they are, similar to a well-known list of the most common ways regular websites get hacked, but specifically written for AI systems.

It functions as the scoring baseline for AI application security the way the original OWASP Top 10 does for web; use this list as your primary structured checklist when conducting or commissioning a security review of any LLM-based application, since it represents current community consensus on the highest-priority risk categories.

A useful, credible reference to ask any AI vendor or internal team about directly: has your system been assessed specifically against this list, and what is the current status of each identified risk category? This is a concrete, checkable question rather than a vague assurance about "AI security."

A widely recognized, community-developed consensus reference for AI application security risk categories, providing a consistent baseline that supports more comparable security assessment across different organizations' AI systems and vendors.

terms.origin: OWASP, first released 2023.
terms.example: Structuring an AI application security review as a walk through the ten categories.
terms.definition: The consensus list of the highest-priority security risks in LLM applications, from prompt injection through unbounded consumption. It functions as the scoring baseline for AI application security the way the original OWASP Top 10 does for web.

lenses.body: Checking whether an AI agent is actually allowed to do something at the exact moment it tries to do it, instead of just trusting that it was given broad permission once, in advance, and never checking again after that.

Enforcement, not documentation: the policy engine sits in the execution path and can say no. Implement this as an active runtime control point, not merely as a documented policy that describes intended behavior, since only an actively enforcing system can actually prevent an unauthorized action rather than just having a rule about it.

A meaningfully stronger control than a documented policy alone; ask whether your agent systems actually enforce permissions at the moment of each action attempt, or whether the "policy" is really just a written description of intended behavior that nothing actively checks against in real time.
