It is the final step before a model commits to a next-token choice; softmax converts raw logit scores into a proper probability distribution, which is what sampling strategies like temperature and top-p actually operate on to decide the next token.

terms.example: Turning logits into the probabilities that sampling draws from.
terms.definition: The function that converts raw scores into a probability distribution summing to one. It is the final step before a model commits to a next-token choice.

lenses.body: An AI that only wakes up and uses the specific relevant parts of itself for each word it processes, instead of using its entire "brain" every single time, which lets it be huge overall while still being fast to actually run.

Sparse models typically require more total memory to hold all parameters even though fewer are active per token, so memory footprint and compute cost need to be evaluated separately when comparing a sparse model against a dense alternative for deployment.

The compute-versus-capacity decoupling sparse models offer is a genuine efficiency gain, but training dynamics for sparse architectures are less well understood and more prone to instability than dense-model training, which remains an active area of methodological research.

Total capacity grows without proportional inference cost, which is how very large models stay servable; this is the general principle behind mixture-of-experts architectures specifically, decoupling total parameter count from per-token compute cost, which dense models cannot do.

terms.example: An MoE model with huge total parameters but modest active compute per token.
terms.definition: A model that activates only a subset of its parameters per token, typically through mixture-of-experts routing. Total capacity grows without proportional inference cost, which is how very large models stay servable.

lenses.body: A newer kind of AI design that keeps a running, compressed summary of everything it has seen so far, instead of comparing every word to every other word directly, which lets it handle very long text more efficiently.

Worth evaluating for genuinely long-sequence use cases where attention-based models' context length and cost become limiting factors; tooling maturity and pretrained model availability remain less developed than the transformer ecosystem as of this writing.

The relative expressiveness of SSMs versus attention for tasks requiring precise, arbitrary long-range token-to-token comparison, as opposed to compressed sequential summarization, remains a genuinely open empirical and theoretical question actively being studied.

The active alternative to attention for very long inputs, scaling linearly with sequence length where attention scales quadratically; this makes SSMs specifically attractive for tasks involving very long documents, audio, or other lengthy sequential data where attention's cost becomes prohibitive.

terms.example: Mamba processing book-length documents at linear cost.
terms.definition: A sequence architecture that maintains a running compressed state, scaling linearly with sequence length where attention scales quadratically. The active alternative to attention for very long inputs.

lenses.body: The AI design used in almost every chatbot today, built around the idea of letting every word in a sentence directly consider every other word at once, which turned out to work amazingly well and can be trained really fast on modern computer hardware.

The default architecture choice for essentially any new NLP or general sequence-modeling project today; deviating from it requires a specific, well-justified reason, like extreme long-context requirements or edge-device constraints, rather than being a neutral starting-point decision.

The 2017 paper's core insight, that attention alone, without recurrence, suffices for strong sequence modeling, remains the foundation nearly all current large-scale language and increasingly vision and audio models build on, making it one of the most consequential single architectural decisions in the field's history.

Its decisive property was parallelizable training, which let model scale grow with hardware in a way recurrent architectures never could; because every position can be processed simultaneously rather than sequentially, transformers can fully exploit modern parallel GPU hardware during training in a way RNNs structurally cannot.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017, "Attention Is All You Need."
terms.example: GPT, BERT, Gemini, and Claude are all transformers.
terms.definition: The deep learning architecture built on self-attention, introduced in 2017, that forms the foundation of modern LLMs. Its decisive property was parallelizable training, which let model scale grow with hardware in a way recurrent architectures never could.

lenses.body: An AI design shaped like the letter U, that shrinks a picture down to understand its big shapes, then builds it back up to full size, using shortcut connections between matching shrink and rebuild stages to keep fine details from getting lost.

Largely superseded by diffusion transformer backbones in state-of-the-art image generation systems, but still a solid, well-understood choice for medical imaging and other segmentation tasks where its original design was purpose-built and remains well-suited.

The architectural transition from U-Net to transformer backbones in diffusion models is a specific instance of the broader pattern where domain-specific inductive biases give way to more general, scalable architectures once sufficient data and compute are available.

Built for medical image segmentation, it became the denoising backbone of the first diffusion image generators; the skip connections between matching resolution levels specifically preserve fine spatial detail through the compression bottleneck, which is exactly what image denoising needs to reconstruct sharp results.

terms.origin: Ronneberger et al., 2015.
terms.example: The denoiser inside classic Stable Diffusion.
terms.definition: An encoder-decoder network with skip connections between matching resolution levels, preserving fine detail through the compression bottleneck. Built for medical image segmentation, it became the denoising backbone of the first diffusion image generators.

lenses.body: A version of an autoencoder that learns a smooth, organized internal map of information instead of fixed, rigid codes, which makes it possible to actually generate new, realistic examples from that internal map, not just compress and rebuild existing ones.

If working with a latent diffusion pipeline, the VAE component's reconstruction quality sets a hard ceiling on final output quality, since diffusion operates in the VAE's compressed latent space and any information lost in that compression cannot be recovered later.

The KL-divergence regularization term that enforces a smooth, well-structured latent distribution introduces a well-documented reconstruction-versus-regularization tradeoff, and balancing that tradeoff remains a meaningful design decision across different VAE-based applications.

In image diffusion systems it handles the compression into and out of latent space; the probabilistic rather than fixed encoding is specifically what makes the latent space smooth enough to sample new points from and get coherent output, which a standard deterministic autoencoder's latent space does not reliably support.

terms.origin: Kingma and Welling, 2013.
terms.example: The latent compression stage in Stable Diffusion pipelines.
terms.definition: An autoencoder that learns a probabilistic latent distribution rather than fixed codes, making the latent space smooth enough to generate from. In image diffusion systems it handles the compression into and out of latent space.

lenses.body: A picture-understanding AI design that treats an image like a sequence of small tiles, the same way a language AI treats a sentence as a sequence of words, instead of using the older sliding-filter approach that older picture AIs used.

Favor CNNs over ViTs for smaller datasets or resource-constrained settings, since ViTs generally need more training data to reach comparable performance; the crossover point where ViT advantages emerge depends on dataset scale, which is worth checking against your actual data volume.

The data-scale dependency of ViT performance relative to CNNs is a well-documented empirical finding directly connected to the absence of convolutional inductive biases; understanding this tradeoff remains central to choosing appropriately between the two architecture families for a given vision task.

At sufficient data scale it matched then passed CNNs, unifying vision and language under one architecture family; this required substantially more training data than CNNs to reach comparable performance, since ViTs lack the built-in image-specific assumptions CNNs have, and must learn those patterns from data instead.

terms.origin: Dosovitskiy et al., 2020.
terms.example: Image classifiers and the vision encoders inside multimodal models.
terms.definition: An architecture that applies transformer attention to image patches instead of convolutions, treating a picture as a sequence of tiles. At sufficient data scale it matched then passed CNNs, unifying vision and language under one architecture family.

lenses.body: An AI that can look at pictures and talk about them in words, connecting what it sees in an image to what it can say about it, which lets it answer questions about photos, charts, or screenshots.

Test VLM performance specifically on your actual document or image types, since performance on natural photographs does not reliably predict performance on charts, dense text screenshots, or specialized diagrams, which are meaningfully different visual distributions.

Fine-grained visual grounding, precisely connecting specific language to specific image regions rather than producing plausible but loosely connected descriptions, remains an active evaluation challenge distinct from simply measuring overall description quality or question-answering accuracy.

The bridge that lets a chat model read screenshots, charts, and documents; this capability specifically requires jointly training on paired image-text data so the model learns to connect visual features to language, rather than treating vision and text as entirely separate systems bolted together.

terms.example: CLIP, LLaVA, and GPT-4V-class models describing and reasoning over images.
terms.definition: A multimodal model trained to understand both visual inputs and text, connecting what it sees to what it can say. The bridge that lets a chat model read screenshots, charts, and documents.

lenses.body: A famous hard maths competition for teenagers. Giving it to an AI is like giving a spelling test to a robot: if it can solve these tricky problems without seeing them before, that is real thinking, not just remembering.

A math score is a proxy for structured reasoning ability, not a claim your business problem involves competition maths. Use it to shortlist models for tasks with clear right answers and many steps, then verify on your own cases.

A rising AIME score is real progress on structured problem-solving, but headlines that read it as "AI beats top students at math" skip that these are timed, well-specified competition problems, not the open-ended reasoning most work requires.

Selected because AIME problems require genuine multi-step derivation rather than pattern completion, making score inflation from memorization less likely than on broader benchmarks, though contamination checks are still necessary.

terms.origin: American Invitational Mathematics Examination, adopted as an AI benchmark from 2024.
terms.example: A reasoning model reporting its AIME solve rate as a headline capability claim.
terms.definition: A competition mathematics exam repurposed to test advanced multi-step reasoning in models. Its problems resist pattern-matching, which is why reasoning-model releases lead with AIME scores.

lenses.body: Puzzle grids that are brand new every time, so the AI cannot have secretly seen the answer before. It has to actually figure out the pattern, like a puzzle book nobody has ever solved.

A model that scores well broadly but poorly here may be strong on recalled knowledge and weak on novel problem-solving, which matters if your use case involves situations the model has not effectively seen before.
Worth checking before quoting: a model's ARC-AGI score and its score on knowledge-heavy tests like MMLU can diverge sharply, and conflating the two produces a misleading capability claim either way.

Its resistance to memorization makes it one of the few current benchmarks that plausibly measures generalization rather than recall, which is why a low score alongside high scores elsewhere on knowledge tests is informative rather than contradictory.

terms.origin: Fran\u00e7ois Chollet, "On the Measure of Intelligence," 2019.
terms.example: Models scoring far below humans on puzzles a child solves by inspection.
terms.definition: An abstract reasoning benchmark built from novel visual puzzles that cannot be solved by recalling training data. It is deliberately resistant to memorization, making it one of the few tests that measures generalization rather than recall.

lenses.body: A score for how good a computer is at telling two things apart, like sorting emails into "junk" and "not junk." A perfect sorter gets a perfect score; a random guesser gets a middling one.

A single number for "how good is this classifier overall," useful for comparing models before anyone decides how aggressive the system should be. It does not tell you the right threshold for your business; that decision comes after.

A high AUC-ROC does not mean a system performs well at the threshold actually deployed. Ask what threshold was chosen and what the precision and recall look like there, since a strong overall score can hide a bad choice of cutoff.

Threshold-independence is the useful property: it summarises separability across every possible decision boundary rather than one chosen cutoff, which is why it precedes precision/recall analysis at a specific operating point.

terms.example: Comparing two fraud models without committing to an alert threshold.
terms.definition: The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, a threshold-independent measure of how well a classifier separates classes. It answers "how good is the model overall" before anyone picks an operating point.

lenses.body: A test that lots of different AI systems take, so people can compare their scores fairly. Like every school in the country sitting the same exam paper.

A comparison score, not a guarantee of fitness for your use. A model that leads a public leaderboard may still underperform on your documents, your formats and your edge cases. Treat published numbers as a shortlist filter, and decide with an evaluation built from your own tasks.

Before quoting a score, establish who ran it, on what date, with what scaffolding, and whether the developer submitted its own result. Vendor-reported figures and independent evaluations of the same benchmark often differ, and a jump usually reflects a change in method or harness as often as a change in capability.

A fixed task set with a scoring protocol, valuable only while it remains a proxy for the capability it claims to measure. Watch for contamination of test items into training data, saturation as headroom disappears, and harness differences that make two reported numbers on the same benchmark incomparable.

terms.example: MMLU scores quoted in every model release announcement.
terms.definition: A standardized test used to compare model performance on a defined task set. Useful for ranking and dangerous for deciding: a benchmark measures the test, and vendors optimize for exactly that.

lenses.body: A way to check if a computer's translation matches a human's translation, by counting how many of the same word-groups they both used. It is not perfect, since two good translations can use totally different words.

Still useful as a fast regression check during development because it is deterministic and free, but do not treat it as a quality gate on its own; pair it with a smaller human-reviewed sample before shipping a translation feature.

A legacy metric known within the field to reward surface word overlap over meaning. A reported BLEU improvement is evidence of something, but it is not evidence that translations read better to a human.

An n-gram overlap score against reference translations, cheap and standardized but blind to meaning: a fluent, accurate translation using different phrasing than the reference can score lower than a stilted, literal one.

terms.origin: Papineni et al., 2002.
terms.example: Scoring a translation system against reference translations in a research paper.
terms.definition: An n-gram overlap metric for machine translation quality, scoring how much generated text matches reference translations. A legacy NLP metric: cheap, standardized, and known to reward surface overlap rather than meaning.

lenses.body: Before saying a computer definitely cannot do something risky, safety testers try really hard to get it to do that thing, using their best tricks. If skilled effort still fails, that is a more trustworthy "no."

If a vendor claims a model cannot perform some risky task, ask what elicitation effort was applied before that conclusion. A model that refuses under casual testing can still comply under more determined prompting.

Relevant to any pre-deployment capability claim used to justify a lower risk tier: a claim of inability is only as strong as the elicitation effort behind it, and testing under default settings alone is not sufficient evidence.

Naive prompting systematically undercounts capability; elicitation protocols including fine-tuning, scaffolding and adversarial prompting are now standard in frontier safety evaluations specifically to avoid false negatives that a refusal under casual testing would produce.

terms.origin: Frontier-lab safety evaluation practice.
terms.example: Red-teamers using optimized prompts before certifying a capability absent.
terms.definition: The effort to draw out a model's maximum ability before concluding it cannot do something. It exists to prevent false negatives in safety testing: a model that "cannot" assist with a dangerous task under naive prompting may comply under skilled prompting.

lenses.body: A chart that shows exactly which mistakes a computer made, not just how many. Did it call a cat a dog, or a dog a cat? Those are different problems even though both count as "one wrong answer."

Always look past the headline accuracy number at the off-diagonal cells: which specific classes get confused with which, since that pattern usually points directly at the fix, whether it is more training data or a threshold change.

Two systems can share the same accuracy score while making very different kinds of mistakes. Ask to see this breakdown before approving a system whose error types have different costs, like flagging a good customer as fraud versus missing real fraud.

The evidentiary basis for a documented risk assessment on a classification system: aggregate accuracy alone does not show whether errors are evenly distributed across protected classes or concentrated in ways that raise a disparate-impact concern.

terms.example: Discovering a model's errors concentrate in one costly direction.
terms.definition: A table of true and false positives and negatives that shows exactly how a classifier errs, not just how often. The off-diagonal cells are where the operational story lives.

lenses.body: Instead of grading answers with a test, this counts wins and losses when two AIs answer the same question and people vote for the better one, the same way chess players get ranked by who beats whom.
Reflects what people preferred in head-to-head chat, which correlates with helpfulness and tone but not necessarily with factual accuracy or task completion on your specific workflow.

An Elo leaderboard position is a preference ranking from a specific pool of voters and prompts, not an objective capability score; who voted and on what prompts shapes the result as much as the models do.

Captures relative human preference from pairwise comparison rather than absolute correctness on a fixed task set, which makes it a different and complementary signal to accuracy benchmarks, not a replacement for them.

terms.origin: Arpad Elo's chess rating system, applied to LLMs by LMSYS from 2023.
terms.example: Arena leaderboards ranking chat models by win rate against each other.
terms.definition: A relative skill score derived from pairwise comparisons, imported from chess into model evaluation. It ranks models by human preference in head-to-head matchups rather than absolute test scores.

lenses.body: One number that balances two kinds of mistakes: missing things you should have caught, and falsely flagging things that were fine. It rewards a system that is good at both, not just one.

The harmonic mean punishes imbalance more than a simple average would, so a model with high precision and low recall (or vice versa) will not hide behind a decent-looking average the way it might with arithmetic mean.

A balanced summary score, useful when false alarms and missed cases cost you roughly the same amount. If one type of error is far more expensive than the other in your business, ask for precision and recall separately rather than the blended F1.

terms.example: Evaluating an entity-extraction system with one balanced figure.
terms.definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, a single number balancing the two. Standard for classification tasks where both false alarms and misses matter.

lenses.body: Really hard science questions written so that even looking them up online will not help, because the answer is not sitting there waiting to be found. The AI has to actually reason it out.
A strong GPQA score is a signal of reasoning depth on expert-level problems, relevant if your use case involves genuinely novel analysis rather than retrieving and restating known information.
Worth naming in coverage because it is one of the few benchmarks explicitly built to resist the "the model just looked it up" objection, which makes a high score a more specific claim than most.

The "Google-proof" construction is specifically designed to separate genuine graduate-level reasoning from retrieval, addressing the contamination concern that undermines knowledge-heavy benchmarks whose answers can appear verbatim in training data.

terms.origin: Rein et al., 2023, "GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark."
terms.example: Frontier models scored on questions PhDs answer near 70 percent.
terms.definition: Graduate-level science questions designed so that even skilled web search does not yield answers, isolating genuine reasoning from lookup. Its "Google-proof" construction is the point.

lenses.body: The actual correct answer, checked and confirmed by a person, that gets used to grade the computer's answer. Getting this right answer key made is usually the hardest and most expensive part of testing an AI.
Ask how a vendor's claimed accuracy number was verified. A benchmark scored against weak or automatically generated ground truth is measuring something, but not necessarily what the marketing claims.

A documented, verified ground-truth methodology is what separates a defensible accuracy claim from an unverifiable one; conformity assessments and audits should ask specifically how reference answers were produced and validated.

Every evaluation is only as trustworthy as its ground truth; without verified labels an eval measures agreement between the model and whatever produced the reference, not accuracy against reality, which matters when the reference itself was AI-generated or crowd-sourced cheaply.

terms.example: Subject-matter experts labeling a golden set before an eval run.
terms.definition: The verified correct answer used as the reference for scoring. Every real evaluation needs it, and producing it is usually the expensive part: without trusted ground truth, an eval measures agreement, not accuracy.

lenses.body: Instead of one test score, this checks a computer on lots of different things at once, being right, being fair, being fast, being tough to trick, because no single number tells the whole story about how good it is.

If you are choosing a model based on one headline benchmark, a multi-dimensional evaluation like this is worth a look, since it can reveal that a leaderboard leader on one axis is mediocre on robustness or fairness.

A holistic evaluation is harder to summarise in a headline than a single leaderboard number, which is exactly why it is more informative and why coverage collapsing it back into one score loses the point of it.

Its premise, that no single score characterises a model, motivated a multi-metric multi-scenario design that trades leaderboard simplicity for a fuller picture, which is why HELM results are reported as a profile rather than a rank.

terms.origin: Stanford CRFM, 2022.
terms.example: Reading a model's full HELM profile instead of one headline benchmark.
terms.definition: A holistic evaluation framework scoring models across many scenarios and metrics at once, accuracy, robustness, fairness, efficiency, rather than one leaderboard number. Its premise is that no single score describes a model.

lenses.body: Real people read two answers and pick the one they like better. It is good at catching whether an answer feels helpful and friendly, but people can be fooled by an answer that sounds confident even when it is wrong.

Captures tone and perceived helpfulness, which benchmarks cannot, but the raters' preference for confident-sounding answers means a model can win on likability while being wrong more often than a less polished competitor.

A model winning on human preference is a real result worth reporting, but note for readers that raters measurably favour confidence and length, so a preference win is not the same claim as an accuracy win.

Documented biases include a preference for longer and more confident-sounding responses independent of correctness, which is why preference scores are triangulated against accuracy-based evaluations rather than used alone as a capability measure.

terms.example: Pairwise ratings feeding a reward model during alignment training.
terms.definition: Scoring models by having human raters compare outputs and pick the better one. It measures what benchmarks cannot, helpfulness and tone, and inherits every bias of the raters, including a documented preference for confident answers.

lenses.body: A coding test where the computer has to write a small program, and then the program either passes or fails automatic checks, no human needed to grade it. Very clear right and wrong.

Useful as a quick sanity check on raw code-generation ability, but it tests isolated function writing, not the multi-file, multi-step engineering that SWE-bench-style benchmarks measure, so a strong HumanEval score does not predict agentic coding performance.

A model's HumanEval score speaks to writing a correct short function, not to fixing a bug in your actual codebase. For engineering-relevant procurement decisions, look for benchmarks built from real repository tasks instead.

Superseded in relevance by larger and harder software-engineering benchmarks as frontier models saturated it, illustrating the general pattern where a benchmark's useful life ends once top models cluster near the ceiling.

terms.origin: OpenAI, 2021, "Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code."
terms.example: Reporting pass@1 on HumanEval in a model card.
terms.definition: A Python coding benchmark scored by unit-test pass rate: the model writes a function, the tests decide. It set the early standard for code capability measurement before larger software-engineering benchmarks arrived.

lenses.body: Millions of people chat with two mystery AIs at once and vote for the better one, without knowing which is which. It is like a giant, ongoing taste test for chatbots.
The closest thing to a live market price for general chat quality, driven by real user preference at scale, but it reflects casual conversational use rather than your specific enterprise task.

A live, crowd-sourced ranking is a legitimate and citable signal, more resistant to a single vendor gaming it than a static benchmark, though the voter pool is self-selected rather than representative of all users.

The scale and anonymisation reduce some selection bias present in curated evaluations, but the voter pool and prompt distribution still shape rankings, which is why Arena results are read alongside, not instead of, task-specific benchmarks.

terms.origin: LMSYS Org, 2023.
terms.example: Checking Arena rankings the week a new model ships.
terms.definition: A crowd-sourced evaluation where users chat with two anonymous models and vote for the better answer, producing an Elo ranking from millions of matchups. The closest thing to a live market price for model quality.

lenses.body: A huge quiz covering everything from history to physics to law, all multiple choice. For a while it was the main way people compared how "smart" different AIs were.

Still a reasonable floor check for broad knowledge, but a near-saturated headline number no longer meaningfully differentiates leading models; look at more recent, harder benchmarks for comparisons among frontier systems.

An MMLU score quoted today carries less information than it did two years ago, precisely because most frontier models now score similarly high; a genuinely differentiating comparison needs a benchmark with headroom left.

Saturating as frontier models cluster near the ceiling, which reduces its discriminative power for comparing top-tier systems and is why newer benchmarks such as GPQA and ARC-AGI have taken over the role MMLU played earlier.

terms.origin: Hendrycks et al., 2020.
terms.example: Model launches quoting MMLU alongside newer, harder benchmarks.
terms.definition: The massive multitask language understanding benchmark: multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects from law to physics. For years the default headline number for model knowledge, now saturating as frontier models cluster near the top.

lenses.body: A test that hides one important sentence inside a giant pile of text and checks whether the AI can still find it, no matter where it is buried. It proves a big "memory" actually works everywhere, not just at the start.

Run this before trusting an advertised context window in production: a model can accept a long input without reliably using all of it, and this test specifically catches attention degradation at the far end or middle of long contexts.

An advertised context-window size is a capacity claim, not a usage guarantee. This test is what verifies the model can actually retrieve information from anywhere in that window, which matters for any long-document use case.

A vendor advertising a large context window without publishing needle-in-a-haystack results at that length is making an unverified capacity claim; ask for the retrieval curve across the full advertised range before crediting the number.

terms.example: A retrieval check at 200 thousand tokens, with the fact buried mid-document.
terms.definition: A long-context test that plants one fact in a large document and asks the model to retrieve it. It validates that an advertised context window actually functions across its full length and at every depth.

lenses.body: Instead of asking the AI to write code once, this lets it try k times and checks if at least one attempt works. Trying ten times and succeeding once shows the ability exists, even if it is not reliable yet.

Pass@1 is what matters for a single-shot production feature; pass@10 or higher tells you whether the capability exists at all, which is the right metric when your system can sample multiple attempts and pick the best, such as an agent with a verifier.

The gap between pass@1 and pass@k for the same model is itself informative: a large gap indicates the model can solve the problem but is inconsistent, which points at sampling and search strategies rather than further pretraining as the fix.

terms.example: A model with modest pass@1 but strong pass@10, usable with retry loops.
terms.definition: The probability that at least one of k sampled attempts is correct, the standard code-generation metric. Pass@1 measures reliability; pass@10 measures whether the capability exists at all.

lenses.body: A score for how surprised the AI is by real text, lower meaning less surprised, which usually means it understood the pattern well. It is an old-school way to check training, not how helpful the AI actually is.
If a vendor cites perplexity as evidence of a better product, treat it as a training metric, not a usefulness claim; ask for task-based or preference-based evaluation results instead.

Still used during pretraining as a fast, cheap proxy for language modelling quality, but it is well established that lower perplexity does not reliably predict downstream task performance or human-judged helpfulness, so it is a training-time signal, not an evaluation of the finished assistant.

terms.example: Tracking perplexity on a validation set during pre-training.
terms.definition: A measure of how well a model predicts a text sample, lower being better. The classic language-modeling quality metric, still used in training but disconnected from downstream usefulness: a lower-perplexity model is not automatically a better assistant.

lenses.body: Precision is "of the things I flagged, how many were actually right." Recall is "of the things that were actually right, how many did I catch." A system can be great at one and bad at the other.

The tradeoff is tunable through the decision threshold, so the choice of operating point, not just model quality, determines which of precision or recall you get more of; report both, not just the one that flatters the system.

Whether you want higher precision or higher recall is a business decision about which error is more expensive, missing a real fraud case, or wrongly flagging a good customer, not a modeling decision, and it should be made explicitly rather than defaulted to.

A single accuracy figure can obscure a system that has high recall and low precision or the reverse; for any deployed detection or screening system, both figures should be reported and justified against the cost of each error type.

terms.example: Tuning a compliance monitor toward recall because misses cost more than false alarms.
terms.definition: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct; recall is the share of true cases found. Every detection system trades one against the other, and the right balance is a business decision, not a modeling one.

lenses.body: Running the exact same set of questions through an AI system every time something changes, to make sure it did not quietly get worse. Like re-checking your recipe still tastes right after switching one ingredient.

Essential given that provider-side model updates can silently change behaviour on a fixed API; a maintained regression suite with pinned expected outputs or scoring rubrics is the only reliable way to catch a quality regression before users do.

A silent quality drop after a vendor pushes a model update is a real and recurring risk. Ask whether your AI vendor or internal team runs a regression suite against every model version change, and what happens when it fails.

If you rely on an AI tool for a repeated task, keep a short list of test questions with known good answers and spot-check them occasionally. Vendors update their models without warning, and quality can shift.

terms.example: A nightly suite catching a tone shift after a model version bump.
terms.definition: Rerunning a fixed prompt suite after any change, model version, prompt edit, retrieval update, to detect quality loss. It guards against the silent regressions that provider model updates routinely introduce.

lenses.body: A way to check if an AI's summary shares the same important word-groups as a human's summary. It counts overlapping words, but two good summaries can use completely different words and both be right.

Useful for fast automated regression checks during development, but pair it with a faithfulness check, ideally a sample of human review or an entailment-based metric, before shipping a summarization feature, since ROUGE cannot catch a fluent but inaccurate summary.
Like BLEU, a legacy metric known to reward wording overlap over accuracy; a reported ROUGE improvement is not itself evidence that summaries became more faithful to their sources.

Like BLEU for translation, ROUGE is a standardized overlap metric for summarization, cheap to compute and blind to whether a summary is actually faithful to the source, so a high ROUGE score does not rule out a summary that misrepresents the original.

terms.example: Scoring summarizers in research papers before LLM-as-judge methods.
terms.definition: An overlap metric for summarization quality, counting shared n-grams between generated and reference summaries. Like BLEU, a legacy metric: standardized, cheap, and blind to whether the summary is actually faithful.

lenses.body: A coding test built from real bugs that real programmers actually reported on GitHub. The AI has to fix the bug well enough that the project's own tests pass, the same bar a human engineer would be held to.

The defining coding-agent benchmark because it measures end-to-end engineering against a repository's own test suite rather than isolated snippet generation, which is why leaderboard entries here report the specific agent scaffold used alongside the base model.

A high score here is closer to a real signal for "can this help with actual software maintenance" than most coding benchmarks, since it tests fixing real, previously unsolved issues rather than writing new small functions.

Because scores vary substantially by agent scaffold rather than model alone, comparing two reported SWE-bench numbers is only valid if the harness is comparable; a higher number from a heavier, more expensive scaffold is not a fair like-for-like comparison.

terms.origin: Jimenez et al., 2023.
terms.example: Coding agents ranked by percentage of real issues resolved.
terms.definition: A software engineering benchmark built from real GitHub issues: the model must produce a patch that passes the repository's own tests. It measures end-to-end engineering, not snippet writing, which made it the defining coding-agent benchmark.

lenses.body: A written rule book that says which AI tools employees are allowed to use, what kind of information they can put into them, and what tasks they can use AI for at work.

The baseline governance artifact for AI use, and one that provides zero protection if nobody has actually read it. A policy that exists only as a document is not a control; distribution and acknowledgment matter as much as the content.

A due-diligence checkpoint worth asking about directly: an AI-dependent company with no written AUP is operating without a basic governance artifact that most regulators and enterprise customers will eventually expect to see.

Even a short, one-page version covering which tools are okay, what customer data should never go into an AI tool, and who to ask before trying a new one is far better protection than having nothing written down.

terms.example: A one-page policy naming approved tools and the data classes barred from prompts.
terms.definition: The policy defining permitted and prohibited employee AI use: which tools, which data, which tasks. It is the baseline governance artifact, and an AUP nobody has read governs nothing.

lenses.body: How often people actually keep the AI's suggestion instead of ignoring it or writing their own. If people stop keeping the suggestions, that is a warning sign even before anyone stops using the tool completely.

The leading indicator worth tracking over the lagging one: a falling acceptance rate reveals eroding trust in the tool weeks or months before overall usage numbers actually decline, giving you time to investigate and fix the cause.

A more honest adoption signal than raw usage or seat counts for any assistive AI product; ask a vendor for acceptance rate trends specifically, since it is much harder to game favorably than a login count.

If your team has an AI writing or coding assistant, notice how often they actually use its suggestions versus ignoring them. A low or falling rate usually means the tool is not fitting how they actually work.

terms.example: Tracking what fraction of code-completion suggestions developers accept.
terms.definition: The share of AI suggestions users actually keep. It is the leading adoption indicator for assistive tools: a falling acceptance rate says the tool is losing the user's trust long before usage numbers drop.

lenses.body: Keeping track of how much money AI is costing a company and making sure that cost is actually worth what the company gets back from it, the same way businesses already track other spending.

Its unit is cost per outcome, not cost per token: what matters is what a resolved support ticket or a drafted contract actually costs end to end, not the raw API bill, which by itself tells you almost nothing about value.

A company with mature AI FinOps can tell you cost per resolved outcome; a company without it can usually only tell you total spend. The gap between those two answers is a real signal about operational maturity.
Even informally, try to connect your AI subscription costs to a specific outcome, cost per customer response, per document drafted, rather than just watching the monthly bill in isolation.

terms.origin: Extension of the FinOps Foundation discipline to AI workloads.
terms.example: A dashboard showing cost per resolved support ticket by model and team.
terms.definition: The discipline of tracking and optimizing AI spend against business value, extending cloud FinOps to inference costs. Its unit is cost per outcome, not cost per token: what matters is what a resolved ticket or drafted contract costs.

lenses.body: Everyone at a company understanding the basics of what AI can and cannot do well, and knowing the rules for using it, so people are not just guessing or assuming AI is either magic or useless.

No longer just good practice: under the EU AI Act it is now a legal requirement for providers and deployers, which means workforce AI literacy needs to be a documented, deliberate program rather than an assumed byproduct of tool rollout.

A company operating in or selling into the EU with AI-touching products should be able to demonstrate an AI literacy program as a compliance matter, not just a training nicety; its absence is a real regulatory gap worth flagging in diligence.

Make sure your team actually understands the basics: what the AI tool is good at, where it commonly gets things wrong, and what the rules are for using it. Assuming everyone already knows this is usually wrong.

terms.origin: EU AI Act Article 4, in force since February 2025.
terms.example: Annual training covering hallucination, data handling, and the approved-tool list.
terms.definition: Baseline workforce understanding of AI capability, limits, and policy: what the tools can do, where they fail, and what the rules are. Under the EU AI Act it is now a legal requirement for providers and deployers, not just good practice.

lenses.body: A way to rate how far along a company is with using AI well, from just messing around with it, all the way up to having it fully built into how the business actually runs.

Its value is diagnostic honesty: knowing accurately which stage your organization is actually at, rather than the stage leadership assumes or wants to be at, is what determines which investment actually makes sense next.

A useful diligence lens for any AI-forward company: ask them to self-assess against a maturity model rather than accepting a general claim of "we use AI extensively," since the two can diverge sharply.

Be honest with yourself about which stage you are actually at, early experimenting versus real embedded use, since that honesty determines whether your next investment should be more tools or better process around the tools you already have.

terms.example: A readiness assessment placing a firm at stage two of five, with a path to three.
terms.definition: A staged framework rating an organization from ad hoc experimentation to an embedded operating model. Its value is diagnostic honesty: knowing which stage you are actually at determines which investments make sense next.

lenses.body: When a company exaggerates how much AI is really in their product just to sound impressive to customers or investors, even though the actual AI part is small or barely there.

Now an active SEC enforcement target: regulators treat inflated AI claims the same as any other material misstatement to investors, which means marketing language about AI capability needs the same scrutiny as any other public claim about the business.

A real and growing enforcement risk worth checking directly: ask specifically what AI does in the product, how it was built, and whether that description would survive regulatory scrutiny, rather than accepting a general "AI-powered" claim.

If you market your business as "AI-powered," make sure that claim is honest and specific; overstating it is not just a reputational risk anymore, it is an enforcement risk regulators are actively pursuing.

terms.origin: SEC enforcement actions beginning 2024.
terms.example: Enforcement actions against firms claiming AI capabilities they did not have.
terms.definition: Overstating the AI content of a product or company to attract customers or capital. It is now an SEC enforcement target: regulators treat inflated AI claims the same as any other material misstatement.

lenses.body: The difference between AI doing a whole job by itself, replacing a person, versus AI just helping a person do their job faster or better while they still do it.

This distinction directly determines role design, headcount planning, and the change-management burden of any AI initiative; conflating the two in planning leads to either overpromising job elimination or underpreparing staff for genuine role change.

Ask an AI company specifically which side of this line their product sits on for its core workflow; a company claiming both full automation and easy adoption is often understating the change-management cost their customers will actually face.

Be clear with your team, and yourself, about which one you are actually implementing. Telling people a tool will "help them" when it is really designed to replace their task creates trust problems that are hard to undo.

terms.example: A decision to augment underwriters rather than automate underwriting.
terms.definition: The distinction between AI replacing a task outright and AI increasing a person's output on that task. The line determines role design, headcount planning, and the change-management burden of an initiative.

lenses.body: The choice a company faces between building its own AI system from scratch or just buying and using one that already exists from another company.

Complicated specifically by AI's pace of change: a capability that only a custom build could deliver last year may ship as a standard product feature this year, which means a build decision needs to account for how fast the vendor market is likely to catch up.

Ask a company defending a build decision whether they have re-evaluated it recently against current vendor offerings; a build choice that was correct eighteen months ago may now represent unnecessary ongoing engineering cost.

For almost any small business, buying an existing AI tool is the right call over building your own; the pace of change in this space makes a custom build a maintenance burden most small teams cannot sustain.

terms.example: Choosing a vendor contract-review tool over an internal build after pricing the maintenance.
terms.definition: The decision between developing an AI capability in house and licensing a vendor solution. The standard portfolio decision, complicated by AI's pace: what only a custom build could do last year ships as a product feature this year.

lenses.body: Splitting work between a person and an AI so each one does the part they are actually best at: the AI handles scale and remembering lots of information, the person handles judgment and takes responsibility for the final decision.

Named for the chess format where human-computer teams beat both grandmasters and engines playing alone; the useful management lesson is that the best combination is rarely "most AI" or "most human," it is a deliberate split by comparative advantage.

A well-designed centaur workflow, where the split between AI scale and human judgment is deliberate rather than accidental, is usually a better indicator of durable operational quality than a claim of "fully autonomous AI."

Think about which parts of a task the AI genuinely does better, handling volume, remembering details, and which parts a person should still own, judgment calls, relationships, final responsibility, rather than assuming AI should do as much as possible.

terms.origin: From advanced chess, popularized by Garry Kasparov in the late 1990s.
terms.example: An analyst directing AI research sweeps, then making the recommendation personally.
terms.definition: A division of labor where human and AI split work by comparative advantage: machine scale and recall paired with human judgment and accountability. Named for the chess format where human-computer teams beat both grandmasters and engines.

lenses.body: A central team inside a company whose job is to set the rules and provide the tools for AI, while the rest of the company actually uses AI to do their work day to day.

The hub-and-spoke model balances consistency against speed, and drifts toward becoming a bottleneck when the hub tries to do the work itself rather than enabling business units to do it; watch for that drift as a specific warning sign.

Ask whether a company's AI CoE is an enabling function, providing standards and tooling, or a gatekeeping bottleneck that every AI initiative has to pass through; the second pattern predicts slower adoption than the org chart suggests.

At smaller scale, this can just mean one person whose job includes keeping AI tool choices consistent and sharing what works across the team, rather than everyone experimenting independently with no coordination.

terms.example: A CoE publishing the golden path while product teams build on it.
terms.definition: A central team setting AI standards, tooling, and enablement while business units execute. The hub-and-spoke operating model that balances consistency against speed, and drifts toward bottleneck when the hub tries to do rather than enable.

lenses.body: Helping people actually change how they work, what their job involves, and how they are rewarded, when a company starts using AI, since just giving people a new tool does not automatically change how they do their job.

The actual constraint on ROI in most AI initiatives: the technology usually works reasonably well, and the organization around it has not changed enough to actually capture the value, which means underinvesting here is the most common cause of a disappointing return.

A company reporting strong AI capability but weak realized ROI is often describing a change-management failure, not a technology failure; worth probing whether roles, incentives, and workflows actually changed alongside the tool rollout.

Rolling out a new AI tool without talking to your team about how their actual job and daily habits need to change is the most common reason adoption fails; the tool alone rarely does the work of changing behavior.

terms.example: Redesigning review workflows and incentives alongside the tool deployment.
terms.definition: The structured approach to shifting behavior, roles, and incentives during AI rollout. It is the actual constraint on ROI: the technology usually works, and the organization around it usually has not changed enough to capture the value.

lenses.body: An AI helper built right into software you already use, that suggests things for you to accept or reject, rather than doing the whole job on its own without asking.

The dominant enterprise adoption pattern precisely because it upgrades an existing workflow rather than replacing it, which lowers the change-management burden compared to a standalone tool that requires people to adopt an entirely new process.

Copilot-style products generally see faster and less contested adoption than fully autonomous alternatives, since they preserve human control and existing habits; worth weighing that adoption-speed advantage against the smaller efficiency ceiling compared to full automation.

A copilot-style tool embedded in software you already use is usually easier for a small team to adopt than a standalone AI product, since it fits into existing habits rather than requiring a new workflow to learn.

terms.origin: Popularized by GitHub Copilot, 2021.
terms.example: A coding copilot completing functions inside the developer's editor.
terms.definition: An AI assistant integrated directly into existing software, suggesting rather than acting autonomously. The dominant enterprise adoption pattern because it upgrades a workflow without replacing it.

lenses.body: A rule that certain data has to physically stay stored and processed in a specific country or region, which limits which AI companies and tools you are even allowed to use for that data.

Directly constrains model and provider choice: a capability that only runs in a data center outside the required jurisdiction is a capability the regulated workload simply cannot use, regardless of how good the model itself is.

A company operating under strict data residency requirements has a narrower vendor selection than one without; worth checking whether their AI stack was chosen with this constraint in mind or retrofitted after the fact.

If you handle data subject to residency requirements, like certain healthcare or financial information, check specifically where an AI vendor actually processes and stores data before adopting it, not just where the company is headquartered.

terms.example: Choosing an EU-region deployment to keep customer data inside the jurisdiction.
terms.definition: The requirement that data be stored and processed within a specific jurisdiction. It constrains model and provider choice directly: a capability that only runs in another region is a capability the regulated workload cannot use.

lenses.body: How many customer questions an AI support system fully solves on its own, without a human needing to step in. But solving a problem badly and having it come back later does not really count as success.

The core support-AI metric, and one that specifically punishes gaming: a deflection that leaves the underlying problem unresolved returns as an escalation or churn later, so a high deflection rate paired with rising churn is a warning sign, not a win.

Ask for deflection rate alongside downstream churn and re-contact rate, not in isolation; a vendor reporting an impressive standalone deflection number without those companion metrics may be reporting a gamed statistic.

Track not just how many support questions your AI handles alone, but whether those customers come back with the same problem later. A high deflection number paired with repeat complaints means the AI is closing tickets, not solving problems.

terms.example: A support bot resolving six of ten contacts end to end, measured by no-reopen rates.
terms.definition: The share of support contacts fully resolved without a human. The core support-AI metric, and one that punishes gaming: deflection that leaves problems unresolved returns as escalation and churn.

lenses.body: Thinking about AI helpers as buying finished work, like a certain number of solved customer problems, instead of just buying software licenses that a person still has to use.

Reshapes budgeting and vendor pricing directly: you are buying resolved tickets or processed claims, not licenses, which means procurement and financial planning need a different model than traditional software spend, closer to outsourced labor cost than SaaS subscription cost.

A vendor pricing on this model is making an implicit claim about reliability, since outcome-based pricing only works if the AI genuinely completes the work; ask what happens, financially, when it does not.

If a vendor offers to price their AI service based on results delivered rather than a flat subscription, that can be a good deal, but check what counts as a completed result and what happens when the AI gets it wrong.

terms.origin: Emerging vendor pricing model, 2024 onward.
terms.example: A vendor quoting per-resolution pricing instead of per-seat subscriptions.
terms.definition: The framing of AI agents as capacity purchased in units of work rather than software seats. It reshapes budgeting and vendor pricing: you buy resolved tickets or processed claims, not licenses.

lenses.body: Connecting an AI to a company's own real information, like its documents and records, so its answers are based on actual company facts instead of general knowledge that might not apply.

Where most enterprise AI value actually sits, and also where most of the integration cost sits; a model with no connection to internal systems of record can only ever give generic answers, however capable the underlying model is.

Ask specifically how a company's AI product connects to internal data sources; a product with strong model capability but weak grounding infrastructure will underdeliver in practice compared to its benchmark performance.

A generic AI chatbot cannot answer questions about your specific business unless it is connected to your actual documents and records. Ask any AI tool vendor exactly how that connection works before expecting company-specific answers.

terms.example: An assistant answering from the firm's own contracts and policies, with citations.
terms.definition: Connecting a model to internal systems of record so its answers reflect company data rather than general knowledge. It is where most enterprise value sits, and most integration cost.

lenses.body: The official, supported, easy way for teams inside a company to build things with AI, using approved tools and safety rules already set up for them. Making the safe way also the easy way stops people from going around it.

Reduces shadow AI more effectively than prohibition, because it makes the sanctioned route the easiest route; a governance approach relying purely on rules against unapproved tools, without an easy approved alternative, predictably fails as people route around friction.

A company with a well-adopted golden path has effectively solved much of its shadow AI risk through design rather than enforcement, which is a more durable and scalable solution than policy alone; worth asking whether one exists and how widely it is actually used.

If you want your team to use AI safely, make the safe, approved option also the easiest and most convenient one to use. Rules alone rarely beat convenience when people are trying to get work done quickly.

terms.origin: Platform-engineering vocabulary, notably from Spotify.
terms.example: A platform team shipping templates that make the compliant architecture the default.
terms.definition: The approved and supported way to build AI applications internally: sanctioned models, patterns, and guardrails packaged for teams. A good golden path reduces shadow AI more effectively than prohibition, because it makes the sanctioned route the easiest route.

lenses.body: How much it costs, in people's time, to check and fix what AI produces before it is used. If checking and fixing takes a long time by a highly paid person, that cost can cancel out the time AI saved.

Heavy review can erase ROI entirely: an AI that drafts in seconds but requires an hour of senior review may cost more in total than the manual process it replaced, which is why review cost must be included in any honest AI cost calculation.

Ask any AI vendor's ROI claim to include the reviewer time and seniority required to check the output; a fast-generation claim without this figure is systematically understating the real total cost of the workflow.

Factor in the real cost of the time your team spends reviewing and correcting AI output, especially if that review requires someone senior or specialized, before concluding the tool is actually saving you money.

terms.example: A contract pipeline repriced after counting reviewer hours per document.
terms.definition: The labor cost of reviewing and correcting AI output. Heavy review erases ROI: an AI that drafts in seconds but requires senior review in hours may cost more than the process it replaced.

lenses.body: The strange pattern where AI is amazing at one task but bad at another task that seems almost identical. It explains why AI can feel brilliant one moment and frustrating the next, doing similar-looking things.

Explains inconsistent user experience directly, and is the reason task-level piloting beats general intuition for deciding what to deploy; two seemingly similar tasks can sit on opposite sides of this uneven capability boundary, so test the specific task, not the category.

A company assuming AI capability generalizes smoothly across similar tasks is likely to be surprised by this unevenness in production; ask whether their deployment decisions were based on task-specific piloting or general capability assumptions.

Do not assume that because AI is great at one task, it will be equally good at a similar-seeming one. Test each specific task you actually want to use it for; capability does not generalize as smoothly as it seems like it should.

terms.origin: Coined in the 2023 Harvard Business School and BCG field study of consultant AI use.
terms.example: A model acing complex analysis while fumbling a simple formatting request.
terms.definition: The uneven capability boundary where AI excels at some tasks and fails at adjacent, seemingly similar ones. It explains inconsistent user experience and why task-level piloting beats intuition for deciding what to deploy.

lenses.body: When lots of different AI tools get adopted by different teams across a company with nobody keeping track, leading to wasted money, duplicated work, and no clear picture of what AI the company is even using.

Drives cost and duplicates spend directly, and makes producing a defensible AI inventory impossible until consolidated; an organization cannot govern, secure, or accurately cost what it has not centrally tracked, which is the practical reason sprawl matters beyond tidiness.

A company with significant model sprawl cannot give you an accurate AI cost or risk picture in diligence, which is itself informative; the sprawl is often evidence of weak overall operational governance, not just a tooling inefficiency.

Periodically ask each team what AI tools they are actually using; you may discover more overlapping subscriptions and unmanaged tools than you expected, which usually means wasted spend and unclear risk.

terms.example: An audit finding four departments running four overlapping AI subscriptions.
terms.definition: The uncontrolled proliferation of models and AI tools across an organization, each adopted locally and governed nowhere. It drives cost, duplicates spend, and makes a defensible AI inventory impossible until consolidated.

lenses.body: Paying for AI based on what it actually accomplishes, like each problem it solves, instead of paying a flat fee no matter how well it works. It puts more of the risk on the company selling the AI, not the one buying it.

Vendors adopt this model where outcomes are reliably countable, resolved support tickets, qualified leads, and it shifts real performance risk from buyer to vendor, which is a meaningfully different commercial relationship than a traditional seat-based license.

A vendor confident enough in their product to price on outcomes rather than seats is making a credible signal about their own belief in reliability; conversely, a reluctance to offer outcome pricing where outcomes are clearly countable is worth asking about directly.

If a vendor offers to charge you per result delivered instead of a flat subscription, and your use case has clearly countable outcomes, that can be a genuinely lower-risk deal for you; just be clear on exactly how a successful outcome is defined and verified.

terms.example: A support-AI contract billing per ticket the AI fully resolves.
terms.definition: Charging per resolved task or achieved result instead of per seat or per token. Vendors adopt it where outcomes are countable, support resolutions, qualified leads, and it shifts performance risk from buyer to vendor.

lenses.body: A company announcing big AI plans and putting out press releases about it, without actually changing how anyone works day to day. It looks like progress, but nothing real is different.

Activity without outcomes: the press release ships, the operating model does not, and the value never arrives. Distinguish genuine adoption from this pattern by checking whether roles, incentives, or decision rights actually changed, not just whether an announcement was made.

A company's AI narrative should be checked against operational evidence, changed workflows, measured outcomes, altered incentive structures, rather than accepted at the level of press releases and stated strategy, since the two frequently diverge.

Announcing that your business "uses AI now" without actually changing how work gets done does not create value; it just creates a claim. Make sure the announcement is backed by a real, specific change in a process.

terms.example: An "AI-first" announcement followed by unchanged processes a year later.
terms.definition: Announcing AI initiatives without changing workflows, incentives, or decision rights. Activity without outcomes: the press release ships, the operating model does not, and the value never arrives.

lenses.body: When a company keeps starting new AI test projects, but none of them ever actually become real, permanent parts of the business. Lots of experiments, nothing sticks.

The dominant enterprise AI failure mode, and it is usually rooted in a specific cause: pilots designed to demonstrate a capability rather than to actually integrate into a real workflow. Design every pilot with a defined path to production from the outset, or expect it to stall here.

A high count of AI pilots with a low count of production deployments is a red flag worth probing directly; it usually indicates pilots were designed for demonstration rather than integration, which predicts continued stalling rather than eventual breakthrough.

If you have tried several AI tools that never became a real, ongoing part of how your team works, the problem is likely how the pilots were set up, not the tools themselves. Design the next one with a specific plan for what "success" actually means and what happens after.

terms.example: Twelve proofs of concept, zero production deployments, two years running.
terms.definition: The condition where AI pilots multiply but none reach production. The dominant enterprise failure mode, usually rooted in pilots designed to demonstrate rather than to integrate.

lenses.body: A small test to check whether an idea can even technically work, before spending a lot more time and money on it. It answers "can this be done," not "will this actually work well for us."

Answers "can this work" technically, which is a genuinely different and easier question than "will this work here" operationally, the question the follow-on pilot must actually answer; treating a successful POC as proof of business readiness is a common and costly mistake.

A successful POC alone is weak evidence of business viability; ask whether it was followed by a real operational pilot answering the harder question of fit within actual workflows, incentives, and scale.

A proof of concept just tells you the technology can technically do the thing; it does not tell you it will fit well into how your business actually operates. Do not skip the next step of testing it in a real, if small, part of your actual workflow.

terms.example: A two-week POC confirming extraction accuracy on real documents.
terms.definition: A small, scoped test validating technical feasibility before larger investment. It answers "can this work," which is a different question from "will this work here," the question the pilot must answer next.

lenses.body: Breaking a whole job down into its smaller individual pieces to figure out which pieces AI can actually help with, since a whole job is rarely something AI can do entirely, but specific tasks inside it often are.

The basis of honest adoption planning: jobs are rarely automatable as a whole, tasks within them often are, and this split determines the real available opportunity, which is usually smaller and more specific than an initial "automate this role" framing suggests.

A company describing AI opportunity at the job level rather than the task level is likely overstating the addressable opportunity; ask for the task-level breakdown to get a more grounded picture of what is actually automatable.

Instead of asking "can AI do this person's job," break the job into its individual tasks and ask which specific tasks AI can genuinely help with. The realistic opportunity is almost always at the task level, not the whole-job level.

terms.example: Decomposing a paralegal role into twenty tasks and finding eight AI-suitable.
terms.definition: Breaking a job into constituent tasks to identify which are AI-suitable. The basis of honest adoption planning: jobs are rarely automatable, tasks often are, and the split determines the real opportunity.

lenses.body: How long it takes from starting an AI project to actually seeing a real business benefit from it. A project that pays off quickly is worth more than one that takes years, even if they eventually deliver the same total benefit.

A key portfolio filter for comparing initiatives: two projects with equal eventual returns are not equal if one pays back in a quarter and the other in two years, since the faster one frees capital and builds organizational confidence sooner.
Ask for time to value alongside total expected return on any AI initiative; a long payback period carries real opportunity cost and execution risk that a headline ROI figure alone does not capture.

When choosing between AI projects to invest in, favor ones that will show a real benefit quickly over ones that promise a bigger payoff far in the future; faster feedback lets you course-correct before too much is spent.

terms.example: Prioritizing the document-automation project that shows returns within one quarter.
terms.definition: The elapsed time from project start to measurable business benefit. A key portfolio filter: two projects with equal returns are not equal if one pays back in a quarter and the other in two years.

lenses.body: A spending limit set for how much a team is allowed to use an AI tool, so costs do not spiral out of control without anyone noticing or being responsible for it.

Converts open-ended, unpredictable inference cost into a governed resource with a named owner; without an explicit budget, AI spend tends to grow silently until it surfaces as a surprising line item, rather than being actively managed like other operating costs.
A company without any form of token or usage budgeting for its AI spend is likely to show volatile and hard-to-forecast costs as usage scales; ask specifically how AI spend is governed and by whom.

Set a clear spending limit for your AI tool usage and check it periodically, the same way you would monitor any other recurring business expense, rather than letting it run unmonitored until the bill surprises you.

terms.example: A monthly token allocation per team, with alerts at 80 percent.
terms.definition: An allocated spend ceiling on model usage for a team or workload, the FinOps control for AI. Budgets convert open-ended inference cost into a governed resource with an owner.

lenses.body: The real price of something is not just what it cost to buy. It is also what you spend keeping it working, year after year.

The full cost of an AI capability over its life: licences and compute, but also integration, data preparation, evaluation, monitoring, human review, retraining and the eventual migration off it. Pilots are usually priced on the first item only, which is why the production bill so often surprises the sponsor.

What separates a reported gross margin from a durable one. Ask what is excluded from cost of revenue, particularly human review, evaluation and support, since those often sit in operating expense while being functionally part of delivering the product, and they do not fall with scale the way compute does.

Add up more than the monthly subscription: the hours spent learning it, cleaning up its mistakes, and the cost of the work not done while you set it up. A cheaper tool that needs constant correction is usually the more expensive one.

terms.example: A TCO model where human review and integration dwarf the model bill.
terms.definition: The full lifetime cost of an AI capability: inference, integration, oversight labor, evaluation, and retraining. Routinely understated because the visible API price is the smallest line.

lenses.body: Rebuilding how a job actually gets done around what AI is good at, instead of just bolting AI onto the old way of doing things. Just adding AI to a bad process usually just makes the bad process happen faster.

Where the real gains actually come from: automating a bad process yields a faster bad process, not a better one. The organizations capturing the most AI value are the ones willing to redesign the workflow itself, not just insert AI into an unchanged process.

A company layering AI onto unchanged legacy workflows will show smaller and less durable gains than one that redesigned the workflow around AI capability; ask which approach they actually took before crediting a reported efficiency number.

Before adding AI to a process, ask whether the process itself should change now that AI is available, rather than just inserting AI into the exact same steps you used before. The redesign is usually where the real benefit is.

terms.example: Collapsing a five-handoff approval chain once AI handles the assembly steps.
terms.definition: Rebuilding a process around AI capabilities rather than layering AI onto the existing process. It is where the real gains come from: automating a bad process yields a faster bad process.

lenses.body: A promise from an AI company that they will not keep or store what you send them or what they respond with, once they are done processing it, so your information does not sit around in their system afterward.

A common enterprise contract term, and one worth verifying against the vendor's actual technical architecture rather than accepting on the strength of the sales deck alone; ask for the specific technical mechanism that enforces it, not just the contractual promise.

A vendor offering ZDR as a contractual term without being able to describe the technical enforcement mechanism is making a promise that is harder to actually verify; worth probing this gap directly in any diligence involving sensitive customer data.

If data privacy matters for your use case, ask any AI vendor specifically how zero data retention is technically enforced, not just whether they offer it as a contract clause; a vague answer is a reason for caution.

terms.example: A ZDR clause negotiated before routing client data through a model API.
terms.definition: A vendor commitment not to store prompts or outputs after processing completes. A common enterprise contract term, and one worth verifying against the vendor's actual architecture rather than the sales deck.

lenses.body: A recipe of exact steps a computer follows to solve a problem, like a set of instructions for making a sandwich, but for math or decisions instead of food.

Choice of learning algorithm shapes what the resulting model can express and how much data it needs, independent of the specific dataset; picking one is an architectural decision worth documenting alongside hyperparameters.

When someone says "the algorithm decided," ask which one: the training algorithm that built the model, or the model itself making a prediction. The distinction matters for accountability, since they fail differently and are fixed differently.

In machine learning specifically, the algorithm is the recipe for learning from data, while the model is what that recipe produces after training. People often use the words interchangeably, but they mean different things.

terms.example: Gradient descent and decision trees are algorithms; a trained classifier is their output.
terms.definition: A set of step-by-step rules or instructions a computer follows to solve a problem or perform a calculation. In machine learning the algorithm is the recipe for learning from data; the model is what the recipe produces.

lenses.body: Teaching a computer what "normal" looks like so it can spot when something unusual happens, like a security guard who does not need photos of every possible burglar, just a good sense of what normal looks like.

Quality depends heavily on how well "normal" is modeled for your specific data distribution; a model trained on one system's normal traffic will flag legitimate but unfamiliar patterns on another, so retrain or recalibrate per deployment rather than reusing a generic model.

Valuable specifically because it catches novel threats that no one has labeled before, unlike systems trained on known attack patterns; the tradeoff is a higher false-positive rate that needs a real review process behind it.

The workhorse of fraud and intrusion detection precisely because it does not require examples of every possible attack, only a good model of normal behavior, which is a meaningfully different and more tractable learning problem than classifying known attack types.

terms.example: A monitoring system flagging a login pattern no employee has ever produced.
terms.definition: Identifying data points that deviate materially from expected patterns. It is the workhorse of fraud and intrusion detection precisely because it does not need examples of every attack, only a good model of normal.

lenses.body: A made-up-so-far kind of AI that could learn and understand anything a person can, not just one specific skill. Nobody agrees exactly when we would know it had actually arrived.

As an engineering term it is nearly useless, since there is no benchmark that constitutes proof of arrival; focus technical roadmaps on specific, measurable capabilities rather than progress toward an undefined destination.

Treat any vendor claim about AGI timelines with real skepticism, since there is no industry-agreed definition or test; a specific, falsifiable capability claim is more useful for planning than a prediction about AGI arrival.
