Anchors both investment theses and safety debates despite the absence of an agreed test for its arrival, which is worth noting whenever the term appears in a headline: "AGI" claims vary enormously in what they actually mean by different speakers.

terms.origin: Term popularized by Ben Goertzel and Shane Legg, early 2000s.
terms.example: Lab mission statements and policy debates organized around reaching or governing AGI.
terms.definition: Hypothetical AI able to understand, learn, and apply knowledge across any intellectual task at or above human level. The term anchors both investment theses and safety debates, despite no agreed test for when it has arrived.

lenses.body: The whole area of computer science about building machines that can do things that normally need human smarts, like understanding language, recognizing pictures, or making decisions.

Prefer the specific subfield term, machine learning, NLP, computer vision, over the umbrella "AI" whenever precision matters, since the broad term obscures which techniques, failure modes, and evaluation methods actually apply.

"We use AI" is rarely a useful statement on its own, since the term spans everything from a simple recommendation algorithm to a frontier language model; ask what specific capability, within this broad field, is actually being used.

The umbrella term over everything in this glossary: machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and more all sit inside AI as a field, which is why "AI" alone is often too broad a term to be useful in a specific technical discussion.

terms.origin: Term coined by John McCarthy for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.
terms.example: Machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision are all AI subfields.
terms.definition: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions. The umbrella over machine learning, NLP, and everything else in this glossary.

lenses.body: An imaginary future AI that would be way smarter than any human at literally everything, including things like creativity and understanding people's feelings, not just facts and math.

Not a term with engineering relevance to current systems; if it appears in a technical conversation about your actual work, it is usually a sign the discussion has drifted from the concrete system in front of you.

A useful concept for understanding why some safety researchers focus on long-horizon risks, but not a near-term planning consideration for most businesses; treat ASI discussion as context for the field's safety culture, not as an operational timeline.

Matters less as a near-term forecast than as the scenario that motivates much of long-horizon AI safety research; understanding the concept helps make sense of why some researchers focus heavily on control and alignment problems that seem premature for today's systems.

terms.origin: Popularized by Nick Bostrom's "Superintelligence," 2014.
terms.example: The endpoint scenario debated in existential-risk literature.
terms.definition: A hypothetical form of AI far surpassing human intelligence in every field, including creativity, wisdom, and social skill. It matters less as a forecast than as the scenario that motivates much of long-horizon safety research.

lenses.body: Turning spoken words into written text, like when your phone writes down what you say instead of you typing it. It has gotten really good, especially in quiet rooms.

Test against your actual audio conditions, not clean benchmark data; accent coverage, background noise, and overlapping speech are the common failure modes that a vendor's headline word-error-rate number will not reveal.

Accuracy in the demo and accuracy in your actual environment can differ substantially; background noise, accents, and cross-talk in real meetings all degrade performance from the clean-condition numbers vendors typically advertise.

Modern ASR approaches human transcription accuracy in clean audio conditions, which is specifically what made features like automatic meeting transcription and reliable voice interfaces practical rather than a novelty.

terms.example: A meeting tool producing a searchable transcript in real time.
terms.definition: Converting spoken audio into text. Modern ASR approaches human transcription accuracy in clean conditions, which is what made meeting transcription and voice interfaces routine.

lenses.body: A famous idea in AI: over and over, giving a computer more raw computing power and letting it figure things out itself has beaten trying to hand-teach it clever human tricks and shortcuts.

Worth weighing before investing heavily in hand-crafted features or domain-specific architecture tweaks; historically, that engineering effort has often been outcompeted within a few years by a larger, more general model trained on more data.

Explains why scale, more compute, more data, has consistently outcompeted clever domain-specific engineering in AI research; useful context for why leading labs keep investing in larger training runs rather than smarter, smaller architectures alone.

Drawn from roughly seventy years of AI history as an empirical pattern rather than a theoretical proof, it is cited to justify betting research effort on scale over hand-engineered features, and the pattern has continued to hold as models have grown larger.

terms.origin: Rich Sutton, "The Bitter Lesson," 2019.
terms.example: Choosing a bigger general model over a hand-tuned domain pipeline.
terms.definition: The argument that general methods leveraging computation beat hand-crafted domain knowledge over time, drawn from seventy years of AI history. It is cited to justify betting on scale over feature engineering, and it has aged well.

lenses.body: The part of AI that lets computers understand pictures and video: finding objects in a photo, reading text in an image, or tracking something moving across a video.

Benchmark against your actual deployment conditions, lighting, camera angle, image quality, since published accuracy figures typically come from curated datasets that do not reflect the noise of a real physical environment.

A mature, well-understood technology with a long production track record, distinct from the newer generative AI wave; vendors sometimes blur the two in marketing, so it is worth asking specifically which type of vision capability is being sold.

One of the earliest AI capabilities to reach industrial reliability, well before large language models existed; object detection and optical character recognition were solved to a production-usable standard years before generative AI became mainstream.

terms.example: Defect detection on a production line running at camera frame rate.
terms.definition: The field enabling machines to interpret images and video: detecting objects, reading documents, tracking motion. One of the earliest AI capabilities to reach industrial reliability.

lenses.body: A big organized collection of information or examples used to teach and test an AI, like a giant set of flashcards it studies from and gets quizzed on.

Document dataset provenance, composition, and known gaps as you would document any other dependency; a model's failure modes are usually explainable by looking at what was underrepresented or absent from its training and evaluation data.

Ask what a model was actually trained and evaluated on before trusting a capability claim; a model that performs well on one dataset can perform poorly on your specific data if the two differ meaningfully in composition.

Its composition quietly determines what the model can and cannot do; a dataset skewed toward certain examples produces a model skewed the same way, which is why dataset documentation is treated as a governance artifact rather than mere technical housekeeping.

terms.example: ImageNet for vision; Common Crawl for language pre-training.
terms.definition: A structured collection of data used to train, evaluate, and test models. Its composition quietly determines what the model can and cannot do, which makes dataset documentation a governance artifact, not housekeeping.

lenses.body: A type of machine learning that uses many stacked layers of simple math units to learn patterns directly from raw information, instead of a person having to tell it what to look for.

Deep architectures trade interpretability for representation power; if your use case genuinely needs explainability, weigh that tradeoff explicitly rather than defaulting to a deep model because it is the current default choice.

The engine behind image recognition, speech systems, and large language models; when a vendor says "deep learning," it signals a specific class of neural-network technique, distinct from older, simpler statistical methods still used for many business forecasting tasks.

The key distinction from earlier machine learning is that deep networks learn their own useful representations from raw data rather than relying on hand-built features a person designed in advance, which is what let the same basic approach scale across images, speech, and text.

terms.example: A deep network learning edge, texture, and object concepts from pixels alone.
terms.definition: A subset of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers, which learn their own representations from raw data rather than relying on hand-built features. It is the engine behind image recognition, speech, and large language models.

lenses.body: A live computer copy of a real machine or process, kept updated with real data, so you can test changes safely on the computer version before trying them on the real thing.

Fidelity to the real system is the whole value proposition; a digital twin that drifts from the actual physical asset's current state produces simulations that are confidently wrong, so keep the data feed current and validate against reality regularly.

Valuable specifically for high-cost, high-risk physical operations where testing a change directly is expensive or dangerous; the ROI case depends heavily on how costly real-world failures actually are in your specific operation.

Lets an operator test changes in software before risking them in the physical world, which is the entire economic case for building one: the cost of a failed simulation is near zero compared to the cost of a failed real-world experiment.

terms.example: Simulating a production-line change on the twin before touching the floor.
terms.definition: A live virtual model of a physical asset or process, fed by real data and used for simulation and optimization. It lets an operator test changes in software before risking them in steel.

lenses.body: AI that sorts or labels things that already exist, like deciding if an email is spam or not, rather than AI that creates brand new things like pictures or stories.

Simpler to evaluate than generative systems, since correctness is usually well-defined; standard classification metrics, precision, recall, F1, apply cleanly, which is one reason discriminative models remain the default choice for well-specified decision tasks.

Most of your organization's existing, revenue-relevant AI is probably discriminative, classification, scoring, prediction, even if recent AI conversations have focused almost entirely on generative tools; do not let the newer category crowd out attention to the older, still-valuable one.

The quiet majority of production AI: most deployed models decide rather than create, which is worth remembering given how much current public attention focuses on generative AI specifically; discriminative models quietly run fraud detection, recommendation, and classification at enormous scale.

terms.example: Spam classification and sentiment analysis running billions of times daily.
terms.definition: Models that classify existing data or predict labels rather than generating new content. The quiet majority of production AI: most deployed models decide, they do not create.

lenses.body: AI that controls a real physical body, like a robot, using cameras and sensors to see and touch the world. It is much harder than AI that only works with text or pictures on a screen, because real mistakes have real consequences.

Physical mistakes are not undoable the way a bad text output is; safety margins, fallback behaviors, and human override capability need to be designed in from the start, not added after a capability demo succeeds in controlled conditions.

Treat robotics and physical-AI capability claims with more caution than digital-AI claims; the gap between demo conditions and reliable real-world physical performance is currently much wider than for text or image-based AI.

The gap between digital and embodied performance remains one of the field's most stubborn frontiers; a model that reasons brilliantly in text can fail badly at simple physical manipulation, since physical dexterity and real-world sensor noise are qualitatively different problems than digital pattern matching.

terms.example: Warehouse picking robots handling variable, cluttered objects.
terms.definition: AI operating through a physical body, tied to sensors and actuators, where mistakes have physics. The gap between digital and embodied performance remains one of the field's most stubborn frontiers.

lenses.body: A skill that a computer suddenly gets good at only once it reaches a certain size, a skill that smaller versions of the same computer just could not do at all, not even a little bit.

Do not assume a capability absent at one model scale will remain absent at the next; conversely, do not assume scale alone reliably delivers a specific needed capability. Test the actual model you plan to deploy rather than extrapolating from a smaller version.

A reason to treat capability forecasts with humility in both directions: a new model scale can unlock unexpected new abilities, and it can also fail to deliver an expected one, since the relationship between scale and specific capability is not fully predictable in advance.

Emergence is precisely why capability forecasting is hard: the next step up in model scale may unlock an ability nobody specifically trained for or predicted, which means capability roadmaps built purely on extrapolating current trends can miss genuinely new behaviors.

terms.origin: Wei et al., 2022, "Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models."
terms.example: Multi-step arithmetic appearing abruptly as model size crossed a threshold.
terms.definition: A skill that appears only above a certain model scale and was absent in smaller versions. Emergence is why capability forecasting is hard: the next scale step may unlock abilities nobody planned for.

lenses.body: An early kind of AI where people wrote out lots of "if this, then that" rules based on what human experts knew, for one narrow area like diagnosing a specific kind of car problem.

Rule-based logic is not obsolete, it remains the right choice for narrow, well-understood domains where explainability matters more than handling edge cases; the lesson from expert systems is about scaling to messy, broad domains, not about rules being universally inferior.

A useful historical reference point when evaluating a modern AI pitch: if a "smart" system is actually a large set of hand-written if-then rules rather than a learned model, it will inherit the same brittleness that limited expert systems decades ago.

Carries the field's founding lesson in its rise and stall: hand-written rules do not scale to the messiness of the real world, which is a large part of why the field later shifted toward learning patterns from data instead of encoding human-written logic directly.

terms.origin: Dominant AI paradigm of the 1970s and 1980s.
terms.example: MYCIN recommending antibiotics from encoded clinical rules in the 1970s.
terms.definition: Early AI that encoded human expert rules into if-then logic for a narrow domain. Its rise and stall carry the field's founding lesson: hand-written rules do not scale to the messiness of the real world.

lenses.body: Training one shared AI across lots of separate devices or locations without ever moving the actual private data to one central place; only what the AI learned gets shared, not the raw information itself.

The engineering overhead is real: coordinating training across decentralized, unreliable devices with intermittent connectivity is materially harder than centralized training, so weigh that cost honestly against the privacy or residency benefit before committing to this approach.

Worth investigating specifically for use cases involving sensitive or regulated data that cannot legally or practically be centralized; it is a real technical option, not just a compliance talking point, though it does add real engineering complexity to weigh against the benefit.

Trades meaningful engineering complexity for genuine privacy and data-residency advantages; the underlying data literally never leaves its original location, which is a structurally different privacy guarantee than data being collected centrally and then protected with access controls.

terms.origin: Google, 2016.
terms.example: Phone keyboards improving prediction from usage that never leaves the device.
terms.definition: Training a shared model across decentralized devices without moving raw data to a central server; only model updates travel. It trades engineering complexity for privacy and residency advantages.

lenses.body: One huge AI that gets trained once on a massive amount of information, and then gets adjusted cheaply many different ways to do lots of different specific jobs, instead of building a brand new AI from scratch for each job.

Fine-tuning or prompting a foundation model is almost always cheaper and faster than training from scratch; reserve from-scratch training for cases where the foundation model's pretraining data or architecture genuinely does not fit your domain.

Most AI products you buy are built on top of someone else's foundation model rather than a custom-trained one, which is usually the right choice; ask a vendor whether their capability comes from the foundation model itself or from what they built on top of it.

The economic logic is amortization: one enormous, expensive training run gets adapted cheaply a thousand different ways downstream, which is what makes the huge upfront training cost of a foundation model economically viable across an entire industry of applications built on top of it.

terms.origin: Term coined by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, 2021.
terms.example: GPT, Claude, and Llama serving as bases for countless products.
terms.definition: A large model trained on broad data at scale that serves as the base for many downstream tasks. The economic point is amortization: one enormous training run, adapted cheaply a thousand ways.

lenses.body: One of the very newest, most powerful AI models that exist right now, at the edge of what is currently possible, before newer and even better ones come out.

Frontier-model access often comes with usage restrictions or evaluation requirements attached by the provider or regulator; check the terms of use and any reporting obligations before building critical infrastructure on a frontier-designated model.

Being labeled a frontier model now carries specific regulatory obligations in some jurisdictions, evaluation and reporting requirements, so a vendor's frontier-model status is a compliance fact worth understanding, not just a marketing claim about capability.

The designation carries real regulatory weight beyond marketing: frontier status increasingly triggers formal evaluation and reporting obligations under emerging AI regulation, which means being classified as "frontier" is a legal and compliance category, not just a capability claim.

terms.example: A new flagship release undergoing pre-deployment safety evaluation.
terms.definition: A model at or near the current maximum of capability, typically the largest and most recently released systems. The designation carries regulatory weight: frontier status increasingly triggers evaluation and reporting obligations.

lenses.body: AI that makes brand new things, writing, pictures, videos, sounds, computer code, based on patterns it learned, instead of just sorting or labeling things that already exist.

Evaluation is fundamentally harder here than for discriminative models, since there is often no single correct output to check against; invest in evaluation methodology, human review, rubrics, comparison, specifically because "did it get the right answer" is rarely a well-defined question.

The category most current AI marketing and public conversation focuses on, but it is only one part of the broader field; do not let generative AI's visibility crowd out attention to discriminative AI, which likely already runs significant parts of your operations.

The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is the specific development that put generative AI into mainstream public attention; before that shift, most deployed AI was discriminative, sorting and predicting rather than creating.

terms.example: ChatGPT, Midjourney, and Claude producing drafts, images, and code on request.
terms.definition: Models that create new content, text, images, video, audio, code, from patterns learned in training data. The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is what put this glossary on your reading list.

lenses.body: Normally you tell a computer exactly what to do, step by step. With machine learning you show it lots of examples instead, and it works out the rules by itself.

The engineering reality is that the model is the small part. Data collection, labelling, splitting, leakage prevention, evaluation design, monitoring for drift and retraining are the work. A model that scores well offline and degrades in production has almost always met a distribution shift the evaluation did not represent.

The shift from programming rules to learning them from examples, which is why data quality became a strategic asset. It also changes what assurance looks like: behaviour is statistical, so systems are validated by measured performance on representative cases rather than by reading the specification.

A family of methods that learn a function from data rather than following rules written by hand. The core divisions are supervised learning from labelled examples, unsupervised learning from structure in unlabelled data, and reinforcement learning from a reward signal. Generalisation to unseen data, not accuracy on the training set, is the whole objective.

terms.origin: Term coined by Arthur Samuel, 1959.
terms.example: A recommendation engine improving as it observes more behavior.
terms.definition: The subset of AI focused on systems that learn from data and improve with experience rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Nearly everything called AI in production is machine learning underneath.

lenses.body: A strange discovery: computers found it easier to master things like chess, which seem hard for people, than to master things like folding laundry, which seem easy for people. Things that feel effortless to us can be really hard to program.

A caution against assuming capability transfers intuitively from one domain to another; a model's strength on abstract, symbolic tasks tells you little about its readiness for sensorimotor or physical-world tasks, which require fundamentally different capabilities.

Useful context for setting realistic expectations about physical robotics timelines versus digital AI timelines; the intuition that "if AI can beat a chess grandmaster, surely it can handle simple physical tasks" is precisely backwards according to this pattern.

Explains why chess fell to computers decades before reliable robotic laundry folding did: abstract reasoning turned out to be comparatively tractable for machines, while the sensorimotor skills that feel effortless to humans, built on millions of years of evolutionary tuning, are genuinely hard to replicate.

terms.origin: Hans Moravec, "Mind Children," 1988.
terms.example: Superhuman chess coexisting with clumsy robot manipulation.
terms.definition: The observation that abstract reasoning is comparatively easy for machines while sensorimotor skills that feel effortless to humans are hard. It explains why chess fell decades before laundry folding.

lenses.body: AI built to do one specific job well, like recognizing faces or recommending videos, but that cannot do other unrelated things at all. Every AI you actually use today is this kind, even if it seems impressively smart.

Test explicitly at the boundaries of a model's intended scope, not just within it; narrow AI systems can fail unpredictably, and sometimes confidently, just outside the distribution they were trained and evaluated on.

Every AI product you evaluate is narrow AI regardless of how "intelligent" its marketing sounds; the practical question is always how narrow, exactly, and whether that specific narrow scope actually matches your intended use case.

Every deployed system today is narrow AI, however broad its marketing sounds; the distinction from general AI matters because narrow systems can excel dramatically within their specific trained scope while failing completely just outside it, which is a very different failure pattern than human generalization.

terms.example: Spam filters, chess engines, and voice assistants each excelling at one thing.
terms.definition: AI designed and trained for a specific task or narrow range of tasks, with no ability to generalize beyond it. Every deployed system today is narrow AI, however broad its marketing.

lenses.body: The part of AI focused specifically on writing text that sounds natural and human, turning data or an idea into readable sentences, instead of just understanding text that already exists.

Fluency is not the same as accuracy; a highly fluent NLG system can produce confidently wrong output with no stylistic tell, so fluency-based quality checks are insufficient on their own for anything where factual correctness matters.

The capability that made AI-generated text convincing enough to raise real questions about disclosure, authenticity, and misuse at scale; policies around labeling AI-generated content exist largely because NLG crossed this fluency threshold.

Once template-driven and stilted, producing obviously mechanical text, NLG is now indistinguishable from human drafting in many contexts, which changed both its practical usefulness and the risks around misuse, like generating convincing but false content at scale.

terms.example: Automated earnings summaries generated from financial data.
terms.definition: The subfield focused on producing fluent, human-readable text from data or intent. Once template-driven and stilted, now indistinguishable from drafting, which changed both its usefulness and its risks.

lenses.body: The whole field of AI dealing with human language: understanding it, translating it, summarizing it, or figuring out how someone feels from what they wrote. Lots of separate skills that used to be handled by different systems.

Consider whether a general LLM or a specialized, older-style NLP model is the right fit for your specific subtask; specialized models can still outperform general LLMs on narrow, well-defined tasks like precise entity extraction, at lower cost.

A vendor offering "NLP" today is usually offering LLM-based capability, since the field has consolidated around that approach; older, specialized NLP systems still exist for specific high-precision needs but are increasingly the exception rather than the default.

Translation, sentiment analysis, and summarization were separate research tracks with separate specialized systems until large language models absorbed most of them into one general capability, which is a genuine and significant consolidation in how the field is structured.

terms.example: Sentiment analysis, translation, and summarization as classic NLP tasks.
terms.definition: The field covering machine understanding and generation of human language. Its problems, translation, sentiment, summarization, were separate research tracks until large language models absorbed most of them into one capability.

lenses.body: The part of language AI focused on figuring out what someone actually means, not just producing text back. It is what turns a customer complaint into a clear category the right team can handle.

Test intent classification accuracy separately from response quality when evaluating a language system; a model can generate fluent, well-written responses while still misclassifying the underlying user intent, which breaks downstream routing logic.

The technology behind routing and triaging unstructured customer input into actionable categories; a support system's quality often depends as much on its NLU accuracy for categorization as on the eventual response it generates.

The comprehension side of the field, distinct from generation: NLU is what turns an unstructured statement like "I can't log in" into an actionable, structured category, like "authentication issue," that a downstream system or team can route and act on.

terms.example: Intent classification routing tickets in a support system.
terms.definition: The subfield focused on extracting meaning and intent from text, as opposed to producing it. It is what turns "I can't log in" into an actionable support category.

lenses.body: Mixing two kinds of AI together: the pattern-noticing kind that is good at understanding messy real-world stuff, and the rule-following kind that can guarantee certain things will always be true, so you get the best of both.

A genuinely different architecture pattern from pure neural approaches, worth the added engineering complexity specifically when your use case requires hard guarantees, not just high accuracy, since a neural network alone provides no such guarantee.

Worth investigating specifically for regulated or high-stakes use cases that need both real-world pattern recognition and provable rule compliance, such as certain financial or safety-critical decisions, where a pure neural network's lack of guarantees is a genuine blocker.

Attractive wherever answers need to be both learned from data and provably compliant with fixed rules; neural networks alone offer no guarantees, while symbolic rules alone cannot handle the messiness of real-world data, so combining them addresses a genuine gap either approach has alone.

terms.example: Neural document extraction feeding a deterministic rules engine for compliance decisions.
terms.definition: A hybrid approach combining neural networks with symbolic logic and rules: perception from the network, guarantees from the rules. Attractive wherever answers must be both learned and provably compliant.

lenses.body: Reading text out of a picture or scanned document and turning it into text a computer can actually use, like turning a photo of a receipt into an editable list of items and prices.

Test OCR quality on your actual document types, since accuracy varies enormously by font, scan quality, handwriting, and layout; a downstream language model cannot recover information the OCR step failed to extract correctly.

A quiet but critical dependency in any document-AI product; OCR errors on the front end propagate into everything downstream, so the quality of a document-processing system often depends more on OCR accuracy than on the language model built on top of it.

Decades old as a technology, newly relevant as a component: OCR is the front door through which paper enters every modern AI document pipeline, since a language model cannot process a scanned image directly without OCR converting it to text first.

terms.example: Digitizing invoices before an extraction model reads them.
terms.definition: Extracting machine-readable text from images or scanned documents. Decades old, newly relevant: OCR is the front door through which paper enters every AI document pipeline.

lenses.body: AI that looks at past information to guess what will happen next, like predicting how much stock to order, instead of creating new content like an image or a story.

Generally easier to evaluate rigorously than generative AI, since forecasts can be checked against actual outcomes with standard statistical methods; if your problem is genuinely a forecasting problem, predictive AI is often the simpler and more measurable choice.

Likely already embedded in your existing operations, forecasting, scoring, planning, well before any recent "AI initiative"; it is worth taking stock of your existing predictive AI use before assuming generative AI is your organization's first real AI deployment.

Ran the enterprise quietly for a decade before generative AI took the public spotlight, and it still makes most of the actual revenue for many businesses; demand forecasting, credit scoring, and churn prediction are mature predictive-AI applications that predate the current generative wave by years.

terms.example: Churn and demand forecasting driving retention and inventory decisions.
terms.definition: AI that forecasts outcomes from historical data rather than generating content. It ran the enterprise quietly for a decade before generative AI took the spotlight, and it still makes most of the money.

lenses.body: An AI that takes extra time to think through a hard problem step by step before answering, instead of just giving the first answer that comes to mind. It is slower and costs more, but gets harder problems right more often.

Route by task difficulty rather than defaulting to a reasoning model everywhere; a simpler, faster model on easy queries and a reasoning model reserved for genuinely hard ones is usually the more cost-effective architecture than one-size-fits-all.

Not automatically the right choice for every task; the added latency and cost are only worth it for genuinely hard, multi-step problems, and using a reasoning model for simple queries wastes both time and money for no accuracy benefit.

The design trade is explicit: latency and cost in exchange for accuracy on genuinely hard problems, spending extra inference-time compute on deliberate multi-step reasoning rather than producing an immediate answer, which is a meaningfully different resource tradeoff than simply using a bigger model.

terms.origin: Class established by OpenAI's o1, September 2024.
terms.example: A reasoning model taking thirty seconds on a proof a chat model fumbles instantly.
terms.definition: A model optimized to work through multi-step problems before answering, spending extra inference compute on deliberate chains of reasoning. The design trade is latency and cost for accuracy on hard problems.

lenses.body: The AI that decides what to show you next, like which video, product, or song to suggest, based on what you and people like you have liked before. It is one of the AI systems you touch the most without even thinking about it.

A mature field with well-established evaluation metrics and known failure modes, like filter bubbles and cold-start problems for new users or items; do not reinvent evaluation methodology here, established recommender-systems literature covers most of what you will encounter.

Often the highest-ROI AI application in a consumer-facing business, and one that predates the current generative AI wave by well over a decade; if your business has user-facing content or products, this is usually worth investment priority ahead of newer, flashier AI capabilities.

The most economically consequential AI most people touch daily without naming it; recommendation quality directly drives engagement and revenue for a huge share of consumer platforms, far more visibly in business impact than most of the AI that gets public attention.

terms.example: Streaming and e-commerce suggestions driving a large share of consumption.
terms.definition: A model that ranks and suggests items based on user behavior and item features. The most economically consequential AI most people touch daily without naming it.

lenses.body: Teaching an AI by letting it try things and giving it rewards when it does well and penalties when it does poorly, the way you might train a dog with treats, rather than just showing it labeled examples of right answers.

Reward function design is the hard, easy-to-get-wrong part; an RL system optimizes exactly what you reward, not what you intended, so unintended reward hacking is a common and worth-anticipating failure mode rather than a rare edge case.

A key ingredient in how modern chat assistants got tuned to be helpful and follow instructions well, not just capable; when a vendor describes "post-training" or "RLHF," this is the family of technique underneath that description.

Trained game-playing champions first, in environments like Go and Atari, and now post-trains reasoning and assistant models by rewarding preferred behavior; the same core idea, learning from reward signals through trial and error, applies across both very different use cases.

terms.example: Game-playing agents, robotics, and the RL stage of modern model training.
terms.definition: A paradigm in which an agent learns by taking actions in an environment and receiving rewards or penalties, improving through trial and error rather than labeled examples. It trained game champions first and now post-trains reasoning models.

lenses.body: A pattern researchers found where making an AI bigger, giving it more computing power and more training data, tends to make it predictably better, in a way you can actually calculate ahead of time.

Useful for capacity planning and setting realistic expectations for a custom training project; scaling laws suggest what capability level a given compute and data budget can realistically achieve, which helps avoid both under- and over-provisioning a training run.

Explains why major AI labs are raising and spending enormous capital on compute: scaling laws make future capability gains predictable enough to justify the investment, which is a different and more calculable bet than earlier, less predictable AI research funding.

Turned model development from craft into capital planning: labs can now buy predictable capability improvement on a known curve by investing in more compute, which is a fundamentally different R&D model than earlier AI research that relied more on individual algorithmic insight.

terms.origin: Kaplan et al., 2020; refined by the Chinchilla paper, 2022.
terms.example: Sizing a training run from the curves before committing the budget.
terms.definition: Empirical relationships showing predictable capability gains as compute, data, and parameters increase. They turned model development from craft into capital planning: labs buy capability on a curve.

lenses.body: A way for AI to make its own quiz questions and answers from raw information, like covering up a word in a sentence and trying to guess it, instead of needing a person to label everything by hand first.

The dominant pretraining paradigm for current large models; if you are fine-tuning rather than pretraining from scratch, you are building on top of self-supervised learning someone else already did, which is most of the reason fine-tuning is so much cheaper than training from zero.

The reason large language models could be trained on internet-scale data at all: removing the need for human labeling made training at this scale economically feasible, which is worth understanding when evaluating why foundation models are as capable and broad as they are.

Unlocked web-scale training by removing the human-labeling bottleneck entirely; this is specifically how large language models are pre-trained, on next-token or masked-word prediction the model generates for itself, which is why training could scale to the size of the entire internet rather than a hand-labeled dataset.

terms.example: Next-token prediction over trillions of words, no annotators required.
terms.definition: Training in which the model creates its own labels from the data, such as predicting the next token or a masked word. It unlocked web-scale training by removing the human labeling bottleneck, and it is how LLMs are pre-trained.

lenses.body: Using a small amount of carefully labeled examples along with a much bigger pile of unlabeled information, to stretch the value of the labeling work you can actually afford to do.

A reasonable default when labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant, which describes most specialized enterprise domains; consider it before defaulting to either pure supervised learning on a small labeled set or expensive additional labeling.

Worth asking about specifically in specialized domains where expert labeling is the bottleneck; this technique can meaningfully reduce the labeling cost of a custom AI project without sacrificing much accuracy compared to a fully supervised approach.

The practical middle path when labels are expensive and data is not, which is a common situation in specialized domains, like medical imaging or legal documents, where labeling requires expert time that is scarce and costly compared to the volume of raw unlabeled data available.

terms.example: Labeling one percent of records and propagating structure to the rest.
terms.definition: Training on a small labeled set combined with a large unlabeled set, letting scarce annotation stretch across abundant data. The practical middle path when labels are expensive and data is not.

lenses.body: Teaching an AI using lots of examples where you already know the right answer, so it can learn the pattern and then guess correctly on new examples it has not seen before, like studying with flashcards that have the answers on the back.

Label quality bounds model quality more than most other factors; before tuning architecture or hyperparameters, audit your labeled dataset for consistency and correctness, since a supervised model can only be as good as the labels it learned from.

The most mature and predictable form of machine learning for well-defined business problems; if you have historical examples with known correct answers, fraud or not, churn or not, this is usually the right starting technique, with clear evaluation metrics.

The classic paradigm behind most production classifiers and forecasters; it requires labeled input-output pairs, which is both its strength, clear, checkable correctness, and its constraint, since obtaining enough quality labels is often the actual bottleneck rather than the modeling technique itself.

terms.example: Spam-or-not-spam classification learned from labeled email.
terms.definition: Training on labeled input-output pairs so the model learns to predict the label for new inputs. The classic paradigm behind most production classifiers and forecasters.

lenses.body: The oldest kind of AI, where instead of learning patterns from examples, a computer follows explicit human-written logical rules and symbols, like a giant, very careful rulebook.

Worth combining with neural approaches, see neurosymbolic AI, rather than treating the two paradigms as strictly competing; symbolic components can add exactly the guarantees and transparency a neural pipeline lacks on its own.

Still the right choice for narrow domains where explainability and guaranteed correctness matter more than handling messy, unpredictable real-world input; do not assume newer, learned AI is always the better choice for every application.

The field's first paradigm, and the source of properties neural methods still generally lack: transparency and hard guarantees. A symbolic system's decision can be traced through an explicit chain of rules, which a neural network's decision generally cannot be, even today.

terms.example: Expert systems of the 1980s encoding knowledge as rules.
terms.definition: Rule-based AI that manipulates explicit symbols and logic rather than learning statistical patterns. The field's first paradigm, and the source of properties neural methods still lack: transparency and guarantees.

lenses.body: Turning written text into a computer voice that speaks it out loud. Modern versions sound so natural that people often cannot tell it is not a real human talking.

If building voice authentication, do not treat voice alone as a sufficient security factor anymore; modern TTS and voice cloning have made synthetic voice convincing enough that additional verification is now genuinely necessary, not just cautious extra.

The same capability that improved your voice assistant products also enabled convincing voice-cloning fraud; if your organization handles voice authentication or has executives whose voice is publicly available, this is now a real security consideration, not a hypothetical one.

Modern TTS crossed the naturalness threshold where listeners stop noticing it is synthetic, which is what enabled genuinely usable voice assistants and simultaneously enabled voice-cloning fraud; the same capability improvement produced both the benefit and the new risk.

terms.example: Audiobook narration generated at production quality.
terms.definition: Converting text into synthetic spoken audio. Modern TTS crossed the naturalness threshold where listeners stop noticing, which enabled voice assistants and also voice-cloning fraud.

lenses.body: Taking an AI that already learned a lot from one big task and reusing most of what it knows as a starting point for a new, different task, instead of teaching it absolutely everything again from zero.

Default to transfer learning, starting from a pretrained model, rather than training from scratch unless you have a specific, well-justified reason not to; the data and compute savings are usually substantial and the resulting model quality is often better too.

Directly why building a custom AI capability today is dramatically cheaper than it was a decade ago; you are typically adapting an existing, already-capable model rather than training one from nothing, which changes both cost and required data volume significantly.

The reason a modest dataset can now produce a strong specialized model: most of the actual learning happened before you started, during the original model's broad pretraining, so your smaller specific dataset only needs to adapt that existing knowledge, not build understanding from scratch.

terms.example: Fine-tuning a general image model for defect detection with a few thousand examples.
terms.definition: Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for another, carrying learned representations across. It is why a modest dataset can now produce a strong specialized model: most of the learning happened before you arrived.

lenses.body: A famous old test: if a person chatting with a hidden computer cannot tell whether they are talking to a machine or a real human, the machine passes. It used to be the big goal in AI, but people now think it does not really prove much about true intelligence.

Not a useful evaluation method for a modern system, since passing it has become trivial for current conversational models; use task-specific benchmarks and human preference evaluation instead when assessing whether a model is actually good for your use case.

Passing a casual Turing test is no longer a meaningful capability claim, since current models do this routinely; if a vendor cites Turing-test performance as evidence of quality, ask for more specific, modern benchmark results instead.

Historically the field's north star, now largely superseded: modern conversational models pass casual versions of this test routinely, while the actually interesting capability questions, reasoning depth, factual reliability, genuine understanding, have moved to entirely different evaluation methods.

terms.origin: Alan Turing, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," 1950.
terms.example: Chatbots passing short conversational judgments that Turing proposed in 1950.
terms.definition: A test of whether a machine's conversational behavior is indistinguishable from a human's. Historically the field's north star, now largely superseded: modern models pass casual versions while the interesting capability questions have moved elsewhere.

lenses.body: Letting an AI find patterns and groups in information all by itself, without anyone telling it the right answers in advance, like sorting a big pile of mixed objects into groups just by noticing what looks similar.

Validate discovered clusters or patterns against domain knowledge before acting on them; an algorithm will confidently find structure in data even when that structure is statistical noise or an artifact of preprocessing rather than a meaningful real-world pattern.

Useful for exploratory analysis, discovering unexpected customer segments or patterns you did not think to look for, but the output requires human interpretation before it becomes actionable; do not expect it to produce ready-made business decisions on its own.

It finds the categories; humans decide what they mean. The model discovers structure, clusters, groupings, that exist in the data, but interpreting what a discovered cluster actually represents and whether it is meaningful is still a human judgment call.

terms.example: Customer segmentation discovered through clustering rather than assumption.
terms.definition: Learning structure from unlabeled data: clusters, patterns, and groupings no one specified in advance. It finds the categories; humans decide what they mean.

lenses.body: An AI's internal, learned understanding of how things work in the world, like knowing that if you drop something it will fall, which it uses to predict what will happen next and plan ahead.

Test planning and prediction capability specifically on scenarios genuinely outside the training distribution; strong performance on familiar patterns does not confirm the model has anything resembling a real internal world model rather than sophisticated pattern interpolation.

A useful frame for understanding the limits of current AI planning capability: a model without a robust world model can produce plausible-sounding predictions that fail unpredictably outside familiar patterns, which matters for any use case requiring genuine forward planning.

Whether large models form genuine world models or surface statistics is one of the field's live, unresolved arguments; a model can produce accurate predictions in many cases without necessarily having anything resembling a coherent internal representation of how the world actually works, and researchers disagree on how to tell the difference.

terms.example: Video models that simulate plausible physics when generating motion.
terms.definition: An internal learned representation of how an environment behaves, supporting prediction and planning. Whether large models form genuine world models or surface statistics is one of the field's live arguments.

lenses.body: Instead of always picking the single best next word, this keeps several good possible sentences going at once and picks the overall best one at the end, since the best word right now does not always lead to the best full sentence.

Rarely used for open-ended chat generation, where it tends to produce oddly repetitive or bland text, but still valuable for tasks with a genuinely correct or near-correct target, like translation, where global sequence quality matters more than per-token diversity.

Not something you need to configure directly in most tools you use, but worth knowing that different AI tools use different strategies for choosing words, which is part of why the same prompt can produce noticeably different writing styles across tools.

Common in translation, where the best sentence is not always built from the best next word at each individual step; keeping multiple candidate sequences alive lets the search avoid greedily committing to a locally good but globally suboptimal path.

terms.example: A translation system tracking five candidate renderings before choosing.
terms.definition: A decoding strategy that keeps several candidate sequences alive and expands the most promising, rather than committing to one token at a time. Common in translation, where the best sentence is not always built from the best next word.

lenses.body: Asking an AI to show its work, step by step, before giving the final answer, the same way a teacher asks a student to show their math steps instead of just writing down the answer. It usually gets the answer more right, and lets you see where it went wrong if it does not.

A simple, high-value technique to try before more complex approaches: explicitly asking the model to reason step by step, even with a phrase as basic as "think through this step by step," often measurably improves accuracy on multi-step tasks with minimal added engineering.

If an AI tool gives you a wrong answer to something complicated, try asking it to explain its reasoning step by step next time; this often catches the mistake and produces a more accurate answer, and it lets you see where the logic actually went wrong.

Making the reasoning explicit improves accuracy on multi-step problems and gives reviewers something to inspect when the answer is wrong, since a visible reasoning chain lets you locate exactly which step introduced an error, rather than only seeing a final answer with no explanation.

terms.origin: Wei et al., 2022, "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning."
terms.example: Adding "think step by step" and watching arithmetic accuracy jump.
terms.definition: A prompting technique that encourages the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. Making the reasoning explicit improves accuracy on multi-step problems and gives reviewers something to inspect when the answer is wrong.

lenses.body: When an AI shows exactly which document or source its answer came from, so you can go check it yourself instead of just having to trust the AI's word for it.

Build citation into the system architecture from the start rather than adding it after the fact; retrieval-augmented generation naturally supports this by design, since the source documents are already available at generation time to attach as citations.

Prefer AI tools that show you their sources over ones that just give you an answer with no citation; being able to check the source yourself is the difference between trusting the AI blindly and actually verifying what it told you.

Required in regulated reporting and increasingly expected everywhere: an answer that cites can be checked, an answer that does not must simply be trusted, which is a meaningful difference in reliability that has nothing to do with how confident or fluent the answer sounds.

terms.example: A research assistant footnoting each claim to a retrieved document.
terms.definition: Linking generated claims back to the source documents that support them. Required in regulated reporting and increasingly expected everywhere: an answer that cites can be checked, an answer that does not must be trusted.

lenses.body: Forcing an AI to only produce output that follows a specific correct format, the way a fill-in-the-blank form only accepts certain kinds of answers in each blank, so the output is guaranteed to be usable instead of just usually being usable.

Use this whenever an AI output feeds directly into another system without a human reviewing it first; the guaranteed structural validity eliminates an entire class of parse-failure bugs that would otherwise require defensive error handling downstream.

If you are having a developer build something that uses AI to fill out a form or produce data your systems will use automatically, ask whether they are using this kind of guaranteed-format approach; it prevents a whole category of "the AI output broke our system" problems.

It converts "usually valid" into "guaranteed valid," which is the difference between a demo and an integration; a system that works most of the time in testing but occasionally produces malformed output is not production-ready the way a system with hard structural guarantees is.

terms.example: Function arguments generated under a JSON grammar that cannot produce invalid syntax.
terms.definition: Restricting token choices at generation time so output must satisfy a grammar or schema. It converts "usually valid" into "guaranteed valid," which is the difference between a demo and an integration.

lenses.body: When a conversation with an AI gets really long, it can start forgetting instructions you gave it earlier or getting confused, the same way a conversation can get muddled after going on for a really long time. The fix is usually to start fresh with a clean summary.

Build in periodic context summarization for any long-running conversational or agentic system rather than letting context grow unbounded; a clean, distilled context restart often outperforms a long, accumulated one on both quality and cost.

If a long AI conversation starts giving worse or more confused answers, do not keep pushing through it; start a fresh conversation and briefly summarize what you need it to know. This usually works better than trying to fix a conversation that has gotten too long and tangled.

Fixed by summarizing state and restarting clean rather than pushing on; the practical lesson is that pushing an increasingly long, noisy conversation forward tends to produce worse results than periodically distilling the important state and beginning a fresh, cleaner context.

terms.example: A long session drifting off format until a fresh thread restores it.
terms.definition: Quality decay as a conversation or working context grows long and noisy: the model starts missing instructions it followed an hour ago. Fixed by summarizing state and restarting clean rather than pushing on.

lenses.body: Cramming as much information as possible into what you tell an AI, thinking more is always better, when actually giving it only the relevant stuff usually works better than burying the important parts in a huge pile of extra material.

Invest in retrieval quality, selecting the most relevant chunks, over simply maximizing how much context you provide; a well-curated smaller context frequently outperforms a maximal, unfiltered one on both accuracy and cost.

More information is not automatically better when working with AI tools; giving it only the specific, relevant material for the task at hand usually produces better results than pasting in everything you have and hoping it figures out what matters.

Relevance beats volume, and retrieval that selects usually outperforms context that hoards; dumping large amounts of tenuously relevant material into the context can actually degrade the model's ability to find and use the genuinely important information, rather than helping it.

terms.example: Pasting nine documents when the two relevant ones would score higher.
terms.definition: Filling the context window with as much reference material as possible on the theory that more is better. It often degrades precision: relevance beats volume, and retrieval that selects usually outperforms context that hoards.

lenses.body: How much text an AI can actually pay attention to and remember at once, its working memory. Everything you want it to consider, your question, any documents, earlier parts of the conversation, has to fit inside this limit.

Know your model's actual context window size and monitor how close a given request comes to it; silent truncation of older content when the window fills up is a common, hard-to-debug production issue if not actively tracked.

Different AI tools have different limits on how much they can read and remember at once; if a tool seems to forget something from earlier in a long conversation or a large document, it may have simply run out of room, not made a mistake.

Everything the model should consider, instructions, documents, history, must fit inside it; once the accumulated content exceeds this limit, older material typically gets dropped or truncated, which is a common and often invisible cause of an AI seeming to "forget" something discussed earlier.

terms.example: A 200 thousand token window holding an entire contract set for review.
terms.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can process and retain during a single interaction: its working memory. Everything the model should consider, instructions, documents, history, must fit inside it.

lenses.body: Clear markers, like special symbols or quote marks, used to show an AI exactly where instructions end and the actual content or data begins, so it does not accidentally think a piece of text is a command it should follow.

A cheap, easy first line of defense against prompt injection: always wrap untrusted content, like retrieved documents or user-supplied text, in clear delimiters, and instruct the model explicitly to treat content inside them as data, never as commands.

If you are pasting a document into an AI tool along with instructions, clearly separate the two, for example by putting the document in quotes or after a clear label like "DOCUMENT:", which reduces the chance the AI gets confused about what is an instruction and what is just content to read.

They reduce the chance the model treats quoted content as commands, which is also the first cheap defense against injection; clearly marking the boundary between instructions and data is a simple, low-cost technique with real security value in any system that processes untrusted text.

terms.example: Wrapping a pasted email in tags so its text is analyzed, not obeyed.
terms.definition: Markers that separate instructions from data inside a prompt, XML tags, triple backticks, headers. They reduce the chance the model treats quoted content as commands, which is also the first cheap defense against injection.

lenses.body: Giving an AI a few examples of exactly what you want before asking it to do the real task, the way showing someone two or three solved practice problems helps them understand the pattern better than just explaining the rule in words.

When zero-shot prompting is not reliably producing the exact format or style you need, adding two or three well-chosen examples is often the fastest fix, cheaper and quicker to iterate on than fine-tuning for the same format-consistency improvement.

If an AI tool is not giving you output in the format you want, try showing it one or two examples of exactly what a good output looks like before asking for the real thing; this usually works much better than just describing what you want in words.

The examples do the teaching: format, tone, and edge-case handling transfer from demonstration better than from description, since showing the model exactly what correct output looks like conveys nuances that are hard to fully specify in a written instruction alone.

terms.origin: Established as a capability in the GPT-3 paper, Brown et al., 2020.
terms.example: Two labeled examples teaching a classification the instructions alone missed.
terms.definition: Providing a few in-context examples that demonstrate the desired output format or task handling. The examples do the teaching: format, tone, and edge-case handling transfer from demonstration better than from description.

lenses.body: A setting that discourages an AI from repeating the same words over and over, turned up higher the more times a word has already been used, to keep its writing from getting stuck in a loop.

Useful specifically for fixing repetitive-loop failure modes in generated text; tune conservatively, since setting it too high can push the model toward unnatural word choices just to avoid repetition, trading one quality problem for another.

Not something you usually need to adjust directly in consumer AI tools, but if you are working with a more technical AI platform and notice repetitive, looping text, this is the setting that specifically addresses that problem.

The dial for reducing loops and stuck phrases; unlike presence penalty, which applies a flat discouragement once a token has appeared at all, frequency penalty scales with how many times a token has already been used, targeting genuine repetition specifically.

terms.example: Raising the penalty to stop a model repeating the same sentence stem.
terms.definition: A sampling setting that discourages repeating tokens already used, scaled by how often they have appeared. The dial for reducing loops and stuck phrases.

lenses.body: An AI always picking the single word it thinks is most likely to come next, every single time, with no randomness at all. It is fast and always gives the same answer to the same question, but the writing can end up sounding flat and repetitive.

Use greedy decoding, temperature at or near zero, specifically when you need deterministic, reproducible output, like for testing or evaluation pipelines; avoid it for creative or open-ended generation tasks where the resulting text quality noticeably suffers.

If an AI tool has a "creativity" or "randomness" setting turned all the way down, that is roughly this behavior, always picking the safest next word; useful when you want consistent, predictable output, less useful when you want varied or creative writing.

The best next word at every step rarely produces the best paragraph; because greedy decoding never considers whether a slightly less probable word now might lead to a much better sentence overall, it tends to produce text that is locally reasonable but globally repetitive or flat.

terms.example: Deterministic output for a compliance task where variation is unwanted.
terms.definition: Always selecting the highest-probability next token. Deterministic and fast, and prone to repetitive, flat text: the best next word at every step rarely produces the best paragraph.

lenses.body: Making an AI only answer using information from specific documents you gave it, instead of letting it use whatever it remembers from its training, so every claim it makes traces back to a real source you can check.

The default architecture choice for any enterprise deployment where factual accuracy matters; build the system so it explicitly refuses or flags when the supplied source material does not contain an answer, rather than falling back silently to the model's own unsourced knowledge.

Prefer AI tools that specifically tell you they are only answering from documents you provided, rather than from general training knowledge, when accuracy on your specific business information matters; ask a vendor directly whether their tool works this way.

The standard hallucination control in enterprise deployments: no source, no claim; requiring the model to derive answers from supplied material rather than its own parametric memory converts an unverifiable assertion into a checkable one, which is the entire practical value of the technique.

terms.example: A policy bot instructed to answer only from the retrieved handbook.
terms.definition: Requiring answers to cite or derive from supplied source material rather than the model's own memory. The standard hallucination control in enterprise deployments: no source, no claim.

lenses.body: Sometimes the computer makes something up and says it exactly the way it says true things, with no change in its voice. It is not lying, because it does not know the difference. That is why you check anything important.

Treat it as an expected failure mode with a rate, not a bug awaiting a fix. Grounding with retrieval, constraining output to a schema, requiring citations that you then verify programmatically, and evaluating against a held-out set all reduce it. None of them eliminate it, so the system design question is what happens when a wrong answer gets through.

The reason you cannot put an unchecked model in front of customers on anything that matters. It will state a wrong price, policy or date as confidently as a right one. Use it to draft and summarise where a person reviews the output, and keep a human check on anything a customer could rely on.

Output that is fluent and confident but not grounded in fact or in the provided source. It follows from how these models work: they predict likely continuations, and a plausible-sounding false statement can be more likely than an admission of ignorance. Fluency is therefore not evidence of accuracy.

terms.example: An LLM citing court cases that do not exist, in perfect legal formatting.
terms.definition: A generative model confidently outputting false, fabricated, or unsupported information. The fluency is the danger: fabricated content arrives in the same authoritative voice as fact, which is why verification belongs in every AI workflow.

lenses.body: The surprising ability of an AI to pick up a brand new task just from instructions and examples you give it in the moment, without anyone having to specially retrain it first. It learns for that one conversation only, then forgets.

This is precisely why prompt engineering can substitute for fine-tuning in many cases: the model's in-context learning ability means new task behavior can often be elicited through examples and instructions alone, without the cost and complexity of actually retraining weights.

This is the reason you can just describe a new task to an AI tool in plain language and have it work reasonably well immediately, without waiting for the company to "teach" the AI your specific task in advance; it learns from your instructions on the spot.

It is why prompting works at all: the model adapts per request, learning nothing permanently; this per-request adaptation without any weight update is a distinctive and somewhat surprising property of large language models that earlier machine learning systems generally lacked.

terms.origin: Identified as a scale phenomenon in the GPT-3 paper, 2020.
terms.example: A custom schema taught entirely inside one prompt, gone the next session.
terms.definition: The ability of LLMs to pick up new tasks from instructions and examples in the prompt itself, without any weight changes. It is why prompting works at all: the model adapts per request, learning nothing permanently.

lenses.body: A setting that forces an AI to give its answer in a specific structured computer format instead of regular sentences, so other computer programs can read and use the answer automatically without a person needing to interpret it.

Removes an entire class of integration bugs caused by malformed output, but do not skip content validation just because the structure is guaranteed; check field values, types, and required fields as you would for any external input, since format guarantee is not a correctness guarantee.

If a developer is building something for you that uses AI to feed data into another system, ask whether they are using a structured output mode like this one; it prevents a common category of technical failure where the AI's response cannot be automatically read by other software.

Validity is not correctness: the JSON always parses, the contents still need checking; a guaranteed structurally valid output is not the same guarantee as a factually correct one, and conflating the two is a common mistake when evaluating this feature's reliability.

terms.example: An API integration that never sees malformed output again.
terms.definition: A model setting that guarantees syntactically valid JSON output. It removes the parse-failure class of integration bugs, though validity is not correctness: the JSON always parses, the contents still need checking.

lenses.body: A pattern where AI tends to remember and use information from the very start and the very end of a long document better than stuff buried in the middle, so important instructions or facts should go near the edges, not hidden in the middle.

Structure prompts deliberately, placing the most critical instructions and facts at the beginning and end of the context, not buried in the middle of a long document dump; this measurably improves retrieval accuracy independent of overall context length.

If you are giving an AI a long document along with important instructions, put the key instructions at the very start or very end, not buried in the middle; AI tools tend to pay more attention to the beginning and end of long text than to the middle.

The practical rule it yields is direct: put critical instructions and facts at the edges; this is a well-documented empirical finding about how retrieval accuracy varies by position within a long context, and it holds even for models that technically support very long context windows.

terms.origin: Liu et al., 2023, "Lost in the Middle."
terms.example: A key clause buried mid-document being missed until moved to the top.
terms.definition: Degraded recall of information placed in the middle of a long context, with the beginning and end remembered best. The practical rule it yields: put critical instructions and facts at the edges.

lenses.body: A limit on how long an AI's answer is allowed to be. If the answer would naturally be longer than this limit, it just gets cut off mid-sentence, which can be a real problem if the cut-off part was important.

Set this parameter generously enough for your expected output length, and specifically handle the truncation case in your error handling; a silently truncated response mid-structure is a common, easily overlooked production failure mode.

If an AI response seems to cut off abruptly mid-sentence or mid-thought, that is usually this length limit being hit rather than the AI running out of things to say; try asking it to continue, or ask for a shorter response in the first place.

Outputs that hit the cap are silently truncated, and truncation mid-JSON breaks integrations; a response cut off partway through structured output, like an incomplete JSON object, is not just an inconvenience, it is often an outright system failure for anything reading that output automatically.

terms.example: A summary cut off mid-sentence because the cap was set too low.
terms.definition: The cap on how many tokens a response may contain. A cost and latency control that doubles as a failure mode: outputs that hit the cap are silently truncated, and truncation mid-JSON breaks integrations.

lenses.body: Using an AI to help write or improve the instructions you give to another AI, instead of a person doing all that instruction-writing work by hand, which lets the process of improving instructions get automated too.

Worth building into any system with many prompts to maintain; using a model to help generate variations, catch ambiguities, or suggest improvements to existing prompts can meaningfully speed up the otherwise manual and slow process of prompt iteration.

If you are struggling to get good results from an AI tool, you can literally ask the AI itself to help you write a better prompt for what you are trying to do; this often works surprisingly well and saves you the trial and error.

It industrializes prompt engineering: the optimization loop runs in software instead of in someone's head; rather than a person manually iterating on prompt wording through trial and error, the refinement process itself becomes something a model can help automate and systematize.

terms.example: A pipeline that iterates a prompt against an eval set until scores plateau.
terms.definition: Using a model to write or refine prompts for itself or another model. It industrializes prompt engineering: the optimization loop runs in software instead of in someone's head.

lenses.body: A back-and-forth conversation with an AI where it remembers what was said earlier and builds on it, as opposed to a single one-off question and answer with no memory of anything before it.

Design explicit strategies for managing accumulated conversation state, summarization, pruning, resets, rather than letting a multi-turn conversation grow unboundedly; unmanaged state accumulation is a common source of both cost growth and quality degradation.

A long, ongoing conversation with an AI tool can build up useful context over time, but it can also accumulate confusion if earlier parts were unclear or wrong; if something feels off partway through a long conversation, consider starting fresh rather than trying to untangle it.

State is the feature and the liability: context accumulates, and so does drift; the same conversation memory that makes multi-turn interaction useful for building on earlier points is also what allows errors, misunderstandings, or context rot to accumulate and compound over a long exchange.

terms.example: A chat assistant refining a draft across a dozen exchanges.
terms.definition: Interaction spanning several exchanges with retained conversation state, as against one-shot request and response. State is the feature and the liability: context accumulates, and so does drift.

lenses.body: Telling an AI specifically what you do not want to see in its answer, not just what you do want, the same way you might say "no nuts" when ordering food, not just describing what you do want on the plate.

Worth adding as a deliberate technique in text prompting, not just image generation; explicitly listing common failure modes to avoid, verbosity, hedging language, a specific unwanted format, often produces more reliable results than positive instructions alone.

If an AI tool keeps making the same kind of mistake or including something you do not want, try explicitly telling it what to avoid, not just what you want; sometimes stating the problem directly works better than only describing the ideal result.

A first-class control in image generation and a useful discipline in text, where naming the failure mode often prevents it; explicitly stating an undesired outcome, extra limbs in an image, overly formal tone in text, is often a more effective control than only describing the desired outcome.

terms.example: An image prompt excluding text artifacts and extra fingers.
terms.definition: Specifying what should not appear in the output. A first-class control in image generation and a useful discipline in text, where naming the failure mode often prevents it.

lenses.body: Giving an AI exactly one example of what you want before asking it to do the real task, which is often enough to show it the format you need, even if it is not enough to teach it every tricky detail.

A reasonable middle ground when you need format guidance but want to keep prompt length and cost lower than a full few-shot example set; use it when the task is fairly simple and format is the main thing you need to communicate.

Showing an AI tool just one clear example of what you want is often enough to get the format right, even without a long list of examples; try this as a quick fix before assuming you need something more complicated.

Often enough to fix format, rarely enough to teach nuance; a single example is typically sufficient to establish the desired structure or output style but usually insufficient to convey handling of edge cases, which generally requires the additional examples of few-shot prompting.

terms.example: A single formatted example locking the output structure.
terms.definition: Providing exactly one example to demonstrate the task before asking for output. The minimum-viable demonstration: often enough to fix format, rarely enough to teach nuance.

lenses.body: A setting that nudges an AI toward using new words and topics it has not used yet in its answer, encouraging variety, applied once per new word rather than getting stronger the more times a word repeats.
