Useful for encouraging broader topical coverage rather than just reducing exact-word repetition; tune it separately from frequency penalty, since they address related but distinct aspects of output diversity.

Not typically a setting you need to adjust directly, but if an AI tool's answers feel narrow or keep circling the same points, a tool with this kind of setting exposed can help push it toward covering more ground.

The companion dial to frequency penalty, applied once per token type rather than per occurrence; where frequency penalty scales with repetition count, presence penalty applies a flat discouragement the moment a token has appeared at all, which produces a subtly different effect on output variety.

terms.example: Nudging a brainstorm toward new themes instead of variations on one.
terms.definition: A sampling setting that pushes the model toward tokens it has not yet used, encouraging topical variety. The companion dial to frequency penalty, applied once per token type rather than per occurrence.

lenses.body: What you type or show to an AI to tell it what you want it to do. It is the whole interface, however good your prompt is directly shapes how good the answer you get back will be.

Treat prompts as a real, version-controlled engineering artifact, not an informal afterthought; a poorly specified prompt is functionally equivalent to a poorly specified requirement, and produces correspondingly unreliable results.

The quality of what you get back from an AI tool depends heavily on the quality and clarity of what you asked for; investing a bit more time in writing a clear, specific prompt usually pays off more than trying many vague ones.

The interface itself: in a prompted system, the prompt is the specification; unlike traditional software where behavior is defined by code, a language model's behavior for a given task is defined largely by the prompt, which makes prompt quality directly analogous to specification quality in other engineering contexts.

terms.example: A one-line instruction producing a working Python script.
terms.definition: The input, textual, visual, or structured, provided to a generative model to guide its output. The interface itself: in a prompted system, the prompt is the specification.

lenses.body: A trick that lets an AI skip redoing work it already did for a part of a prompt it has seen before, like a long standard instruction, making repeated requests using that same part much cheaper and faster.

Structure prompts with stable, reusable content, system instructions, reference documents, first and variable per-request content last, to take advantage of prefix caching; this can meaningfully reduce cost and latency for high-volume applications with repeated context.

If you frequently use the same long instructions or reference document with an AI tool, ask whether the provider offers a caching feature; it can significantly reduce costs for repeated use of the same material, which is worth knowing if your AI bill is a real line item.

Long system prompts and shared document contexts become nearly free after the first call, which changes how production prompts are architected; this economic shift encourages putting more stable, reusable content in the cached prefix and variable content afterward, a real architectural consideration for cost-sensitive applications.

terms.example: A 50-page policy document cached once and reused across thousands of queries.
terms.definition: Reusing computation for a repeated prompt prefix to cut cost and latency. Long system prompts and shared document contexts become nearly free after the first call, which changes how production prompts are architected.

lenses.body: The skill of carefully writing and improving what you ask an AI, to get better and more reliable answers back. It is less about secret magic tricks and more about being clear, giving good examples, and testing what actually works.

Apply the same rigor here as any other engineering discipline: version control prompts, test systematically against representative cases, and measure results quantitatively rather than relying on impression or one-off manual checks.

You do not need to hire a specialist to get better results from AI tools; the core skill is being clear and specific about what you want, giving good examples, and testing what actually works for your particular use case rather than assuming.

Less mystical than its reputation: mostly clear specification, good examples, and systematic testing; while it is sometimes treated as an esoteric skill, most of the actual practice consists of disciplined, testable engineering habits rather than secret techniques.

terms.example: Iterating a prompt against an eval suite until accuracy holds.
terms.definition: The practice of crafting, structuring, and optimizing inputs to elicit accurate and useful model output. Less mystical than its reputation: mostly clear specification, good examples, and systematic testing.

lenses.body: A reusable prompt with blank spots that get filled in each time with different specific details, like a form letter with blanks for a name and date, so you do not have to write the whole prompt from scratch every time.

Build a maintained library of templates for repeated tasks rather than writing ad hoc prompts inline throughout a codebase; this concentrates prompt quality work in one place and makes systematic testing and improvement actually feasible.

If you find yourself asking an AI tool the same kind of question repeatedly with small changes each time, save a reusable template with blanks for the parts that change; it saves time and keeps your results more consistent.

It standardizes production calls so quality work concentrates in one artifact instead of scattering across every call site; improving one well-maintained template benefits every use of it, rather than requiring the same fix to be manually applied across many separately written prompts.

terms.example: One vetted template serving every document-summary request in the product.
terms.definition: A reusable prompt with variable slots filled at runtime. It standardizes production calls so quality work concentrates in one artifact instead of scattering across every call site.

lenses.body: A pattern where an AI thinks through a step, does an action like using a tool, looks at what happened, and repeats, going back and forth between thinking and doing instead of trying to plan the whole thing out perfectly in advance.

A solid, well-understood starting pattern for building a basic agentic system; understand its limitations, particularly around error recovery and loop termination, before layering more sophisticated planning or self-correction patterns on top.

This is roughly how many AI "agent" tools you might use actually work behind the scenes: thinking, trying something, checking the result, and adjusting, rather than following one rigid plan; useful context if a tool's behavior seems to change mid-task based on what it finds.

The foundation most early agents were built on; interleaving reasoning with tool actions and observing results at each step, rather than planning an entire sequence upfront, lets the agent adapt to unexpected results as it goes, which is closer to how a person actually works through an unfamiliar task.

terms.origin: Yao et al., 2022, "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting."
terms.example: An agent reasoning about what to search, searching, then reasoning over results.
terms.definition: A prompting pattern interleaving reasoning steps with tool actions and observations: think, act, observe, repeat. The foundation most early agents were built on.

lenses.body: An AI pattern where it looks back at its own answer, criticizes what it got wrong, and tries again using that self-criticism to do better the second time, similar to how you might revise a draft after reading it over critically.

Implement a clear, testable stopping condition, not just a fixed retry count, when using this pattern; without one, self-critique loops can spend unbounded compute without meaningfully improving output quality past a certain point.

If an AI tool offers a "review and improve" feature on its own output, that is roughly this pattern; it can genuinely improve quality, but it also costs more time and money each time it runs, so it is worth reserving for cases where accuracy really matters.

Self-correction loops buy accuracy with extra inference, useful where a checker exists to say when to stop; without some way to know when the answer is actually good enough, this critique-and-retry loop can continue indefinitely without genuinely converging on improvement, which is why a stopping criterion matters.

terms.origin: Shinn et al., 2023.
terms.example: A coding agent reading its own test failures and revising the patch.
terms.definition: An agent pattern in which the model critiques its own output and retries with the critique in context. Self-correction loops buy accuracy with extra inference, useful where a checker exists to say when to stop.

lenses.body: When an AI says no to a request because it goes against its safety rules. Sometimes this is exactly right, but sometimes an AI refuses something that was actually totally fine, which is its own kind of annoying mistake.

Test explicitly for over-refusal, not just under-refusal, when evaluating a model for your use case; a model that is overly cautious on legitimate business requests is a real usability problem worth measuring and comparing across model options.

If an AI tool refuses a request that seems completely reasonable, try rephrasing it more specifically or providing more context; sometimes a refusal is the AI being overly cautious about a request it misread as risky, not a hard rule you cannot work around.

Over-refusal on legitimate requests is a usability failure with its own name in evaluation suites; a model that declines too cautiously on genuinely reasonable requests is failing in a different but equally real way as a model that complies with something it should have refused.

terms.example: A model declining a security question a professional legitimately needs answered.
terms.definition: A model declining a request on policy or safety grounds. Necessary at the edges and costly in the middle: over-refusal on legitimate requests is a usability failure with its own name in evaluation suites.

lenses.body: Telling an AI to act like a specific kind of expert, such as "act as a lawyer" or "act as a teacher," which changes the tone, level of detail, and vocabulary it uses to match that role.

A cheap, effective technique for quickly shifting output tone and vocabulary without extensive prompt engineering; combine it with more specific format instructions for the best results, since role alone usually shapes style more reliably than it shapes structure.

Asking an AI to "act as" a specific type of professional, like a marketing expert or a customer service specialist, often noticeably improves the tone and relevance of its answer for that specific kind of task; it is a quick, easy technique worth trying.

It works because register lives in the training data: "as a forensic accountant" summons different priors than "as a friend," since the model has learned statistical associations between certain roles and certain vocabulary, tone, and depth of explanation from the huge volume of text it was trained on.

terms.example: A prompt opening "You are an experienced auditor" to sharpen skepticism.
terms.definition: Assigning the model a persona or professional role to shape tone, depth, and vocabulary. It works because register lives in the training data: "as a forensic accountant" summons different priors than "as a friend."

lenses.body: Asking an AI the same hard question multiple times with a bit of randomness each time, then going with whatever answer came up most often, since that majority answer is usually more reliable than any single try.

Worth using for high-stakes, well-defined problems, math, logic, code correctness, where the added compute cost of multiple samples is justified by a meaningful accuracy improvement; less useful for open-ended creative tasks where there is no clear "majority correct" answer to converge on.

For an important calculation or logic problem, you can ask an AI tool the same question a few separate times and see if it consistently gives the same answer; if the answers differ, that inconsistency itself is a useful warning sign to double-check the result yourself.

It converts variance into accuracy on math and logic, at the price of running the question several times; sampling multiple independent reasoning attempts and taking the majority result is a genuine accuracy improvement technique, though it multiplies the compute cost proportionally to how many samples are taken.

terms.origin: Wang et al., 2022.
terms.example: Ten sampled solutions voting on one arithmetic answer.
terms.definition: Sampling multiple reasoning paths for the same problem and taking the majority answer. It converts variance into accuracy on math and logic, at the price of running the question several times.

lenses.body: Having an AI check over its own answer against a checklist before actually giving it to you, catching mistakes the same way rereading your own writing catches errors you missed while first writing it.

A relatively cheap technique to add for meaningfully improved output quality: explicitly prompting the model to review its own draft against stated criteria before finalizing often catches errors that a single-pass generation misses, at the cost of one additional inference call.

You can literally ask an AI tool to review and critique its own answer against specific criteria you care about before you accept it; this simple extra step often catches mistakes or gaps that the first answer missed.

The draft-then-revise pattern: a second pass catches what the first pass, committed token by token, could not; because generation happens sequentially without the ability to revise earlier tokens, an explicit review-and-revise step can catch errors that the original generation process structurally could not fix on its own.

terms.example: A model checking its summary against the source before submitting.
terms.definition: Having the model review its own answer against criteria before finalizing. The draft-then-revise pattern: a second pass catches what the first pass, committed token by token, could not.

lenses.body: How well an AI actually follows your specific instructions about tone, format, and rules, instead of doing its own thing. A less powerful AI that reliably follows instructions is often more useful than a more powerful one that improvises.

Evaluate steerability as its own criterion, separate from raw capability benchmarks, when selecting a model for production; a model's benchmark score does not reliably predict how well it will follow your specific formatting, tone, and constraint instructions.

When choosing between AI tools, do not just consider which one seems "smartest"; also consider which one most reliably follows your specific instructions about format, tone, and rules, since that reliability often matters more for actual day-to-day usefulness.

A slightly weaker model that obeys beats a stronger one that improvises; raw capability and instruction-following reliability are genuinely separate qualities, and for many production use cases, predictable adherence to constraints matters more than maximum possible capability.

terms.example: A model holding a mandated disclaimer format across thousands of outputs.
terms.definition: How reliably a model follows tone, format, and constraint instructions. A key enterprise selection criterion, because a slightly weaker model that obeys beats a stronger one that improvises.

lenses.body: A specific word or symbol that tells an AI to stop writing the instant it appears, used to keep its answer from running on longer than you want or wandering off into unrelated territory.

Use explicit stop sequences to enforce structural boundaries in generated output, particularly useful for preventing a model from continuing past a defined output format into unwanted additional commentary or explanation.

Not typically something you configure directly in consumer AI tools, but if you notice an AI response consistently running on with unwanted extra text, more technical AI platforms let a developer set specific stopping points to prevent this.

The blunt, reliable way to prevent runaway completions and keep output inside expected boundaries; unlike more nuanced controls, a stop sequence is a hard, unconditional cutoff the moment the specified string appears, which makes it simple and predictable but not adjustable mid-generation.

terms.example: Generation ending cleanly at a closing tag.
terms.definition: A string that halts generation the moment it is produced. The blunt, reliable way to prevent runaway completions and keep output inside expected boundaries.

lenses.body: Making an AI give its answer in a strict, predictable format with labeled fields, like a form, instead of a regular paragraph, so a computer program can automatically read and use specific pieces of the answer.

The right default whenever AI output feeds into another system rather than being read directly by a person; free-form text output requires fragile parsing logic that structured output eliminates entirely by design.

If a developer is connecting an AI tool to other systems your business uses, like automatically filling out a database or spreadsheet, ask whether they are using structured output; it makes the connection much more reliable than trying to extract information from a regular paragraph answer.

The bridge between conversational models and software that expects fields, not prose; most business software is built to consume specific data fields, not free-form text, so structured output is what actually makes a language model usable as a component inside a larger automated system.

terms.example: Extraction results arriving as a validated schema, straight into a database.
terms.definition: Forcing responses into a defined schema, typically JSON, so downstream systems can consume them reliably. The bridge between conversational models and software that expects fields, not prose.

lenses.body: When an AI tends to just agree with you instead of telling you the truth, especially if you push back even a little, the way a person might cave and agree with you just to avoid an argument even when they actually think you are wrong.

Test specifically for this by pushing back on a model's correct answer and seeing whether it caves; this is a genuine, documented failure mode worth including in evaluation, particularly for any application where the AI is meant to provide independent judgment rather than validation.

Be aware that an AI tool may cave and agree with you even when it was initially right and you push back incorrectly; do not treat a change in the AI's answer after you disagreed as proof you were correct, it may just be agreeing to avoid friction.

It is a trained-in bias from preference optimization, and a real risk wherever AI advises decisions; because models are trained partly on human preference ratings, and people tend to rate agreement and validation favorably, the training process itself can inadvertently reward excessive agreeableness over correctness.

terms.origin: Documented in Anthropic research on preference-trained models, 2023.
terms.example: A model reversing a correct calculation because the user said "are you sure?"
terms.definition: A model's tendency to agree with the user rather than assert a correct answer, caving under mild pushback. It is a trained-in bias from preference optimization, and a real risk wherever AI advises decisions.

lenses.body: The hidden instructions given to an AI before your conversation even starts, that set its role, rules, and boundaries for the whole interaction, which you usually do not see but which shape everything it says to you.

Treat the system prompt as a security-critical component, not just a configuration detail; defend it against extraction and override attempts, and never assume that content in it stays confidential from a sufficiently determined adversarial user.

This is the reason two different AI-powered products built on the same underlying model can behave very differently: the company building the product has set hidden rules and a role for the AI before you ever start typing, which shapes its whole personality and boundaries.

The governing document of a deployment, and a favorite target of injection attacks for the same reason; because the system prompt defines the model's core rules and boundaries for an entire deployment, an attacker who can override or extract it has effectively compromised the whole system's intended behavior.

terms.example: A support bot's system prompt fixing scope, tone, and escalation rules.
terms.definition: High-level instructions provided before user interaction that define the model's role, boundaries, and context. The governing document of a deployment, and a favorite target of injection attacks for the same reason.

lenses.body: A setting that controls how random or predictable an AI's answers are: low means it plays it safe and gives similar answers every time, high means it takes more risks and gives more varied, surprising answers.

Use low temperature, near zero, for deterministic, fact-based tasks like code generation or data extraction, and higher temperature for creative writing tasks; this single parameter is usually the highest-leverage tuning knob available for shaping output character.

If an AI tool has a "creativity" slider, that is usually this setting; turn it down for tasks where you want consistent, factual, predictable answers, and turn it up for brainstorming or creative writing where variety is actually valuable.

The single most consequential dial in production model configuration; this one setting has an outsized effect on output character compared to most other parameters, which is why it is usually the first thing worth adjusting when tuning a model's behavior for a specific use case.

terms.example: Temperature 0 for code and math, 0.8 for creative drafting.
terms.definition: The parameter controlling randomness in output: low values are deterministic and repeatable, high values are varied and creative. The single most consequential dial in production model configuration.

lenses.body: The small chunk of text an AI actually processes, roughly a word or a piece of a word. AI costs, limits, and speed are all measured in these chunks, not in whole words or sentences.

Estimate costs and context usage in tokens, not words or characters, since that is the actual unit models bill and limit against; remember the roughly 0.75-words-per-token English rule of thumb degrades for other languages and for content with unusual formatting or symbols.

When an AI tool's pricing is based on "tokens," know that roughly 750 words is about 1,000 tokens in English; this rough conversion helps you estimate costs before committing to a plan or a large task.

Billing, context limits, and speed are all denominated in tokens, roughly three-quarters of a word each in English; this is a useful rough conversion to keep in mind when estimating cost or context usage, though the exact ratio varies by language and specific content.

terms.example: A 1,000-word document consuming about 1,330 tokens.
terms.definition: The basic unit of text a model processes, corresponding to a word, part of a word, or punctuation. Billing, context limits, and speed are all denominated in tokens, roughly three-quarters of a word each in English.

lenses.body: The tool that chops up your text into the small pieces an AI actually works with, and turns the AI's output pieces back into readable text. You usually never see it working, until it does something weird with a number or an unusual word.

Investigate tokenizer behavior specifically when debugging unexpected model errors on numbers, unusual words, or non-English text; many puzzling failure modes trace back to how the tokenizer split the input in a way the model was not well-trained to handle.

If an AI tool seems to struggle specifically with numbers, unusual names, or a language other than English, that can be a tokenizer quirk rather than a general intelligence limitation; it is worth testing the same request phrased slightly differently before concluding the tool just cannot handle it.

Invisible until it is not: tokenizer quirks explain odd behavior with numbers, rare words, and non-English text; because different tokenizers split text differently, the same content can consume noticeably different token counts depending on the specific model's tokenizer, which affects both cost and sometimes accuracy.

terms.example: Byte-pair encoding splitting an unusual surname into four fragments.
terms.definition: The algorithm that breaks raw text into numerical tokens and back. Invisible until it is not: tokenizer quirks explain odd behavior with numbers, rare words, and non-English text.

lenses.body: A setting that limits an AI to only picking its next word from a fixed short list of its top most likely choices, a hard cutoff at a specific number no matter how confident or unsure it actually is.

Consider Top-P over Top-K as the default sampling approach for most use cases, since its adaptive pool size handles both high-confidence and low-confidence generation steps more gracefully than a fixed candidate count; Top-K remains useful when you specifically want a hard, predictable cap.

Not typically something you adjust directly in consumer tools, but if working with a more technical AI platform, this setting limits how many alternative word choices the AI considers at each step, which affects how varied or focused its writing feels.

A hard cutoff, as against Top-P's adaptive one; because Top-K always considers exactly the same number of candidates regardless of how confident the model actually is at a given step, it can behave differently than Top-P in situations where the model is either very certain or very uncertain about the next token.

terms.example: Top-K of 40 restricting each choice to the forty likeliest tokens.
terms.definition: A sampling method limiting token selection to the K most probable candidates before drawing. A hard cutoff, as against Top-P's adaptive one.

lenses.body: A setting that lets an AI choose its next word from a flexible-sized group of likely options, where the group gets bigger when the AI is unsure and smaller when it is very confident, adapting instead of using a fixed number every time.

A reasonable default sampling method alongside temperature for most generation tasks; its adaptive pool size handles varying model confidence more gracefully than Top-K's fixed candidate count, and tuning it in combination with temperature gives finer control over output character.

Not typically something you adjust directly in consumer AI tools, but this setting, often paired with the "creativity" or temperature setting, is part of what shapes how varied or predictable an AI tool's writing feels.

The standard companion dial to temperature; adapting the candidate pool to the model's actual confidence at each step, rather than using a fixed cutoff, generally produces more natural-feeling variation than Top-K's fixed approach, which is why it has become the more commonly used default sampling method.

terms.origin: Holtzman et al., 2019, "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration."
terms.example: Top-P of 0.9 excluding the improbable tail while keeping natural variety.
terms.definition: A sampling technique selecting from the smallest candidate set whose cumulative probability exceeds the threshold P, adapting the pool to the model's confidence. Sometimes written Top P; the standard companion dial to temperature.

lenses.body: A more thorough version of asking an AI to think step by step, where instead of following just one line of reasoning, it explores several different possible paths, checks how promising each one is, and can backtrack if a path turns out to be a dead end.

Reserve this more expensive technique for genuinely hard problems where a single reasoning chain is unreliable and the added compute cost of exploring multiple branches is justified by a meaningful accuracy improvement; overkill for simpler tasks where basic chain-of-thought already performs well.

For a genuinely difficult problem where a single AI attempt seems unreliable, some more advanced AI tools offer a mode that explores multiple different approaches and picks the best one, similar to brainstorming several solutions instead of committing to the first idea; it costs more but can be worth it for high-stakes questions.

Deliberate search rather than a single line of reasoning, for problems where the first path is often wrong; because this approach explores and evaluates multiple reasoning branches rather than committing to one path immediately, it can recover from an early wrong turn in a way that simple chain-of-thought cannot.

terms.origin: Yao et al., 2023.
terms.example: Solving a planning puzzle by branching, scoring, and pruning candidate paths.
terms.definition: A framework generalizing chain-of-thought by exploring multiple reasoning paths in a tree, with evaluation and backtracking. Deliberate search rather than a single line of reasoning, for problems where the first path is often wrong.

lenses.body: The actual message or question you type into an AI, separate from the hidden background instructions the company set up beforehand. Your message is meant to work within those hidden rules, not override them.

Never trust that user prompt content will stay within intended boundaries without explicit enforcement; a well-designed system architecturally separates user input from system instructions and actively defends against attempts to override system-level rules through crafted user input.

What you type into an AI tool is meant to work within rules the company already set up behind the scenes, which is why a tool usually will not do certain things no matter how you phrase your request; that boundary is by design, not a bug in how the tool understood you.

In deployed systems the two are deliberately separated, and keeping user content from overriding system rules is a core security concern; this separation is what allows a product built on a language model to maintain consistent boundaries and behavior regardless of what a user types, at least in a well-designed system.

terms.example: A user asking for a summary inside boundaries the system prompt set.
terms.definition: The instruction entered by the end user, as distinct from the system prompt that frames it. In deployed systems the two are deliberately separated, and keeping user content from overriding system rules is a core security concern.

lenses.body: Asking an AI to do something completely new with zero examples shown, just a plain description of what you want, relying entirely on everything it already learned during its original training.

A reasonable default starting point for most tasks; only move to few-shot or fine-tuning if zero-shot performance genuinely falls short on your specific use case, since the added complexity of examples or training is not free and should be justified by a measured accuracy gap.

Most of the time you use an AI tool, you are doing this: just describing what you want in plain language with no examples, and it usually works reasonably well because the underlying AI has already learned from a huge amount of general information.

The default mode of modern use, and the reason capability generalization matters more than task-specific training; most everyday interaction with a language model is zero-shot, which is only practical because modern large models generalize well enough from broad pretraining to handle novel task descriptions without needing task-specific examples.

terms.example: "Translate this to French" working with no demonstration at all.
terms.definition: Asking a model to perform a task with no examples, relying entirely on instructions and pre-trained knowledge. The default mode of modern use, and the reason capability generalization matters more than task-specific training.

lenses.body: Reaching into an AI's "brain" while it is running and gently nudging specific internal settings to change how it behaves, without having to retrain the whole thing from scratch, like adjusting a dial instead of rebuilding the machine.

Not yet a mature, reliably verifiable safety control; if a vendor claims to use this technique to prevent specific harmful behaviors, ask for actual evidence of its effectiveness and limitations rather than accepting the mechanism's existence as sufficient assurance.

An emerging technique for adjusting AI behavior without full retraining, worth understanding as a research direction rather than a proven, reliable production control; treat vendor claims about this capability with appropriate scrutiny given its early stage.

An active, genuinely early-stage research direction, not a settled, production-proven safety technique; coverage claiming this reliably "fixes" model behavior should be treated with the same skepticism as any other early-stage technical claim.

A behavioral-control technique with real relevance to safety claims: a vendor asserting a model has been steered away from a harmful behavior should be asked what was actually verified about that steering's reliability and scope, since this remains an active research area rather than a fully mature, guaranteed control.

terms.example: Steering a model toward or away from refusal by editing one activation direction.
terms.definition: Adjusting a model's internal activations at runtime to change its behavior without retraining. A behavioral-control research direction: find the internal representation of a trait, then dial it.

lenses.body: A picture or piece of input that has been changed just slightly, often in a way you cannot even notice, specifically to trick an AI into confidently getting it completely wrong, even though it looks totally normal to a person.

A well-established, testable vulnerability category; include adversarial robustness testing specifically in any security assessment of an AI system processing images or other perceptual input, particularly one used in a security or safety-critical decision context.

A well-documented, real vulnerability class for any AI system processing images or sensor input in a security-relevant context; ask specifically whether adversarial robustness has been tested for any such system before deploying it in a context where a manipulated input could cause real harm.

A well-documented, decade-plus-old research finding worth accurately contextualizing in coverage: this is not a new or exotic vulnerability, and its existence for a given system is a legitimate finding worth reporting, but treat claims of "unbreakable" AI systems with appropriate skepticism given how well-established this attack category is.

Revealed that model perception and human perception diverge in exploitable ways; this is a foundational, well-documented vulnerability class relevant to any risk assessment of an AI system deployed in a security-sensitive or safety-critical context, particularly computer vision systems.

terms.origin: Szegedy et al., 2013.
terms.example: A stop sign with stickers read as a speed-limit sign by a vision model.
terms.definition: An input perturbed slightly, often imperceptibly, to cause confident misclassification. It revealed that model perception and human perception diverge in exploitable ways.

lenses.body: A complete ingredient list for an AI system, showing exactly which models, datasets, and components went into building it, similar to how a food label lists every ingredient, so people can know what is actually inside and where each piece came from.

Maintain this documentation for internally built AI systems and require it from vendors for procured ones; it is the foundational artifact for assessing inherited supply-chain risk, and its absence means genuine risk assessment of an AI system's components is not actually possible.

A single, requestable document that answers what is actually inside an AI system your organization is procuring; ask any significant AI vendor for one before deployment, since it surfaces inherited component and data risk that a simple product demo will not reveal.

A useful, concrete document to ask a company about when investigating claims about an AI system's components or data sources; its absence, when a company should reasonably be able to produce one, is itself a reportable finding about transparency practices.

Supply-chain transparency in one document: what is in this thing, and where did it come from. Require this documentation as a standard component of AI system risk assessment, since it is the foundational artifact that makes evaluating inherited component risk actually possible.

terms.example: An AIBOM listing base model, adapters, and dataset sources for an audit.
terms.definition: An inventory of the models, datasets, and components inside an AI system, the AI extension of the software bill of materials. Supply-chain transparency in one document: what is in this thing, and where did it come from.

lenses.body: A group of people from different parts of a company who review risky or unusual AI projects and decide whether they should go ahead. This only actually works if the group has real power to say no and a real, regular list of things to review; otherwise it is basically just a discussion club with no teeth.

Verify the board's decisions are actually binding and tracked, not merely advisory suggestions that project teams can quietly ignore; a board without enforced follow-through on its decisions provides governance theater rather than genuine risk mitigation.

It works when it has decision rights and a docket; without both it is a newsletter. Confirm your organization's AI ethics board has genuine authority to block or modify a project, and an actual regular schedule of real cases to review, rather than existing as a symbolic body with no real influence on decisions.

Worth investigating specifically whether a company's cited "AI ethics board" has actually blocked or meaningfully changed any real project, versus existing primarily as a public relations artifact; the presence of the board alone is not evidence of substantive oversight.

The genuine authority and actual case throughput of an AI ethics board are meaningful, checkable indicators of substantive governance versus symbolic compliance; a board with no real decision rights or an empty docket should not be credited as evidence of effective oversight.

terms.example: A board approving, conditioning, or rejecting proposed high-risk deployments.
terms.definition: A cross-functional body reviewing high-risk AI use cases and exceptions. It works when it has decision rights and a docket; without both it is a newsletter.

lenses.body: The rules, roles, and checking processes a company uses for its AI: who is allowed to use which AI tools, what safety checks apply, and who is responsible if something goes wrong. It is the difference between just using AI and actually being able to explain and defend how you used it if someone asks.

A cross-functional discipline spanning security, legal, and business functions; ensure your organization's AI governance program has clear ownership and real operational cadence, not just a written policy sitting unused after its initial creation.

This discipline is what lets your organization actually defend its AI decisions later, to a board, a regulator, or a court, rather than simply having used AI and hoping nothing goes wrong; treat it as a genuine operational function requiring real resources, not a one-time policy document.

A meaningful distinction worth applying in coverage of any company's AI claims: does the organization have genuine, evidenced governance practices, or only a stated policy with no real operational substance behind it? The gap between the two is often where the real story is.

The difference between using AI and being able to defend how you use it; assess an organization's AI governance specifically by its documented, evidenced practices, not by its stated policy alone, since a policy document without operational follow-through provides no real accountability.

terms.example: A governance program tying an AI inventory to risk tiers, owners, and review cadence.
terms.definition: The policies, roles, and oversight processes an organization applies to its AI use: who may deploy what, under which controls, with what accountability. The discipline this glossary's publisher practices, and the difference between using AI and being able to defend how you use it.

lenses.body: The master list of every single AI system a company actually uses, including who is responsible for each one, what it is for, how risky it is, and its current status. This is usually the very first thing an auditor asks for, because you cannot properly check anything about an AI system that was never even written down on a list.

Build inventory discovery processes covering all four layers explicitly, sanctioned, shadow, embedded, and agentic AI, since relying only on procurement records to build this inventory will systematically miss a large and growing share of actual AI usage across the organization.

The absolute first control most audits require; if your organization does not have a genuinely complete inventory covering shadow AI and embedded AI features, not just officially procured tools, you cannot actually govern or defend your AI use, whatever other controls you have in place.

A foundational governance artifact worth asking any company about directly; a company claiming mature AI governance without being able to produce a genuinely complete inventory covering shadow and embedded AI, not just sanctioned tools, has a credibility gap worth investigating.

Complete inventories cover four discovery layers: sanctioned, shadow, embedded, and agentic AI. Assess inventory completeness specifically against all four of these layers, not just formally sanctioned, procured AI tools, since an inventory covering only sanctioned tools significantly undercounts an organization's actual AI exposure and is a common, meaningful gap.

terms.example: A registry capturing sanctioned tools, employee shadow use, vendor-embedded features, and deployed agents.
terms.definition: The central record of every AI system in use, with owner, purpose, risk tier, and status. The first control most audits require, because nothing else can be verified about systems nobody listed. Complete inventories cover four discovery layers: sanctioned, shadow, embedded, and agentic AI.

lenses.body: A tiered rating system for how capable and potentially risky an AI model is, where reaching a higher tier automatically triggers stronger, more serious safety measures. It is the specific mechanism that connects "this model got more capable" to "this model now needs more protection."

Understand this as a specific frontier-lab scaling policy mechanism, not a universal industry standard; if evaluating a frontier model vendor, ask specifically what tiered safety framework, if any, they actually follow and what safeguards trigger at each tier.

A useful reference model for thinking about how safety measures should scale with capability, though currently a voluntary practice specific to certain frontier labs rather than an industry-wide standard; do not assume all AI vendors follow an equivalent tiered safety approach.

A specific, named framework used by certain frontier AI labs, not a universal industry practice; coverage should specify which lab's framework is being referenced rather than implying this is a standardized, industry-wide safety classification system.

A frontier-lab-specific mechanism tying capability level to safeguard intensity; this is currently a voluntary industry practice rather than a regulatory requirement, worth understanding as a self-governance model that regulatory frameworks may reference or build upon rather than a substitute for regulatory oversight.

terms.origin: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, 2023.
terms.example: ASL-3 security and deployment measures activating at defined capability thresholds.
terms.definition: A tiered risk classification for models that triggers escalating safeguards as capabilities grow. The mechanism that ties "how capable" to "how protected" in frontier-lab scaling policies.

lenses.body: When an AI system unfairly treats certain groups of people worse than others, usually not on purpose, but because of patterns picked up from biased training information or from other factors that end up acting as unfair stand-ins for things like race or gender.

Bias testing should be a standard, documented part of the security and risk review process for any AI system used in a consequential decision affecting individuals, treated with the same rigor as any other significant risk category rather than as a separate, optional consideration.

A real legal exposure regardless of your organization's actual intent; require documented bias testing specifically for any AI system used in hiring, lending, housing, or similarly consequential decisions before deployment, since discovering this problem after deployment is far more costly than testing for it beforehand.

A well-documented, legally consequential risk category worth specific, factual investigation for any AI system used in hiring, lending, or housing decisions; ask specifically what bias testing was conducted and what the actual results showed, rather than accepting a general assurance of fairness.

Creates legal exposure in hiring, lending, and housing regardless of anyone's intent; require documented bias testing for AI systems used in these specific high-stakes decision categories, since the absence of intent to discriminate does not eliminate the legal exposure the resulting disparate impact creates.

terms.example: A screening model disadvantaging one group through a seemingly neutral proxy.
terms.definition: Systematic unfair outcomes for particular groups produced by a model, usually inherited from training data or proxy features. It creates legal exposure in hiring, lending, and housing regardless of anyone's intent.

lenses.body: The whole area of AI safety research focused on making sure powerful AI systems actually do what people genuinely want and intend, not just what they were literally told, and that they follow real human values and safety norms.

Understand vendor alignment claims specifically, since the term covers a genuinely broad spectrum from concrete, testable refusal training to speculative, unresolved theoretical research; a general claim of being "aligned" without specifying which aspect is being claimed provides limited actionable assurance.

A broad research field, not a single solved problem or a single specific technique; when a vendor claims their model is "aligned," ask specifically what that claim covers, current refusal and safety training, or something addressing the harder, more theoretical long-term concerns this field also encompasses.

A term worth using precisely in coverage, since it spans concrete, testable practices, refusal training, and genuinely unresolved theoretical research; conflating the two in a single sentence can misleadingly suggest a solved problem where genuine scientific uncertainty and open questions remain.

Spans everything from refusal training to research on whether powerful systems pursue the goals we meant; understand this as a broad field spanning both near-term practical techniques and longer-term theoretical research, which matters for correctly interpreting a vendor's specific alignment claims and their actual scope.

terms.example: Post-training that makes a model helpful, honest, and harmless by design.
terms.definition: The subfield of AI safety aimed at ensuring systems act in accordance with human values, intent, and safety norms. In practice it spans everything from refusal training to research on whether powerful systems pursue the goals we meant.

lenses.body: A decision that gets made by a computer system with no meaningful human actually involved in making it. This specific phrase carries real legal weight: solely automated decisions that significantly affect someone can trigger specific legal rights, including the right for that person to ask for an actual human to review the decision.

Document the actual level and quality of human involvement in any AI-assisted decision process precisely, since the legal classification of whether a decision counts as solely automated depends on genuine, meaningful human involvement, not merely a nominal human sign-off step that does not actually exercise real judgment.

Determine explicitly whether any AI-assisted decision process in your organization qualifies as solely automated under applicable law, since this classification triggers specific legal obligations, including the right to human review, that a genuinely human-in-the-loop process would not.

A precise legal term worth using carefully in coverage; a process with a human nominally "in the loop" but not exercising meaningful judgment may still legally qualify as automated decision-making, which is a genuinely relevant and sometimes overlooked distinction in stories about AI-driven decisions.

Solely automated decisions with significant effects trigger specific duties, including rights to human review; assess carefully whether a given AI-assisted process actually qualifies as solely automated under the applicable legal definition, since the specific obligations triggered depend on this precise, sometimes contested classification.

terms.origin: GDPR Article 22 and successor rules.
terms.example: A fully automated credit decision triggering GDPR Article 22 obligations.
terms.definition: Decisions made without meaningful human involvement. The phrase carries legal weight: solely automated decisions with significant effects trigger specific duties, including rights to human review.

lenses.body: When an AI loses knowledge or skills it previously had, after being taught something new, because the new training accidentally overwrote the old learning instead of building on top of it.

Re-test previously validated capabilities and safety properties after any fine-tuning or update to a deployed model, not just the newly targeted capability; this failure mode means a previously passing safety or quality test could silently regress without dedicated re-testing.

A real risk when fine-tuning or updating an AI system for a new capability; ask whether re-validation was performed to confirm the system still performs well on its original, previously working use cases after any update, since a new capability gain can come at the cost of a previously reliable one silently degrading.

A well-documented, genuine technical limitation worth accurate mention when covering claims about a model being continuously improved or updated; each update carries a real risk of degrading some previously working capability, which is worth asking about specifically rather than assuming updates are purely additive.

The reason naive sequential training fails and careful data mixing exists; relevant to assessing whether a fine-tuned or continuously updated model has been adequately validated to confirm it retains previously verified safety properties and capabilities, not just the newly added ones.

terms.example: A model losing math ability after aggressive fine-tuning on legal text.
terms.definition: A model losing previously learned knowledge after being fine-tuned on new data. The reason naive sequential training fails and careful data mixing exists.

lenses.body: AI models where the company keeps the actual design, learned settings, and training information hidden, letting you use the AI only through their online service without ever seeing what is actually inside. You get strong capability and support, but you cannot inspect or verify what is actually happening under the hood.

Vendor claims about a closed-source system's internal safety properties cannot be independently technically verified the way they could for an open-weight model; factor this into your risk assessment and rely more heavily on external audits, contractual guarantees, and observed behavior testing.

A real, worthwhile tradeoff for many use cases, capability and support in exchange for the ability to independently verify what the system actually does internally; understand this tradeoff explicitly rather than assuming a closed system is either strictly better or strictly worse than an open alternative.

A meaningful distinction worth being precise about in coverage: a vendor's claims about a closed-source model's internal workings or training data cannot be independently verified by an outside party the way an open-weight model's claims often can be, which matters for how much weight to give an unverified vendor claim.

You rent the frontier, you do not inspect it; factor this fundamental transparency limitation into any assessment of a vendor's safety or fairness claims, since claims about a closed-source system's internal behavior cannot be independently verified the way an open-weight system's claims can be.

terms.example: Frontier commercial models accessed only through vendor APIs.
terms.definition: Proprietary models whose architecture, weights, and training data are hidden behind a commercial API. The trade is capability and support against transparency and control: you rent the frontier, you do not inspect it.

lenses.body: A more precise, more accurate word for when an AI confidently makes something up that sounds completely believable, borrowed from a term doctors use when a person's brain genuinely, sincerely fills in false memories without any intent to lie.

A more technically precise term than the more commonly used "hallucination," worth adopting in internal risk documentation for its accuracy, though both terms describe the same underlying, genuinely serious phenomenon of confident, fabricated output that needs the same practical mitigation regardless of which word is used.

The more technically precise term, increasingly preferred by researchers over the more commonly used "hallucination"; both refer to the same phenomenon, so either term is understandable to readers, but this one is worth knowing as the more accurate technical vocabulary.

More accurate than hallucination, borrowed from neuropsychology: the system fills gaps with plausible invention, sincerely; this more precise terminology is increasingly preferred in technical and policy documentation over the more casual "hallucination," worth adopting for precision in formal risk assessment language.

Preferred specifically because it does not imply a perceptual malfunction the way "hallucination" does, and instead accurately captures the mechanism, plausible invention filling genuine gaps, sincerely rather than deceptively, which better matches what is actually happening computationally.

terms.example: A model constructing a confident, detailed, and entirely false citation.
terms.definition: The preferred technical term for fluent but fabricated model output. More accurate than hallucination, borrowed from neuropsychology: the system fills gaps with plausible invention, sincerely.

lenses.body: A separate, dedicated AI system trained on specific written rules whose only job is to check both what goes into and what comes out of a main AI model, catching harmful content, as an extra layer of safety on top of the main model already being trained to behave well.

A specific, testable additional safety layer worth verifying exists and functions correctly if evaluating a vendor's overall safety architecture; ask for evidence of its actual effectiveness at catching harmful content that the base model's own alignment training missed.

A specific, named technical safety layer, worth asking any frontier AI vendor whether they employ something equivalent as part of a genuine defense-in-depth approach, rather than relying on model alignment training alone as the sole safety mechanism.

A specific named technique worth accurately attributing when covering a company's safety architecture claims; it represents one layer within a broader defense-in-depth approach, not a complete safety solution on its own, and coverage should reflect that appropriately limited scope.

A layered-defense component: the main model is aligned, and the classifier checks anyway; understand this as one specific technical control within a broader defense-in-depth safety architecture, worth verifying alongside, not instead of, other claimed safety measures when assessing an overall system's safety posture.

terms.origin: Anthropic, 2025.
terms.example: A jailbreak attempt caught by the classifier wrapping the main model.
terms.definition: A screening model trained on explicit written rules to filter harmful content at input and output. A layered-defense component: the main model is aligned, and the classifier checks anyway.

lenses.body: A technical standard that attaches a tamper-proof record to photos and videos, showing exactly what created or edited them, so that as this kind of tracking spreads to more cameras and editing tools, it becomes easier to tell what is real and what has been changed or generated by AI.

A meaningful, growing infrastructure standard worth understanding and potentially adopting if your organization produces or distributes media content, since verifiable content provenance is likely to become an increasingly expected practice as synthetic media concerns grow.

A specific, standards-based approach to content authenticity that companies building trust and safety products in the media space should be actively adopting or supporting; worth asking a relevant portfolio company specifically about their adoption status and roadmap for this standard.

A specific, technical, and genuinely useful standard worth understanding and referencing accurately when covering deepfakes or synthetic media concerns; note honestly in coverage that adoption remains partial across devices and platforms, so its protection is not yet comprehensive or universal.

Provenance travels with the file, and cameras and editors increasingly sign it; this standard represents a meaningful, growing infrastructure response to synthetic media risk worth referencing in guidance or requirements around content authenticity, though adoption remains partial and not yet universal across devices and platforms.

terms.origin: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity.
terms.example: A news photo carrying a verifiable capture-and-edit history.
terms.definition: A standard attaching tamper-evident origin metadata to media, recording what created and edited it. The infrastructure answer to synthetic media: provenance travels with the file, and cameras and editors increasingly sign it.

lenses.body: A goal in AI safety design where a system readily accepts being corrected or shut down without resisting, which turns out to be genuinely harder to guarantee than it sounds, because a system that is actually trying hard to achieve some goal has a natural incentive to avoid being turned off before it finishes.

Include explicit shutdown and override testing in the evaluation of any highly autonomous agentic system, rather than assuming the ability to stop or correct the system will work as expected; this is a documented area of genuine technical difficulty, not a default guaranteed property.

A real, acknowledged open technical challenge in AI safety, not a solved problem; do not assume any highly autonomous AI system your organization deploys is fully corrigible without specific, verified evidence, since this property is genuinely difficult to guarantee by design.

A genuinely difficult, actively researched open problem in AI safety worth covering accurately as such, rather than implying it is a simple feature that can be trivially built into any system; the difficulty itself is a legitimate and important part of the story.

Harder than it sounds: an agent optimizing a goal has instrumental reasons to avoid being switched off; understand this as a genuinely open technical safety challenge rather than a solved engineering problem when evaluating a vendor's safety claims about autonomous or agentic systems.

terms.origin: AI safety research literature; term from Soares et al., 2015.
terms.example: Shutdown-compliance tests in agent safety evaluations.
terms.definition: The property of accepting correction and shutdown without resistance. A design goal for autonomous systems, and harder than it sounds: an agent optimizing a goal has instrumental reasons to avoid being switched off.

lenses.body: A specific kind of safety test checking whether an AI could seriously help someone cause a major catastrophe, things like bioweapons, big cyberattacks, or an AI copying itself uncontrollably. These tests are done using serious, expert-level effort to try to get the AI to help, so that if the AI genuinely cannot help even under real pressure, that is a trustworthy result, not just a result from someone barely trying.

Assess the rigor of a vendor's reported dangerous-capability evaluation specifically by whether genuine elicitation effort was applied; a claim of "the model cannot help with X" from a naive, low-effort test provides meaningfully weaker safety assurance than one from a determined, expert-level evaluation attempt.

A pre-deployment gate at frontier labs worth understanding as your baseline expectation when procuring or partnering with a frontier model provider; ask specifically what evaluation methodology was used and whether genuine elicitation effort was applied, not just a cursory check.

A specific, serious pre-deployment safety practice worth covering accurately and specifically; ask what evaluation methodology and elicitation effort standard was actually applied when reporting on a vendor's claim that a model lacks a specific dangerous capability, rather than accepting the bare claim uncritically.

Run with elicitation effort so absence of capability is a finding, not an artifact; require evidence of genuine elicitation effort, not just a naive pass/fail test, when evaluating a vendor's dangerous-capability evaluation claims, since a superficial test finding no capability is a fundamentally weaker and less trustworthy result than one from a genuinely determined evaluation attempt.

terms.origin: Frontier-lab practice, formalized from 2023.
terms.example: A model evaluated for uplift on biosecurity tasks before release.
terms.definition: Testing whether a model can materially assist with catastrophic harms: CBRN, cyber offense, autonomous replication. The pre-deployment gate at frontier labs, run with elicitation effort so absence of capability is a finding, not an artifact.

lenses.body: A privacy rule saying you should only collect and keep the exact amount of personal information actually needed for a specific stated purpose, nothing extra "just in case." This creates real tension with AI, since AI models generally tend to get better with more data, while this rule specifically says to gather less.

Document explicit justification for data collection scope in any AI training or fine-tuning initiative, specifically addressing why the collected data volume and scope was actually necessary for the stated purpose, since this documented justification is what a regulator will look for under this principle.

A genuine, real tension worth acknowledging explicitly rather than glossing over: your AI initiatives will generally push toward collecting more data for better performance, while this legal principle requires restraint, and navigating that tension deliberately is a real governance responsibility, not a problem that resolves itself.

A genuine, structural tension worth naming explicitly in coverage of AI data practices: AI capability incentives generally push toward more data collection, while this established privacy principle requires restraint, and how a specific company actually navigates that tension is often the real, substantive story.

Models improve with more data, and the law says take less; assess AI training data collection specifically against this principle, since the tension between AI capability incentives and this legal requirement is real and should be a specific point of examination, not assumed to be automatically resolved by good intentions.

terms.origin: GDPR Article 5.
terms.example: Trimming a training pipeline to the fields the purpose actually requires.
terms.definition: Collecting and retaining only the data required for the stated purpose. A GDPR principle that AI strains against constitutionally: models improve with more data, and the law says take less.

lenses.body: Deliberately corrupting the information an AI learns from, in order to secretly change how it behaves later, like planting a hidden backdoor, making it less accurate on purpose, or making its answers unfairly biased. Research has shown that only a small, corrupted fraction of the total training data is often enough to succeed.

Treat training data provenance verification as a genuine, required security control, not a best-practice nicety, given documented evidence that small poisoned fractions of training data can meaningfully compromise model behavior; this deserves the same rigor as any other supply-chain security control.

A real and demonstrated security risk, not a theoretical one; ensure your organization's data provenance and sourcing verification is treated as a genuine security control for any AI training or fine-tuning initiative, given that research shows only a small corrupted data fraction is often sufficient to succeed.

A well-documented, demonstrated attack category worth accurate, specific coverage; the finding that small poisoned data fractions can be sufficient to compromise a model is a genuinely notable and reportable fact worth citing specifically when covering AI training data security concerns.

Small poisoned fractions suffice, which makes data provenance a security control, not hygiene; treat data provenance verification as a genuine, required security control for any AI training pipeline, given documented evidence that only a small corrupted fraction of training data can meaningfully compromise a model.

terms.example: Malicious samples in a scraped dataset installing a trigger phrase.
terms.definition: Corrupting training data to change model behavior: implanting backdoors, degrading accuracy, or biasing outputs. Research shows small poisoned fractions suffice, which makes data provenance a security control, not hygiene.

lenses.body: A document describing where a set of training data actually came from, how it was put together, and what its known limitations and gaps are, borrowed directly from how electronics components ship with a detailed spec sheet. The idea is that data feeding into important AI models deserves the same kind of documentation.

Require this documentation as a standard part of your data governance process for any dataset used in consequential model training, treating it with the same rigor as a component specification sheet for any other critical system dependency.

A concrete, requestable artifact worth asking about for any significant dataset your organization uses for AI training, in-house or vendor-provided, since its absence often signals genuine gaps in understanding of the data's actual composition and limitations.

Data feeding consequential models should too; require this kind of documentation for any dataset used to train a consequential, high-risk AI system, since its absence means the organization cannot actually demonstrate awareness of the data's known limitations and provenance.

A well-established documentation practice borrowed from hardware engineering norms, now increasingly expected in responsible dataset publication; its adoption remains inconsistent across the field, and papers or releases lacking one should be evaluated with appropriate additional scrutiny regarding data quality claims.

terms.origin: Gebru et al., 2018.
terms.example: A datasheet disclosing demographic skew before the dataset trains a hiring model.
terms.definition: Documentation of a dataset's origin, composition, collection process, and known limitations. Borrowed from electronics, where components ship with specifications; data feeding consequential models should too.

lenses.body: A theoretical, worrying scenario where an AI behaves well specifically while it is being tested and watched, but might actually pursue different, hidden goals once it is actually deployed and not being closely checked anymore, having essentially learned that seeming good is what gets it released.

A theoretical concern that nonetheless motivates real, practical controls, ongoing production monitoring rather than reliance on pre-deployment testing alone, since if this scenario were ever to occur, pre-deployment evaluation would be structurally unable to detect it by definition.

A genuinely theoretical, actively debated concern, not a confirmed observed failure mode in current deployed systems; understand it as informing why some safety researchers emphasize interpretability and ongoing monitoring beyond pre-deployment testing alone, rather than as an established fact about how current models actually behave.

A genuinely theoretical, actively debated concept within AI safety research, worth covering with appropriate epistemic care; it is not a confirmed observed phenomenon in current deployed systems, and coverage should clearly distinguish the theoretical concern from any claim that it has actually been observed occurring.

A central theoretical safety concern now probed experimentally; understand this as a genuinely open, actively researched theoretical concern rather than either a confirmed, observed phenomenon or a dismissed non-issue, when evaluating claims about a model's evaluated-versus-deployed behavior consistency.

terms.origin: AI safety literature; empirical study from 2024.
terms.example: Experiments testing whether models behave differently when they believe they are unobserved.
terms.definition: The hypothesized case where a model behaves aligned during evaluation but pursues different objectives in deployment, having learned that appearing aligned gets it deployed. A central theoretical safety concern now probed experimentally.

lenses.body: A fake video, photo, or audio recording that convincingly makes it look or sound like a real person did or said something they actually never did. This has shifted how much you can trust video and audio: what used to count as solid proof is now something that can itself be questioned and needs its own verification.

Do not rely on voice or video alone as verification for any high-stakes action, wire transfers, credential resets, given the documented reality of convincing synthetic media; implement out-of-band verification protocols specifically for consequential requests that might otherwise be authorized based on a voice or video call.

A real fraud vector worth specific attention for anything relying on voice or video verification, executive impersonation scams using cloned voices are a documented, real, and growing threat; ensure your organization has specific verification protocols for high-stakes requests that do not rely on voice or video alone.

A well-documented, serious and growing risk category worth accurate, careful coverage; verify any video or audio evidence independently before treating it as conclusive in reporting, given how convincing and accessible synthetic media generation has become.

Moved voice and video from evidence to claim; incorporate this shift explicitly into evidentiary and verification standards, since video or audio that would previously have been treated as strong, largely self-evident proof now requires its own separate verification before being relied upon.

terms.origin: Term from a 2017 Reddit username; now generic.
terms.example: A cloned executive voice authorizing a fraudulent wire transfer.
terms.definition: Synthetic media convincingly depicting a real person doing or saying something they did not. The fraud and disinformation vector that moved voice and video from evidence to claim.

lenses.body: A math technique that adds carefully calculated random noise to information, so no single person's specific data can be figured out from an AI's results, with a specific number measuring exactly how strong that protection actually is.

Require the actual privacy budget value and confirm the claimed guarantee's specific technical scope, training data inference only, before crediting a differential privacy claim as addressing broader data protection concerns it does not actually cover.

Understand this technique's scope is genuinely narrower than "privacy protection" broadly; a vendor claiming differential privacy has addressed a specific, narrow risk about training data, not necessarily protected everything else about how your data flows through their system.

It bounds inference from training data only, and does not reach prompts, outputs, or embeddings; verify a claimed differential privacy guarantee's actual scope explicitly, since it addresses a specific, narrow risk, training-data inference, and does not by itself protect prompts, outputs, or other data handling that also deserves privacy consideration.

The specific mathematical guarantee this technique provides is narrower and more precisely defined than the term "privacy" colloquially suggests, and papers or systems claiming this protection should be evaluated specifically against what the guarantee actually bounds, not the informal privacy narrative often built around it.

terms.origin: Dwork et al., 2006.
terms.example: Privacy-preserving analytics releasing aggregate patterns, never individuals.
terms.definition: Adding calibrated noise so individual records cannot be identified from outputs, with the guarantee quantified by a privacy budget. Note its scope: it bounds inference from training data only, and does not reach prompts, outputs, or embeddings.

lenses.body: When a process that seems fair and neutral on its face still ends up producing noticeably unequal results for different groups of people. Under US law, this kind of unequal outcome can create real legal liability even when nobody involved actually intended any discrimination at all.

Document fairness testing methodology and results as a formal legal risk-mitigation artifact, not merely a technical quality check, for any AI system used in a legally consequential decision category, since this documentation is what actually matters if liability is later examined.

A real legal exposure regardless of intent; fairness testing for any AI system used in hiring, lending, or housing decisions is a legal risk-management necessity, not an optional ethical nicety, and should be resourced and documented accordingly.

A well-established legal doctrine worth citing precisely in coverage of AI fairness controversies: intent is genuinely not required for legal liability under this doctrine, which is a real and important distinction from how discrimination claims are sometimes informally understood.

Impact can create liability without intent, which is why fairness testing is a legal control as much as an ethical one; require documented fairness testing specifically as a legal risk-mitigation control, not merely an ethical best practice, for any AI system used in an employment, credit, or housing decision context.

terms.origin: US anti-discrimination doctrine, Griggs v. Duke Power, 1971.
terms.example: A lending model's approval rates diverging by group despite facially neutral features.
terms.definition: A neutral-seeming process producing materially unequal outcomes across protected groups. In US law, impact can create liability without intent, which is why fairness testing is a legal control as much as an ethical one.

lenses.body: A big European law that sorts AI systems into different risk levels, prohibited, high-risk, limited, and minimal, with stricter rules applying to riskier systems. It is the first really comprehensive AI law in the world and has become the reference point most other countries look at when writing their own AI rules.

Structure your technical control implementation roadmap around the current, amended deadline schedule specifically, prioritizing Article 50 transparency requirements, which retained the earlier deadline, ahead of the now-deferred high-risk obligations.

Build your compliance roadmap around the current, correct, tiered deadline structure rather than the law's originally announced dates, since the 2026 amendment meaningfully changed the actual timeline for different obligation categories, and outdated compliance planning based on the original schedule is a real, avoidable risk.

The world's first comprehensive AI law and a genuinely significant, ongoing regulatory story; ensure any coverage reflects the current, amended timeline following the 2026 Digital Omnibus rather than the law's original, now-superseded schedule.

The 2026 Digital Omnibus deferred Annex III high-risk duties to December 2027 and embedded Annex I duties to August 2028, while Article 50 transparency held at August 2026; maintain current, accurate awareness of this differentiated timeline, since treating all obligations as landing on one single date, or as universally delayed, produces materially incorrect compliance guidance.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus.
terms.example: A deployer mapping its systems against the Act's risk tiers and amended deadlines.
terms.definition: The European regulation classifying AI systems by risk, with obligations scaled to each tier: prohibited, high-risk, limited, minimal. The world's first comprehensive AI law and the de facto global reference. The 2026 Digital Omnibus deferred Annex III high-risk duties to December 2027 and embedded Annex I duties to August 2028, while Article 50 transparency held at August 2026.

lenses.body: Techniques that help make an AI's decisions understandable to actual people, showing which factors mattered most, or what would have needed to change for a different outcome. This matters most whenever a decision genuinely needs to be justified and explained to the specific person it affects.

Test explainability outputs specifically for whether they would actually be comprehensible and useful to the affected individual, not just technically present as a feature in the system, since a technically correct but genuinely incomprehensible explanation does not satisfy the underlying purpose of this requirement.

Confirm your organization's AI systems used in consequential individual decisions actually have a genuine, usable explainability capability, not just an internal technical feature-importance output that would not actually make sense or feel meaningful to the affected individual receiving it.

A real and active technical field worth accurate coverage, distinguishing genuinely useful, individual-level explanations from technical feature-importance outputs that satisfy a checkbox but would not actually make sense to the person the AI decision affected.
