Report the specific, differentiated dates accurately rather than characterizing this broadly as "the EU delayed its AI law," since the transparency requirement deadline was explicitly left unchanged, and conflating it with the deferred high-risk obligations produces a materially inaccurate account.

A deferral of the heaviest lift, not a dismantling: registration duties and the Act's architecture stand; track the specific new dates precisely, Annex III to December 2, 2027, Annex I embedded systems to August 2, 2028, Article 50 transparency unchanged at August 2, 2026, since treating this as a general delay rather than a specific, tiered rescheduling will produce incorrect compliance timelines.

terms.origin: Adopted by the European Parliament June 16 and the Council June 29, 2026; signed July 8, 2026.
terms.example: A compliance team re-baselining its high-risk roadmap to December 2027 while keeping Article 50 on the original clock.
terms.definition: The 2026 EU amending regulation that deferred the AI Act's high-risk obligations, Annex III standalone systems to December 2, 2027 and Annex I embedded systems to August 2, 2028, while leaving Article 50 transparency at August 2, 2026 and adding a new Article 5 prohibition on AI-generated child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate imagery. A deferral of the heaviest lift, not a dismantling: registration duties and the Act's architecture stand.

lenses.body: A number that checks whether AI is actually producing more real, usable work per hour of human labor, or whether the "time saved" is just being eaten up by extra checking and fixing.

Calculated as net completed output value divided by total labor hours across generation, review, correction, and release. A rising ratio means AI is producing more usable value per labor hour; a flat one means activity without economic change; a declining one means correction debt may be exceeding visible time savings. The discipline: do not scale what you cannot measure.

A more rigorous efficiency signal than headline "hours saved" claims, since it nets out the review and correction time those claims typically omit; ask a portfolio company for this ratio rather than accepting an unaudited time-savings figure.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A proposal team whose NEYR™ fell after an AI drafting tool, because review and correction hours rose faster than drafting time dropped.
terms.definition: The performance ratio measuring whether AI is producing more usable business value per unit of labor, calculated as net completed output value divided by total labor hours across generation, review, correction, and release. A rising NEYR™ means AI is producing more usable value per labor hour; a flat NEYR™ means AI activity is not changing the economics of the workflow; a declining NEYR™ means AI may be creating correction debt or rework that exceeds the visible time savings. Its discipline: do not scale what you cannot measure.

lenses.body: A number that turns the vague complaint "AI is creating more work" into something you can actually measure: how many hidden hours of fixing and double-checking happen for every unit of AI-assisted work produced.

Calculated as total weekly untracked manual correction, verification, reformatting, and bypass hours divided by total weekly AI-supported workflow volume. A rising figure means more hidden administrative drag per unit of output; a flat one means friction persists despite continued use; a declining one is evidence corrective action is working.

If it feels like your team spends a lot of time fixing or reformatting AI output, try to actually count those hours against how much AI-assisted work gets produced. That ratio is more honest than the feeling alone.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: An OLF™ climbing as employees quietly build spreadsheet workarounds around an AI tool nobody trusts.
terms.definition: The friction ratio that turns a vague "AI is creating more work" complaint into a measurable control indicator, calculated as total weekly untracked manual correction, verification, reformatting, and bypass hours divided by total weekly AI-supported workflow volume. A rising OLF™ means the workflow is creating more hidden administrative drag per unit of output; a flat OLF™ means friction is not improving despite continued use; a declining OLF™ means corrective action may be working and the workflow moving toward readiness.

lenses.body: A Colorado law that would have been the first big, comprehensive AI law in the US, but it got repealed before it ever actually took effect. It is still often incorrectly described as a current, live law that other states are copying, which is a common and important mistake to avoid.

The Colorado Privacy Act's profiling opt-out survived the repeal untouched and is what actually binds there today; ensure your compliance documentation reflects this correct, current binding requirement rather than the repealed AI Act, since citing the wrong law as your compliance basis creates a real documentation accuracy problem.

Correct this specific, common misconception if it appears in any compliance briefing your organization receives; the law was repealed before taking effect, and continuing to treat it as a live compliance requirement, or a model other states are actively copying in its original form, reflects genuinely outdated information.

A frequently and incorrectly cited law worth fact-checking carefully before publication; confirm current status before describing this as an active or currently binding law, since its repeal before taking effect is a well-documented but commonly missed fact in AI policy coverage.

It is still widely cited as a live model other states are copying, which is the most common error in US state AI briefings; verify current status explicitly before citing this law in any compliance document, since its repeal is a well-documented but frequently overlooked fact that undermines the credibility of any analysis assuming it is still in force.

terms.origin: Colorado SB 24-205 (2024), repealed by SB 26-189, 14 May 2026.
terms.example: A vendor questionnaire still asking for Colorado AI Act compliance a year after the repeal.
terms.definition: The Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act, SB 24-205, which would have been the first comprehensive US state AI law, repealed by SB 26-189 on 14 May 2026 before it ever took effect. It is still widely cited as a live model other states are copying, which is the most common error in US state AI briefings. The Colorado Privacy Act's profiling opt-out survived the repeal untouched and is what actually binds there today.

lenses.body: A specific European privacy law provision giving people the right not to have important decisions made about them entirely by a computer with no meaningful human involved, when that decision has a real legal or otherwise significant effect on them. This law has been in force and enforceable for years already, well before Europe's newer, dedicated AI law even existed.

Ensure compliance with this specific, already fully enforced requirement is tracked independently from AI Act compliance planning, since the two are separate legal obligations with genuinely different, non-overlapping timelines, and treating them as one combined compliance project risks missing this older, currently binding requirement.

Do not assume EU AI Act deadline extensions provide any relief here; this is a separate, already fully enforced legal obligation that has applied for years and continues to apply regardless of the AI Act's own, more recently deferred timeline for other obligations.

A specific, currently and fully enforced legal provision predating the EU AI Act by eight years, worth citing precisely and distinctly from newer AI Act obligations in any coverage discussing automated decision-making rights, since conflating the two obscures which specific legal protection is actually already active today.

Reaches automated decisions whose AI Act obligations have been deferred to 2027 and 2028; enforce this provision's current, active requirements independent of AI Act deferrals, since organizations sometimes incorrectly assume AI Act deadline extensions provide relief from this separate, already fully enforced GDPR obligation, which they genuinely do not.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 22.
terms.example: An automated credit refusal triggering a right to human intervention and an explanation.
terms.definition: The GDPR provision giving people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects. It predates the EU AI Act by eight years, is fully enforced now, and reaches automated decisions whose AI Act obligations have been deferred to 2027 and 2028.

lenses.body: The specific, named person in charge of managing an organization's AI risks, who bridges the gap between company leaders, lawyers, and technical teams. Unlike some similar roles required by law, this position's actual power depends entirely on what the organization itself decides to give it; without real budget or the power to say no, it is just a title.

Clarify explicitly how this role's authority intersects with security, legal, and technical decision-making, since without a statutory definition, ambiguity about actual authority is a common and genuine governance failure mode for this specific position.

Since this role, unlike the statutorily defined Data Protection Officer, derives its authority entirely from how your organization defines it, ensure it comes with real budget and real veto power over risky deployments; a title alone accomplishes nothing.

Worth investigating specifically whether a company's named AI Officer has genuine authority, budget and veto power over deployment decisions, versus holding a purely titular role with no real operational power; the two are meaningfully different and easily confused in press coverage.

An AI Officer without budget or veto is a title, not a control; assess this role's actual authority, not just its formal existence, when evaluating an organization's AI governance maturity, since a titled but powerless role provides no genuine accountability regardless of how it is described.

terms.origin: Organizational practice; not a statutory role under the EU AI Act.
terms.example: An AI Officer signing off on the risk classification of every new AI deployment.
terms.definition: The named executive accountable for AI risk across an organization, translating between leadership, legal, and technical teams. Unlike the Data Protection Officer under GDPR, the role is not created by statute, so its authority comes entirely from how the organization defines it. An AI Officer without budget or veto is a title, not a control.

lenses.body: The person who actually handles the day-to-day busywork of keeping an organization's AI oversight running: keeping the list of AI tools current, chasing down missing paperwork, scheduling reviews, and making sure records do not go stale.

A distinct operational role from the AI Officer's strategic accountability; without someone specifically doing this administrative maintenance work, an AI inventory and governance program tends to go stale within months, regardless of how well the initial policy was designed.

The role exists because governance fails at the administrative layer far more often than at the decision layer; ensure this role or function actually exists and has real time allocated to it, since a governance policy with no one doing the ongoing administrative maintenance work tends to decay into an outdated document nobody trusts.

The presence of a dedicated operational role maintaining AI governance records is a meaningful, checkable indicator of whether an organization's AI governance program is actually being sustained day to day, versus existing only as a policy document that was written once and never actively maintained.

terms.origin: Organizational practice; not a statutory role.
terms.example: A coordinator keeping the AI register accurate so the officer's decisions rest on real data.
terms.definition: The operational counterpart to the AI Officer, running day-to-day governance: maintaining the AI inventory, chasing documentation, scheduling reviews, and keeping records current. The role exists because governance fails at the administrative layer far more often than at the decision layer.

lenses.body: A part-time or shared leader in charge of a company's AI decisions and safety, for businesses that need someone accountable but cannot afford or justify a full-time person in that role.

The accountability is identical to a full-time in-house role; only the headcount and time commitment differ. For most mid-market organizations, this is the realistic form real AI governance accountability actually takes, not a lesser substitute for it.

A mid-market portfolio company with meaningful AI exposure and no named accountable owner, fractional or full-time, has a real governance gap; the fractional model is a legitimate and cost-appropriate way to close it, worth recommending in diligence follow-ups.

You likely cannot justify a full-time AI executive, but someone should still be clearly accountable for your AI decisions and risk, even part-time or shared with another role. Nobody being accountable is worse than partial accountability.

terms.origin: Advisory market practice, following the fractional CFO and virtual CISO models.
terms.example: A 200-person manufacturer retaining a fractional AI Officer two days a month to chair its AI review board.
terms.definition: A part-time or shared AI Officer engaged by organizations that need accountable AI governance but cannot justify a full-time executive. The accountability is identical to the in-house role, only the headcount differs. For most mid-market operators this is the realistic form the role takes.

lenses.body: A specific, independent privacy job required by European law for organizations doing large-scale monitoring or handling especially sensitive personal information, who reports directly to top leadership and cannot be punished for doing the job properly. This role is very often, and incorrectly, assumed to also cover general AI governance, which it does not automatically do.

Clarify explicit boundaries between DPO responsibilities and AI governance responsibilities in your organization's formal governance structure, since assuming overlap without deliberately confirming it is a common and consequential gap.

Do not assume your DPO automatically covers AI governance; these are related but genuinely distinct responsibilities, and this common conflation is a real governance gap worth explicitly resolving with clear, separate accountability for each.

Worth noting the specific acronym collision in coverage: in a privacy context this means Data Protection Officer, while in a machine learning context the same three letters, DPO, refer to Direct Preference Optimization, an entirely unrelated training technique, and conflating the two in a story is a real and avoidable error.

The role is frequently, and wrongly, assumed to cover AI governance; clarify explicitly in any assessment whether an organization has a properly functioning DPO role and separately whether AI governance is actually being handled by a distinct function, since conflating the two is a common and meaningful gap.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Articles 37 to 39.
terms.example: A DPO advising on a DPIA while an AI Officer owns the AI Act obligations.
terms.definition: The independent privacy role GDPR requires where an organization's core activities involve large-scale systematic monitoring or large-scale special-category processing. The DPO reports to the highest level of management and cannot be penalised for doing the job. The role is frequently, and wrongly, assumed to cover AI governance. Note the acronym collision: in machine learning, DPO means Direct Preference Optimization.

lenses.body: The one specific, named person officially accountable for a particular AI system throughout its whole life: what it is for, how well it performs, its documentation, and any failures. When that specific system misbehaves, this named person is the one who actually gets the call, and every single system on an official AI list needs to have a real, named person in this role, not just the vendor listed instead.

Enforce a strict, no-exceptions policy that every AI system inventory entry requires a specific, named internal owner before it can be considered properly governed, treating "vendor" or a blank field as an unacceptable, incomplete answer that leaves a genuine accountability gap.

Verify every single system in your organization's AI inventory actually has a real, named, internal owner, not simply "the vendor" or an unassigned blank field; a genuinely unowned system is one that nobody is actually accountable for when something eventually goes wrong.

A specific, checkable governance practice worth investigating directly when covering an AI-related incident or failure: was there actually a genuinely accountable, named internal owner for the system in question, or did accountability effectively terminate at an external vendor with no real internal ownership?

The vendor is not an acceptable answer; require a genuine, named internal individual for every system in a compliance-relevant AI inventory, since accountability that terminates at an external vendor rather than a specific internal named person does not satisfy the underlying purpose of this ownership requirement.

terms.origin: Adapted from model risk management practice, notably SR 11-7 and its 2026 successor.
terms.example: The head of talent acquisition listed as model owner for the CV screening tool.
terms.definition: The named individual accountable for one specific AI system across its life: purpose, performance, documentation, and failures. When the system misbehaves, the owner gets the call. Every entry in the AI register needs one, and the vendor is not an acceptable answer.

lenses.body: The AI does its job by itself while a person watches and can step in if something looks wrong, instead of the AI having to stop and ask permission for every single step.

Verify the monitoring is real: check that alerts fire fast enough to matter and that the person assigned to monitor actually has the access and attention to intervene, rather than a role that exists on an org chart but not in practice.

This only functions as a real control if the monitoring interface surfaces problems in time to act; build visibility into what the agent is doing as it happens, not just a log to review afterward, or the "on the loop" oversight is theoretical.

Suits medium-risk, reversible decisions where requiring approval on every step would defeat the point of automating it, but only works if the human monitor genuinely has visibility and time to intervene, not just nominal responsibility.

terms.origin: Control-systems and human-factors engineering, adopted into AI governance vocabulary.
terms.example: An analyst watching an automated pricing engine, able to halt it before the next cycle.
terms.definition: A design where AI executes autonomously while a human monitors and retains the power to intervene mid-run. It suits medium-risk, reversible decisions where approving every step would destroy the value of automating it. The control only works if the monitor can see what the system is doing in time to stop it.

lenses.body: The AI acts completely on its own and a person only checks what happened afterward, if ever. This is only okay for small, easy-to-undo actions where a mistake will not cause real harm.

Defensible only where every action is genuinely low-stakes and reversible and logging is reliable enough to reconstruct what happened; the audit trail is the sole remaining control, so if logging fails, there is no control left at all.

Most organizations arrive here by drift, not decision: approval fatigue quietly turns human-in-the-loop into human-out-of-the-loop over time. Periodically check whether your "supervised" systems are actually still being supervised.

A system operating with no human oversight is defensible only where risk and reversibility genuinely support it, and that determination, along with the logging that substitutes for real-time oversight, should be documented and justified, not assumed.

terms.origin: Control-systems and human-factors engineering; the third rung of the oversight ladder.
terms.example: An AI system auto-tagging support tickets, with a weekly sample review.
terms.definition: A design where AI acts alone and humans review after the fact, if at all. Defensible only for low-risk, easily reversible actions with reliable logging, because the audit trail is the sole remaining control. Most organizations arrive here by drift rather than by decision.

lenses.body: A well-documented human tendency to trust an automatic system's output too much and stop applying your own careful judgment, and this tendency actually gets stronger, not weaker, the more confident and fluent the AI's explanation sounds. This is exactly how a "human checking the AI's work" step can quietly turn into just a rubber stamp.

Design human oversight controls with this specific, documented bias explicitly in mind; a review step that does not actively counteract the tendency toward over-trust in confident-sounding AI output is likely to degrade into rubber-stamping over time, regardless of the original intent behind the control.

A real, well-documented risk that a human review requirement does not automatically solve; ask specifically what your organization does to counteract this tendency, more confident AI output tends to get less scrutiny, not more, which is exactly backwards from what a genuine safety check requires.

A well-documented, named phenomenon worth citing accurately in coverage of AI oversight failures; when a "human in the loop" control fails, this documented bias is often the actual underlying mechanism, worth investigating specifically rather than attributing the failure to simple negligence.

The EU AI Act names it explicitly: human oversight measures for high-risk systems must keep operators aware of it. Require documented, specific mitigation for this named, well-established risk in any human-oversight design for a high-risk AI system, since a human review step alone does not automatically counteract this documented cognitive tendency.

terms.origin: Human-factors research from the 1990s onward; named in EU AI Act Article 14(4)(b).
terms.example: A reviewer approving an AI recommendation they would have questioned from a colleague.
terms.definition: The documented tendency of people to over-trust automated output and under-apply their own judgment, which strengthens the more fluent and confident the system's explanation sounds. The EU AI Act names it explicitly: human oversight measures for high-risk systems must keep operators aware of it. It is the mechanism by which human-in-the-loop quietly becomes rubber-stamp.

lenses.body: A common failure where a person supposedly reviewing and approving an AI's output actually signs off without genuinely checking it carefully, which creates the paperwork and appearance of real oversight without any of its actual substance. This usually happens because reviewing tons of low-stakes items trains people to just quickly approve everything, including the rare, genuinely important item that actually needed real scrutiny.

Design review workload and checkpoint frequency deliberately to actively avoid inducing this well-documented failure mode; excessive low-stakes review volume is the well-established, specific cause, so consider reducing unnecessary review checkpoints on genuinely low-risk items to preserve reviewer attention and scrutiny for the items that actually warrant it.

A genuine, common, and easy-to-overlook failure mode worth actively testing for, not just assuming will not happen; periodically audit whether your organization's human review checkpoints are catching genuine problems in practice, or whether reviewers have quietly settled into automatically approving everything that comes through.

A well-documented, genuinely common failure mode worth investigating specifically when covering an oversight failure story; ask directly whether the human reviewer in question was realistically positioned to catch a genuine problem, or whether review volume and approval fatigue had likely already degraded their actual scrutiny.

It passes an audit that counts approvals and fails one that tests them; design compliance audits specifically to test the actual substance of review decisions, not merely count that an approval step formally occurred, since a purely count-based audit methodology is structurally unable to detect this well-documented, common failure mode.

terms.origin: Descriptive governance term rather than a term of art; the observed failure mode of human-in-the-loop controls.
terms.example: A queue of 400 daily AI recommendations cleared at a rate no one could genuinely review.
terms.definition: The failure mode where a human approver signs off on AI output without real scrutiny, producing the paperwork of governance without the substance. It passes an audit that counts approvals and fails one that tests them. Approval fatigue on low-stakes items is the usual cause.

lenses.body: The category under Europe's AI law with the toughest full set of requirements: careful risk management, good data practices, detailed documentation, logging, real human oversight, and formal compliance checking. Even though the actual deadlines for these specific duties got pushed back to 2027 and 2028, the separate legal responsibility for harm caused by a failing system was not delayed at all.

Continue building toward the full high-risk obligation stack on a genuine urgency basis despite the extended formal deadline, since the strict product liability exposure for a failing system remains fully in effect regardless of the compliance deadline extension.

Do not treat the deferred compliance deadlines as deferred risk; the underlying legal liability for harm caused by a failing high-risk system was not delayed alongside the compliance deadline, so meaningful preparation work should continue on its original urgency even with the extended formal deadline.

A specific and important distinction worth precise coverage: the compliance deadline extension and the underlying legal liability exposure are two genuinely separate things, and characterizing the deadline extension as removing legal risk for a failing system would be a materially inaccurate account.

The 2026 Digital Omnibus deferred these duties to December 2027 and August 2028; it did not defer the strict product liability that attaches to failing them. Communicate this critical distinction explicitly, since organizations may incorrectly assume the deferred compliance deadline also delays their underlying legal exposure for actual harm, which it genuinely does not.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 6 to 27; deadlines amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus.
terms.example: A CV screening tool inheriting the whole high-risk stack because hiring is an Annex III use case.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act tier carrying the full obligation stack: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy and robustness, and conformity assessment. Systems arrive either as safety components of already-regulated products (Annex I) or through the listed use cases in Annex III, such as hiring, credit, education, and essential services. The 2026 Digital Omnibus deferred these duties to December 2027 and August 2028; it did not defer the strict product liability that attaches to failing them.

lenses.body: A category under Europe's AI law where the main requirement is simply telling people clearly, rather than extensive documentation: people must be told they are talking to an AI, and AI-generated content must be clearly labeled as such. This applies to things like chatbots and deepfakes, and its deadline actually landed earlier than the deadline for the more serious high-risk category.

Implement the specific technical disclosure and labeling requirements for this category on the original, unchanged timeline, since it is a genuinely simpler compliance lift than the high-risk tier but still carries a real, binding, and now comparatively nearer-term deadline.

Prioritize compliance with this category's transparency requirements specifically, since its deadline was left unchanged and now actually lands before the more prominent, deferred high-risk obligations; do not let attention to the deferred high-risk timeline cause this nearer, still-binding deadline to be overlooked.

A specific compliance category with its own distinct, unchanged deadline worth accurate coverage, particularly given the counterintuitive fact that this "lighter" category's requirement now lands before the more heavily covered high-risk deadline that was actually deferred.

Its deadline of 2 August 2026 was left untouched by the Digital Omnibus, so it now lands well before the high-risk obligations it was originally scheduled behind; enforce and track this earlier, unchanged deadline with appropriate urgency, since organizations focused primarily on the more prominent, deferred high-risk deadlines may overlook this nearer-term, still-binding transparency obligation.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 50.
terms.example: A customer service chatbot disclosing that it is an AI system at the start of the conversation.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act tier where the duty is disclosure rather than documentation: people must be told they are interacting with AI, and synthetic content must be marked as such. It covers chatbots, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, and deepfakes. Its deadline of 2 August 2026 was left untouched by the Digital Omnibus, so it now lands well before the high-risk obligations it was originally scheduled behind.

lenses.body: A specific list of AI uses that are completely banned under Europe's AI law, and breaking these rules carries the harshest possible penalties, up to a massive percentage of a company's entire worldwide revenue. This list includes things like social scoring systems, scraping facial images without permission, and most real-time facial recognition scanning in public places, and a new ban on certain harmful AI-generated content involving real people was added in 2026.

Screen every AI use case explicitly against this full, current list before deployment, given the severity of penalties attached to any violation; this screening should happen at the earliest possible stage of any AI project, well before other, lower-stakes compliance considerations are addressed.

Confirm explicit legal review of your organization's AI use against this specific, complete, and updated banned-practices list, given the exceptionally severe penalty structure attached to this category; this deserves the highest priority in any AI compliance review, well above lower-tier obligations.

A specific, currently enforced, and recently expanded list worth precise and current coverage; ensure any reporting reflects the 2026 addition specifically, since describing the prohibited list using only its original scope would omit a genuinely significant, recent expansion.

Applicable since 2 February 2025 and carrying the highest penalties, up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of global turnover; maintain current awareness of this list's full, updated scope including the 2026 addition, since this category carries the most severe penalty structure under the entire regulation and any gap in compliance understanding here carries the highest stakes.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 5; extended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus.
terms.example: An employer dropping a sentiment-detection feature that scored staff mood during calls.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act's banned uses, applicable since 2 February 2025 and carrying the highest penalties, up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of global turnover. They include social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, exploitation of vulnerability, and most real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces. The 2026 Digital Omnibus added AI-generated child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate imagery.

lenses.body: A broad, flexible AI model trained on a wide variety of information, capable of doing many different kinds of tasks and getting built into lots of other products by other companies. Under Europe's AI law, most of the actual compliance burden for this kind of model sits with the company that built it, not the businesses that later use it, which is a common point of confusion in both directions.

Verify explicitly which specific compliance artifacts, technical documentation, copyright policy, training content summary, your GPAI model provider is actually required to produce and has actually produced, rather than assuming your organization needs to independently generate documentation the provider is legally responsible for.

Understand precisely which specific obligations, if any, fall on your organization as a deployer of a general-purpose AI model versus which obligations rest entirely with the model provider, since misunderstanding this allocation in either direction, over- or under-estimating your own responsibility, is a genuinely common and consequential mistake.

A specific, technically defined regulatory category worth citing precisely, since the allocation of compliance burden between model provider and downstream deploying business is a real, specific, and commonly misunderstood point worth getting right in any coverage of this regulatory category.

Most of the burden sits with the model provider rather than the business deploying it, which is the point deployers most often get wrong in both directions; clarify this allocation of responsibility explicitly and consistently, since deployers routinely either assume they bear obligations that actually rest with the provider, or conversely assume they bear no obligations at all when some genuinely do apply to them.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(63) and Chapter V.
terms.example: A company building on a frontier model inheriting the provider's documentation rather than producing its own.
terms.definition: A model trained on broad data that can perform a wide range of distinct tasks and be built into many downstream systems. The EU AI Act gives GPAI providers their own obligation set, technical documentation, information for downstream providers, a copyright policy, and a public summary of training content, applicable since 2 August 2025. Most of the burden sits with the model provider rather than the business deploying it, which is the point deployers most often get wrong in both directions.

lenses.body: A stricter, heavier set of rules under Europe's AI law that applies specifically to the handful of general-purpose AI models powerful enough to have a truly significant impact at large scale, based on a specific measured amount of computing power used to train them. Only a small number of the most powerful models actually meet this bar, and essentially none of them are trained by the ordinary businesses that just use AI day to day.

Recognize this classification tier as relevant primarily to a small number of frontier training labs rather than to typical enterprise AI deployment, and focus your organization's own compliance effort on the obligation tiers that actually apply to your deployment context instead.

Understand this heavier obligation tier applies to the small number of frontier labs actually training the largest models, not to your organization as a downstream deployer of AI, unless your organization is itself training frontier-scale models, which is genuinely rare.

A specific, objectively defined regulatory threshold worth citing precisely, given its genuinely narrow scope applying to only a small number of the largest frontier models; coverage implying this tier broadly affects ordinary AI-deploying businesses would misrepresent its actual, genuinely narrow scope.

Presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds ten to the twenty-fifth floating-point operations; apply this specific, objective compute threshold consistently when determining classification, and note that essentially no ordinary AI-deploying business will itself be classified under this tier, since it targets only the small number of actual frontier model training labs.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 51.
terms.example: A frontier lab running adversarial evaluations and reporting incidents to the AI Office.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act's heavier tier for general-purpose models capable of significant impact at scale, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds ten to the twenty-fifth floating-point operations. It adds model evaluation, adversarial testing, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity duties on top of the standard GPAI set. Only a small number of models are in scope, and essentially none are trained by the businesses deploying AI.

lenses.body: An informal, industry term for a per-system record covering an AI system's purpose, owner, data, and risk level, sometimes set up to expire and force a fresh check-up. It is not an official government term, just a useful, catchy vendor phrase for something regulators actually call an "AI inventory" or "system register."

Adopt the expiry concept specifically, regardless of what a given vendor calls the overall artifact, since forcing periodic re-validation of a system's risk profile and controls is a genuinely useful practice independent of the particular branded terminology a vendor is using.

Do not let the catchy vendor terminology distract from the substance; whatever it is called, the useful part is the expiry concept, treating authority to operate as time-limited rather than permanent, which forces periodic re-validation instead of a one-time approval that never gets revisited.

Worth clarifying in coverage that this is vendor marketing terminology for an established underlying concept, an AI inventory or system register, rather than a distinct, officially recognized regulatory requirement, to avoid implying a formal obligation that does not actually exist under this specific name.

Not regulatory terminology; the standard equivalents are the AI inventory and the AI system register. Recognize this as vendor terminology describing a concept your framework already names differently, and evaluate the underlying substance, not the marketing label a vendor happens to use for it.

terms.origin: Practitioner and vendor coinage; no standing in the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, or the NIST AI RMF.
terms.example: A system record that lapses annually unless the owner re-validates its risk assessment.
terms.definition: A vendor and practitioner term for a per-system governance record covering purpose, owner, data, risk tier, and review status, sometimes with an expiry that forces re-validation. It is not regulatory terminology; the standard equivalents are the AI inventory and the AI system register. The expiry idea is the useful part, treating authority to operate as time-limited rather than permanent.

lenses.body: A required check that certain organizations using higher-risk AI in Europe must do before deploying it, looking specifically at who could be affected and how, and what protections will be in place. This applies specifically to public bodies, and to private companies doing certain public-facing or financial decision work, and it is genuinely different from some similarly named privacy assessments, even though people often mix the two up.

Track this as a distinct compliance artifact from both the GDPR DPIA and the provider's conformity assessment documentation, since conflating the three, a common and understandable mistake given their genuine overlap in subject matter, leaves a real, specific compliance gap unaddressed.

Determine explicitly whether your organization actually falls under the specific categories, public bodies, public-service providers, or credit/insurance-pricing deployers, that trigger this specific obligation, since it is distinct from and not automatically satisfied by completing a GDPR DPIA or relying on a vendor's own conformity assessment.

A specific, named legal requirement worth citing precisely and distinctly from the similarly named but genuinely different GDPR DPIA and the provider's conformity assessment; conflating the three in coverage, while an understandable and common mistake, produces a materially inaccurate account of the actual legal landscape.

It is a deployer duty, distinct from the provider's conformity assessment and from the GDPR's DPIA, though the three are routinely conflated; maintain and enforce this specific, three-way distinction, since organizations frequently and incorrectly assume completing one of these three related assessments satisfies the others, which it does not.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 27.
terms.example: A bank documenting affected groups and mitigation before switching on an AI credit model.
terms.definition: The pre-deployment assessment the EU AI Act requires from certain deployers of high-risk systems, covering who could be affected, how, and what mitigation and oversight will be in place. It falls on public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers using AI for credit scoring or life and health insurance pricing. It is a deployer duty, distinct from the provider's conformity assessment and from the GDPR's DPIA, though the three are routinely conflated.

lenses.body: A record specifically of who approved which important AI-assisted decision, when, and why, different from a regular computer log because it captures a real human's actual judgment and reasoning, not just what the software did.

Build this as a distinct logging stream from technical system telemetry, capturing specifically the human decision-maker, timestamp, and stated rationale for consequential AI-influenced decisions; a technical audit trail alone does not substitute for this record when accountability is later questioned.

Named humans, timestamps, and rationale, not just code output. Maintain this specifically and separately from technical system logs, since it is the artifact that answers "who decided this" when a regulator, auditor, or claimant eventually asks, and a system log alone cannot answer that question.

Distinct from and complementary to system logs: it captures human judgment and accountability specifically, which is the evidentiary artifact most directly relevant to questions of accountability for a consequential AI-influenced decision, more so than a purely technical trace of system behavior.

terms.origin: Governance practice; underpins the evidence expectations in ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act's oversight duties.
terms.example: An entry showing the risk lead accepted an AI recommendation, with the reasoning and the date.
terms.definition: The record of who approved which AI-influenced decision, when, and on what reasoning. Distinct from system logs: it captures the human judgment rather than the machine trace, and it is the artifact that answers who decided this when a regulator, an auditor, or a claimant asks. Named humans, timestamps, and rationale, not just code output.

lenses.body: An ongoing log of every AI failure, near-miss, and complaint, tracking what caused it, what it affected, and how it was fixed. The near-misses matter just as much as actual failures, since they are basically free warnings about problems before they cause real damage.

Maintain this register as a living operational artifact reviewed regularly, not a compliance checkbox filled retroactively; its real value is pattern detection across near-misses over time, which requires consistent, disciplined logging as incidents occur, not reconstruction after the fact.

Ensure near-misses, not just full failures, are actually captured in your incident register; near-misses are the cheapest, earliest warning your organization gets about a systemic problem, and a register that only logs full failures is discarding most of that early-warning value.

The EU AI Act separately requires providers of high-risk systems to report serious incidents to authorities, and a register is what makes reporting on a deadline possible; require organizations to demonstrate an actively maintained register as part of any compliance review, since it is the operational foundation for meeting incident reporting obligations.

terms.origin: Governance practice; serious-incident reporting duty at Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 73.
terms.example: A near-miss logged when an AI-drafted client email was caught before sending.
terms.definition: The running log of AI failures, near-misses, and complaints, with cause, impact, and remediation. The near-misses are the point: they are the only cheap warning an organization gets. The EU AI Act separately requires providers of high-risk systems to report serious incidents to authorities, and a register is what makes reporting on a deadline possible.

terms.example: An organisation adopting a third-party scheduling agent from a vendor catalogue without a supplier assessment covering what data it may reach.
terms.definition: A venue where agents, tools, or agent capabilities are published, discovered, and consumed by other parties, sometimes with payment and contractual terms attached. Marketplaces move agents squarely into third-party risk: the operator inherits the behaviour of code it did not write, under terms it may not have read, while the assessment categories for this class of supplier are still forming.

terms.example: Dozens of agents independently searching a codebase for a defect, with attention converging on the files several of them flag.
terms.definition: A multi-agent pattern where many simple, largely interchangeable agents work the same problem in parallel with little central control, and the useful result emerges from their interaction rather than from any one agent's plan. It differs from an orchestrated multi-agent system, where a leader assigns roles, and it is harder to govern for the same reason: there is no single place where the decision was made and no single log that explains it.

terms.example: A planning agent delegating a purchase step to a procurement agent that holds the spending limit, rather than passing the limit along with the task.
terms.definition: The transfer of a task, and the authority to act on it, from a person or one agent to another. Delegation differs from a handoff because it carries permission: the receiving agent may spend, call tools, or commit on the delegator's behalf. The governing question is therefore not what was passed but what authority went with it, whether that authority narrows at each hop, and whether it can be revoked while a run is still in flight.

terms.example: An agent asked to prepare a compliance filing, working through evidence collection, gap analysis, and drafting across several days without being re-briefed.
terms.definition: An agent breaking a long-running objective into a sequence of sub-goals, where each completed step sets the context for the next, so work continues across many cycles without a human restating the aim. It is what makes long-horizon autonomy possible, and it is also where drift begins, because an error early in the chain is inherited by every step after it and rarely re-examined.

terms.example: Building a product taxonomy so a retrieval system can answer questions the raw documents never state directly.
terms.definition: The practice of turning what an organisation knows into structures a machine can use: ontologies, taxonomies, rules, and curated knowledge bases. It predates modern AI and has returned to relevance because retrieval systems are only as good as the structure beneath them, and because a knowledge base can be corrected in one place and audited, where a model's learned behaviour cannot.

terms.example: Rejecting a generated database query that does not parse or touches a table outside the agent's scope, before it reaches the database.
terms.definition: Checking a model or agent's output against rules, a schema, or a second system before it is acted on or shown, so that a wrong answer does not become a wrong action. It is a control point rather than an accuracy technique: validation does not make the model better, it makes the failure visible while it can still be caught, which is why it belongs on the path between generation and execution rather than in evaluation.

terms.example: An assistant recalling a user's preferred report format from earlier sessions, held in a profile store that a deletion request must also reach.
terms.definition: Adapting a system's output to an individual using their history, preferences, or context. In AI systems this usually means retrieval over stored user data rather than a separate model for each person, which is why it sits inside privacy scope rather than beside it: the personalization store is a record about the user, subject to retention schedules, access controls, and erasure requests like any other.

terms.example: An agent finding a required document missing and constructing a new route to the same objective instead of failing the run.
terms.definition: An agent revising or discarding its current plan after the world fails to match its expectations, rather than continuing to execute steps that no longer apply. Replanning is much of what separates an agent from a script, and it is also where cost and loop risk enter, because an agent that may replan without limit can pursue a goal indefinitely and bill for every attempt.

terms.origin: Released as an open-source Python library in October 2022 by Harrison Chase; a JavaScript version followed.
terms.example: A support application that uses LangChain to retrieve relevant policy documents, pass them to a model, and call a ticketing tool if the model decides a ticket is needed.
terms.definition: An open-source framework for building applications that call language models, providing prebuilt pieces for chaining model calls, connecting tools, loading documents, and running agents. It is the orchestration layer: it decides what gets called in what order, rather than supplying the model or the data.

terms.origin: Started as GPT Index in late 2022 by Jerry Liu, renamed LlamaIndex in 2023.
terms.example: Indexing a company handbook so an assistant answers policy questions from the handbook text rather than from model memory.
terms.definition: An open-source framework focused on connecting language models to private data: loading documents, splitting and indexing them, retrieving the relevant pieces, and feeding them to a model. It overlaps with LangChain but is generally simpler for retrieval-heavy applications and broader for document ingestion.

terms.origin: Released by Microsoft in March 2023 with C# and .NET as the primary path; Python and Java followed. Entered maintenance mode in April 2026 when Microsoft shipped Agent Framework 1.0 as its successor.
terms.example: A .NET line-of-business application registering its existing invoice-lookup service as a plugin so a model can call it during a conversation.
terms.definition: Microsoft's open-source orchestration SDK for adding language models to conventional applications through plugins, connectors, memory, and agents. Its distinguishing feature is first-class .NET and Java support, which most competing frameworks lack.

terms.origin: Announced in public preview October 2025, reached Release Candidate February 2026, and shipped version 1.0 on 3 April 2026.
terms.example: Composing a copywriter agent and a reviewer agent into a sequential workflow where each hands its output to the next.
terms.definition: Microsoft's unified agent SDK, built by the same teams as Semantic Kernel and AutoGen and positioned as the successor to both. It combines AutoGen's agent abstractions with Semantic Kernel's enterprise features and adds graph-based workflows for multi-agent orchestration, with native Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent support.

terms.origin: Grew out of the Demonstrate-Search-Predict work at Stanford NLP (research beginning 2022); the DSPy paper was published in October 2023. Name is a backronym for Declarative Self-improving Python.
terms.example: Compiling a classification pipeline against fifty labelled examples so the optimizer finds the instructions and demonstrations that score highest, instead of hand-editing a prompt.
terms.definition: A framework that treats prompting as an optimization problem rather than a writing task. You declare inputs and outputs as a signature, compose modules, supply a metric and example data, and an optimizer compiles the best-scoring prompts and few-shot examples. Changing models means recompiling rather than rewriting.

terms.origin: Representational State Transfer was defined in Roy Fielding's 2000 doctoral dissertation.
terms.example: Posting a JSON body containing a prompt to a provider's completions endpoint and reading the generated text from the JSON response.
terms.definition: An interface style where a client calls a service over HTTP using standard methods against addressable resources, usually exchanging JSON. It is the default way applications talk to AI model providers: nearly every hosted model is reached through a REST endpoint.

terms.origin: Released by Google as open source in 2015, built on HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
terms.example: A model-serving runtime exposing a gRPC endpoint that an internal service calls for low-latency inference, while the public-facing API stays REST.
terms.definition: A remote procedure call framework that uses a binary serialization format and a defined service contract instead of JSON over HTTP verbs. In AI systems it is common between internal services and for model-serving runtimes, where its lower overhead and native streaming matter more than the human readability REST offers.

terms.example: Choosing direct REST calls for a single-purpose feature, and an orchestration framework only once several models, tools, and retrieval steps must be coordinated.
terms.definition: The recurring ways applications connect to models: calling a provider REST API directly, going through an orchestration framework such as LangChain or Semantic Kernel, exposing capabilities to the model as callable tools via function calling, standardising those tools behind the Model Context Protocol, or serving models internally over gRPC. The choice sets what has to be audited, since each pattern puts the boundary between application logic and model decision in a different place.

terms.origin: Formed in 2019 from the merger of the OpenTracing and OpenCensus projects; a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
terms.example: An agent emitting OTel spans for each model call and tool invocation, routed to a self-hosted collector today and a hosted platform tomorrow with no code change.
terms.definition: The vendor-neutral standard for emitting traces, metrics, and logs from software. AI observability tools have converged on it, which means an application instrumented once can send its telemetry to any compatible backend. Instrumenting with OpenTelemetry rather than a vendor SDK is what makes switching observability vendors a configuration change instead of a re-instrumentation project.

terms.example: A single agent run producing one parent span and forty child spans covering model calls, retrievals, and tool executions.
terms.definition: One timed unit of work inside a trace: a single model call, a retrieval step, a tool invocation. Spans nest, so a parent span for an agent run contains child spans for each step it took. Span count is what most observability vendors bill on, and a long agent run can emit thousands, which is why span-based pricing behaves very differently for agents than for chatbots.

terms.example: Opening one trace to find that an agent called the search tool three times, got empty results twice, and answered from its own assumption.
terms.definition: Following one request across every service and step it touches, assembled into a single timeline. For multi-step AI applications this is the difference between knowing an answer was wrong and knowing which retrieval returned the wrong document, which tool failed, and how long each step took. Logs tell you a run finished; a trace tells you what it did.

terms.origin: Developed by Arize AI as a set of OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for LLM applications.
terms.example: Instrumenting a RAG pipeline with OpenInference so any compatible platform can show the retrieved documents as retrieval spans rather than opaque function calls.
terms.definition: A convention layer on top of OpenTelemetry that defines how to describe AI-specific work in a span: what counts as a prompt, a completion, a retrieval, a tool call, token counts. OpenTelemetry says how to emit a span; OpenInference says what the fields inside an LLM span should mean, so different tools read the same trace the same way.

terms.example: Average prompt length creeping up over a month as a retrieval step returns steadily longer chunks, doubling per-request cost with no code change.
terms.definition: A gradual change over time in how many tokens a workload consumes per request, without an intended change to the application. Causes include growing context or history, prompt edits that add examples, retrieval returning longer passages, or a provider changing default behaviour. It matters because cost scales with tokens, so drift shows up as a rising bill before it shows up as a bug.

terms.example: Routing all model traffic through a gateway so cost limits and provider failover are enforced centrally rather than reimplemented in every service.
terms.definition: A service that sits between an application and model providers, handling routing, failover, caching, rate limiting, key management, and usage logging in one place. The trade is architectural: a gateway gives central control and near-zero integration effort, but it sits in the request path, so its availability becomes your availability. SDK-based observability logs alongside your code instead, failing to telemetry loss rather than request failure.

terms.origin: Popularised as a named metric by the Ragas framework (Es et al., 2024); TruLens calls the equivalent measure groundedness.
terms.example: An answer making four claims where three trace to the retrieved documents and one does not scores 0.75.
terms.definition: Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the retrieved context, scored by breaking the answer into individual claims and checking each one against the source. Usually reported 0 to 1 as the fraction of supported claims. It is the direct hallucination measure for a RAG system, and it is reference-free: no human-written gold answer is needed, so it can run on live production traffic.

terms.origin: One of the core Ragas metrics; TruLens carries an equivalent feedback function.
terms.example: Asking for a filing deadline and receiving an accurate but rambling summary of the whole statute: high faithfulness, low answer relevance.
terms.definition: Whether the answer actually addresses the question asked, independent of whether it is true. A response can be perfectly faithful to its sources and still evade the question, or bury the answer in unrequested detail. Typically scored by generating candidate questions from the answer and measuring how closely they match the original.

terms.origin: A core Ragas retrieval metric.
terms.example: Retrieving ten chunks of which three bear on the question, with the best one ranked eighth, scores poorly on precision even if the final answer happens to be right.
terms.definition: What proportion of the retrieved chunks are actually relevant to the question, and whether the relevant ones ranked highly. It measures the retriever, not the model. Low precision means the generator is working through noise, which both raises cost and increases the chance it latches onto an irrelevant passage.

terms.origin: A core Ragas retrieval metric.
terms.example: A legal answer scoring high on faithfulness while context recall sits at 0.62 because the retriever consistently missed the second governing statute.
terms.definition: Whether retrieval fetched everything needed to answer the question. Unlike faithfulness and answer relevance it generally requires ground truth, since something must define what should have been retrieved. It catches the failure the other metrics miss: a confident, well-grounded answer built on half the evidence.

terms.origin: Named by TruLens as a three-part evaluation pattern.
terms.example: Context relevance falling while groundedness holds steady points at the retriever, not the prompt.
terms.definition: Evaluating a retrieval system along three axes at once: is the retrieved context relevant to the question, is the answer grounded in that context, and does the answer address the question. Scoring all three localises a failure to retrieval or generation instead of only recording that output quality dropped.

terms.example: Running faithfulness and answer relevance on production traffic nightly, while a smaller labelled golden set carries the reference-based metrics.
terms.definition: Scoring an output without a human-written correct answer to compare against, using the question and retrieved context as the standard instead. It is what makes evaluation affordable at scale and possible on live traffic, since writing gold answers for thousands of queries is not. The trade is that it measures internal consistency, not truth: a system can score well while the underlying knowledge base is stale or wrong.

terms.example: A pytest suite failing the build if any response omits its citation field, before faithfulness is scored at all.
terms.definition: Checks with one correct answer that do not involve a model judging anything: valid JSON, required field present, cited source appears in the retrieved set, no PII in output, latency under a threshold, refusal on a prohibited prompt. They are cheap, instant, and repeatable, and they belong in CI as hard gates before any model-graded metric runs. Model-graded scores tell you how good an answer is; assertions tell you whether it is even shaped correctly.
